title: Pressure
body: What is Pressure? Pressure can be simply defined as the amount of force per unit area. Mathematically, it can be expressed through two main formulas. Pressure outside of fluids (generally) Pressure in fluids P = F / A, where P stands for pressure, F stands for force and A stands for area. Units: Pa = N/m2. Used mainly when given an applied force. P = h x density x g, where P stands for pressure, h stands for height above the point, density stands for density of the fluid, and g stands for gravitational field strength. Units: Pa = m x kg/m3 x N/kg. Used mainly when no force is given, or when dealing with liquids. Units of Pressure Unit Conversion to other units cmHg / mmHg Pa = N/m2. To convert cmHg to Pa: convert the cm value to m, then multiply by the density of mercury and g (using the formula h x density x g, where h is the height in metres). Pressure: Scalar or Vector? Example: A chair has a mass of 30 kg and rests on a surface on its 4 legs. Each leg has an area of 0.0020 m2 in contact with the ground. What is the pressure exerted by each of the legs, and by all 4 legs combined? Pressure exerted by each leg Pressure exerted by all 4 legs combined Total force (30kg x 10N/kg)/4 = 75N (dividing the chair into 4 parts) 30kg x 10N/kg = 300N Total area 0.0020 m2 0.0020 m2 x 4 = 0.0080 m2 Total pressure 75N/0.0020m2 = 37500 Pa 300N/0.0080m2 = 37500 Pa From this example, it is evident that pressure is a scalar. This is due to: Pressure does not have a direction. Scalars are not added up (scalar rule). Scalar rule: For example, temperature is scalar too, and if 1 thermometer reads the room temperature as 25 degrees C and 2 other thermometers likewise read the temperature as 25 degrees C, the temperature of the room is not 75 degrees C. Similarly, if the pressure exerted by each leg is 37,500 Pa, the total pressure exerted by all legs is not 37,500 Pa x 4. As such, since this scalar rule applies to pressure, pressure is a scalar too. Force vs Area Pressure does not solely depend on how big the force is. If you have a 1.0 N force acting on 1.0 m2 of a surface, the pressure will be 1.0 Pa. If you have a 1.0 N force acting on 0.001 m2 of a surface, the pressure will be 1000 Pa. Common thinking: the greater the force, the greater the pressure. Alternative that must also be considered: the smaller the area, the greater the pressure. Pressure is in relation to area — if there is a great force but spread out over a large area, the pressure will be low, and vice versa.

title: Light: Reflection
body: How Do We See? You can see an object only when light rays are reflected off the object and the reflected light rays can reach your eyes. From this, it is clear that in order for something to be visible to the human eye, two conditions must be fulfilled: Light rays are reflected off the object. Reflected light rays can reach your eyes. Laws of Reflection 1st Law of Reflection The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. 2nd Law of Reflection The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. Characteristics of Reflection Images The image of an object formed by a plane mirror will always be: The same size as the object. The same perpendicular distance from the mirror as the object. Upright and laterally inverted. A virtual image (cannot be formed on a screen). Drawing Ray Diagrams Step Description 1 Locate the image of the eye or object. 2 Join the image of the eye to the object with straight and broken lines, OR join the image of the object to the eye with straight and broken lines. 3 Join the eye/object to the points of incidence with straight and broken lines. 4 Check the diagram for any errors and include all necessary arrows. Things to look out for: All construction lines (imaginary lines that are not real light rays) must be shown and must be drawn as dotted or broken lines. All virtual elements (virtual images, virtual rays, construction lines) should be shown and must be drawn as dotted or broken lines. All lines must be drawn with a ruler. All lines representing light rays must have arrows pointing in the right direction (ensure that light rays are not shown shooting out from the eye). Extend the line representing the mirror (with a broken line), if necessary. What two conditions must be met for us to see an object? Light rays must be reflected off the object, and the reflected light rays must reach your eyes. State the 1st Law of Reflection. The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. State the 2nd Law of Reflection. The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. What size is the image formed by a plane mirror compared to the object? The same size as the object. How does the perpendicular distance of the image compare to the object's distance from the mirror? The image is the same perpendicular distance from the mirror as the object. Describe the orientation of an image formed by a plane mirror. It is upright

title: Light: Refraction
body: What is Refraction? Refraction is fundamentally the bending of light rays when it passes from one medium to another. However, for refraction to occur, two conditions must be met. Condition 1 Condition 2 When a light ray enters a different medium, its speed will change. Light travels slower in an optically denser medium and faster in an optically less dense medium. Essentially, light must slow down or speed up in order to bend. When a light ray enters a medium at an angle, it will bend. For refraction to occur, light must enter at an angle — e.g. if it enters perpendicular to the surface, the angle of incidence would be 0 and refraction will not occur. Similarly, if it enters at an angle larger than the critical angle, total internal reflection will occur and refraction will not occur. How Does Light Bend? If light travels from an optically less dense to an optically denser medium, light bends towards the normal. If light travels from an optically denser to an optically less dense medium, light bends away from the normal. Note: it is very important to draw the normal. Refractive Index Refractive index is the measure of how much refraction will take place (essentially, how much a light ray will bend). Different mediums have different refractive indexes, which then determine if a medium is optically denser or optically less dense. Air/Vacuum → 1.00 Water → 1.33 Glass → 1.48 to 1.96 (depending on the type of glass) Diamond → 2.40 The symbol for refractive index is n. There are multiple formulas to calculate refractive index, and multiple formulas involving refractive index to find other quantities, including Snell's Law and the definition of refractive index. Other notes: Optical density is not the same as mass density — do not confuse the two. There is one more formula that can be used but is not advised, as it does not apply in all circumstances: n = sin i / sin r. Critical Angle The critical angle, represented by the symbol c, is the value of the angle of incidence in an optically denser medium at which the angle of refraction in the optically less dense medium is 90 degrees. For refraction to still occur as a light ray travels from an optically denser medium to an optically less dense medium (only rays which pass through such conditions will have a critical angle), there is a limit to the value of the angle of incidence, known as the critical angle. title: Electromagnetic Waves
body: Properties of Electromagnetic Waves They are all transverse waves. They can all travel through a vacuum. They all travel at a speed of 3 x 10^8 ms-1 in a vacuum. Applications of Electromagnetic Waves Type Uses and Details Radio Waves AM Radio (longer wavelength, lower frequency — 10 m to 2 km); FM Radio (shorter wavelength, higher frequency — 10 cm to 10 m); Submarine communications (longer wavelength — 10 m to 2 km); Over-the-air television (shorter wavelength, higher frequency — 10 cm to 10 m). Radio waves with longer wavelengths can travel around obstructions (e.g. buildings and hills) better than those with shorter wavelengths. For good and uninterrupted reception, radio waves of shorter wavelengths need an unobstructed straight path between the transmitter and receiver. Microwaves Microwave ovens: microwaves penetrate food and cause the water molecules within to vibrate vigorously (millions of oscillations per second), generating heat that spreads throughout the food. Satellite television: microwaves are used for communicating with satellites because they can penetrate the atmosphere and travel through haze, light rain, snow, clouds and smoke; satellite dishes must be positioned in the line of sight, without obstruction between transmitting and receiving satellites. Microwaves also carry signals in mobile phone networks, Global Positioning System (GPS), and mobile phone communications (sending/receiving data like messages and videos). Infrared Radiation Remote controllers. A human body, like any other object, gives out infrared radiation energy which varies with body temperature; ear thermometers work on this principle by measuring infrared radiation emitted from the eardrum to determine body temperature. Intruder alarms are Passive Infrared Detectors (PID) — they do not emit infrared radiation but detect changes in the level of infrared radiation energy in the environment; when an intruder enters a room, the increase in infrared radiation level is detected. Visible Light Optical fibres for medical use and telecommunications. Visible light allows us to see and hence enjoy activities such as watching movies, surfing the internet and reading books. Ultraviolet Radiation Sunbeds are used in artificial tanning, popular in countries with long periods of limited sunlight; however, excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation may lead to premature aging and even skin cancer. Also used for sterilisation of equipment and medical instruments, and detecting fake

title: General Wave Properties
body: What is a Wave? A wave motion is a means of transferring energy from point A to point B without a net transfer of the medium/matter from point A to point B. A wave is made up of periodic motion, whereby an object moves from the extreme highest/most left point to the lowest/most right point, and when it completes such a motion it is known as a period. Hence, the source of any wave is a vibration or oscillation. Motions in a Wave Note that the motion of a wave and the motion of a point on a wave are not equal (they are different things). Examples of wave motions include: waves created by a rope moved up and down; waves created by a spring moved up and down; waves created by a spring moved left and right (forward and back); and waves created on a calm surface (ripples). Types of Waves Transverse Waves Longitudinal Waves Points oscillate perpendicular to the direction of the wave motion. Does NOT consist of compressions and rarefactions. Examples: wave on a rope, water waves, electromagnetic waves. Points oscillate parallel to the direction of the wave motion. DOES consist of compressions and rarefactions. Examples: sound waves, seismic P-waves. Waves in Graphs, Important Terms and Equations Term Definition Wavefront An imaginary line on a wave joining adjacent points on the wave that are in phase. Oscillating in phase (only for transverse waves) Points are always on the same level regardless of the motion of the wave. Oscillating out of phase (only for transverse waves) Points are not always on the same level regardless of the motion of the wave. Displacement-Distance Graph: equivalent to a photograph of a rope at an instant; describes the displacements of all particles at a particular point in time (shows the displacement of every point at one instance in time — a snapshot view). Displacement-Time Graph: describes the displacements of one particle over a time interval (shows how the displacement of one point changes with time — a historical view). Take note: the type of wave does not correspond to the type of graph! The type of wave only indicates the type of displacement, either horizontal or vertical, affecting the values of displacement, not time or distance. Factors Affecting Velocity, Frequency and Wavelength Factor Details Velocity Affected by the medium through which the wave is propagated. Light waves: affected by optical density — higher optical density means the speed of the wave decreases. Sound waves: affected by density of the medium — higher de

title: Sound
body: Production of Sound Key Idea 1: Sound waves (like all waves) are always produced by vibrations from a source. Transmission of Sound Key Idea 2: Sound waves always require a medium to be transmitted, so sound cannot be transmitted through a vacuum. Key Idea 3 (derived from the two ideas above): Sound is transmitted as the vibrations from the source are passed on from molecule to molecule, in a series of compressions and rarefactions. Key Idea 4 (derived from key idea 3): Due to the difference in the spacing of atoms/molecules in a medium, the speed of sound (the rate of transmission of vibrations from molecule to molecule) varies in different mediums. Medium Air Water Iron Approximate speed of sound (ms-1) 300 1500 5000 This is because molecules are spaced further apart in liquids than in solids, so vibrations are less easily passed on from molecule to molecule in liquids than in solids, resulting in a slower speed of sound in liquids than in solids. Graphs of Sound Waves and Longitudinal Waves Sound waves are longitudinal waves. Longitudinal waves (like a spring) consist of compressions and rarefactions; points oscillate parallel to the direction of the wave motion, so displacement is graphed vertically. Since sound waves consist of a series of compressions and rarefactions, identifying compressions and rarefactions is important. Centres of compression and rarefaction are points with zero displacement (NOT crests or troughs, i.e. not the highest or lowest points). For all other points, they are either displaced to the left (negative displacement) or to the right (positive displacement). Looking at the graph, the displacements around a point will indicate whether it is a centre of compression or rarefaction. Pressure-distance graphs can also be used to represent sound waves. Echo Echo is a reflected sound that is distinguishable from the original sound. Echoes can only be heard if the reflected sound is distinguishable from the original sound; otherwise, echo cannot be heard. Example: a boy clapping at certain intervals while standing 125 m from a high wall does not hear any echo, because the interval between claps and the time taken for the echo to travel to the wall and back are equal — hence the reflected sound is not distinguishable and cannot be heard. title: Static Electricity
body: Opening question: What is the difference between current electricity and static electricity? For current electricity, we are focused on the study of charges in motion, whereas for static electricity we are focused on the study of charges on a body. \"Current\" suggests moving/movement while \"static\" suggests stationary. Electric Charges To understand electric charges, we must first know that matter is made of atoms, and each atom consists of a nucleus carrying neutrons and protons, with electrons outside of the nucleus. Big ideas: All matter carries charge through electrons and protons, though they may not necessarily be charged at all times. Electrons carry negative charges while protons carry positive charges. When an atom has an equal number of electrons and protons, it has no net charge, meaning it is electrically balanced and in the neutral state. When an atom (and therefore matter) has an unequal number of electrons and protons, it becomes electrically charged. An unequal number of electrons and protons occurs when electrons are removed or added to the atom. Only electrons can be removed or added, not protons — it is not possible for protons to leave the nuclei, or even the body. If electrons are removed, the number of protons is now greater than the number of electrons, and since protons carry positive charges, the atom becomes positively charged and has a net positive charge. If electrons are added, the number of electrons is now greater than the number of protons, and since electrons carry negative charges, the atom becomes negatively charged and has a net negative charge. The SI unit of electrical charge is the coulomb (C). Electrons are said to carry -1.6 x 10^-19 C while protons are said to carry +1.6 x 10^-19 C. Representing a Charged Body in Diagrams To represent a charged body in diagrams, only show excess charges, not all charges. Like charges repel, and charges also tend to move towards the surface of the body. Hence, excess charges should not be drawn closely packed/concentrated in the centre, but instead should be drawn spaced out, well distributed, and near the surface of the body. Attraction and Repulsion Note: this refers to electrostatic attraction and repulsion, NOT magnetic attraction and repulsion. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract. Repulsion Attraction Takes place when two bodies have like net charge. E.g. two positively charged bodies will repel. Takes place when two bodies have unlike net charge, OR when one body has

title: Current Electricity
body: Electric Current Big ideas: Current occurs only with the movement of electric charges. This is NOT the definition of current — current is NOT the movement of electric charges itself. Instead, electric current is the rate of flow of electric charges. Current is a physical quantity (is measurable) and is given by the equation I = Q / t, where I represents current (in Amperes, A), Q represents charge (in coulombs, C), and t represents time (in seconds, s). 1 Ampere (A) = 1 Coulomb (C) / 1 Second (s). The definition of electric current is the rate of flow of electric charges, where \"rate\" refers to \"per second\" and \"electric charges\" are measured in coulombs (the SI unit for charge, C). The SI unit for electric current is the Ampere, given the symbol A (note: the symbol for the unit is A for Ampere, but the symbol for the physical quantity is I, for current). Hence, electric current can also be defined as: 1 Ampere = 1 Coulomb per second, i.e. A = C/s. Current is measured using an ammeter (by placing an ammeter in series in the circuit). Conventional Current and Electron Flow Previously, we learnt that current occurs only with the movement of electric charges. Most of the time, these electric charges responsible for the movement are: Positive and negative ions (positive and negative charges in conducting fluids like liquids and gases, e.g. water). Free electrons (negative charges in metal conductors). Conventional Current Electron Flow Flows from left to right (positive terminal to negative terminal). When we refer to current, I, with no specific mention of electron flow, it is assumed that the term \"current\" and the symbol \"I\" refer to conventional current, NOT electron flow. Flows from right to left (negative terminal to positive terminal). Conventional current and electron flow flow in the opposite direction to each other. If conventional current is flowing to the right, then electron flow is flowing to the left, and vice versa. Note: scientifically, electron flow is more accurate, as the positive terminal actually lacks electrons (causing it to have more protons than electrons, giving it a net positive charge), and the negative terminal has excess electrons (causing it to have more electrons than protons, giving it a net negative charge). However, since the idea of conventional current was established earlier, it is taken as the convention and what is commonly followed. Conventional current can simply be taken as the flow of positive charges. E.g

title: Electromotive Force (EMF)
body: Electromotive Force (EMF) Big Ideas In an electric circuit, there are electric forces of attraction and repulsion, but electromotive force (EMF) does not measure this force. EMF is not the value or amount of the force of attraction and repulsion in the circuit. It is not energy, otherwise it would be measured in joules (J), which it is not. It is not force, otherwise it would be measured in newtons (N), which it is not. It is energy per unit charge , measured in volts (V). Instead, the electromotive force (of a source/cell/battery etc.) is the work done (by the source/cell/battery etc.) in driving unit charge (1 coulomb) around a complete circuit. The energy for getting this work done comes from energy conversion that takes place within the source/cell/battery etc. Hence, EMF can also be defined as: The amount of other forms of energy that is converted to electrical energy whenever unit charge (1 coulomb) is driven around a complete circuit, OR The energy required to drive unit charge (1 coulomb) around a complete circuit. Equation Electromotive force is given by the equation: ε = W / Q Where ε represents electromotive force (in volts, V), W represents work done/energy (in joules, J), and Q represents charge (in coulombs, C). 1 Volt (V) = 1 Joule (J) / 1 Coulomb (C) The SI unit for electromotive force is volts, given the symbol (V). Notes The symbol for the unit is V, for volts, but the symbol for the physical quantity is ε, for electromotive force. Electromotive force is often also abbreviated as e.m.f, though ε is still the official symbol for electromotive force. Total e.m.f of cells/batteries in series (this concept is referenced as a topic point in the notes). What is the definition of electromotive force (EMF)? The work done by a source (cell/battery) in driving unit charge (1 coulomb) around a complete circuit. Is EMF a force measured in newtons? No. Despite its name, EMF is not a force and is not measured in newtons. Is EMF a form of energy measured in joules? No. EMF is not energy itself, so it is not measured in joules. What is EMF actually measured in terms of quantity type? Energy per unit charge. What is the SI unit of EMF? Volts (V). What is the equation for EMF? ε = W / Q, where ε is EMF, W is work done/energy, and Q is charge. What does 1 volt equal in terms of joules and coulombs? 1 Volt = 1 Joule / 1 Coulomb. title: Potential Difference (P.D.)
body: Potential Difference (P.D.) Big Ideas Simply put, potential difference is the difference in potential between two points, whereby the "potential" refers to "electric potential". At this level, it suffices to know that electric potential is a quantity associated with charge. In a circuit, electrons flow due to potential difference, eventually achieving equilibrium, where all points have the same potential. Potential difference across a component/load is defined as the work done in driving unit charge through the load/component. Similar to electromotive force, the energy for getting this work done comes from energy conversion that takes place in the load/component. Hence, potential difference can also be defined as: the amount of electrical energy converted into other forms of energy in the load/component, when unit charge (1 coulomb) is driven through the load/component. Equation Potential difference is given by the equation: V = W / Q Where V represents potential difference (in volts, V), W represents work done/energy (in joules, J), and Q represents charge (in coulombs, C). 1 Volt (V) = 1 Joule (J) / 1 Coulomb (C) The SI unit for potential difference is volts, given the symbol (V). Notes The symbol for the unit is V, for volts, but the symbol for the physical quantity is also V, for potential difference. Potential difference is often also abbreviated as p.d, though V is still the official symbol for potential difference. Differences between EMF and P.D. Electromotive Force/e.m.f (ε) Potential difference/p.d (V) Strictly for electric power sources/cells/batteries etc. Strictly for potential between any two points Amount of other forms of energy converted into electrical energy to drive unit charge around a circuit. Amount of electrical energy converted into other forms of energy to drive unit charge between the two points. Similarities Both have the same units and are both measured in volts (V) by a voltmeter. e.m.f and p.d. are measured by placing a voltmeter in parallel with the component. Both measure energy converted per unit charge. Both have the same equation (= W/Q). Total p.d of components in series: the sum of all the p.d in series is the e.m.f. Total p.d of components in a parallel circuit: the p.d across separate parallel branches is the same and is equal to the e.m.f. What is potential difference (p.d.)? title: Resistance
body: Resistance Resistance, R, of a component is defined as the ratio of the potential difference, V, across the load to the current, I, flowing through it. It is given by the equation: R = V / I Where R represents resistance (in ohms, Ω), V represents potential difference (in volts, V), and I represents current (in Amperes, A). 1 Ohm (Ω) = 1 Volt (V) / 1 Ampere (A) The SI unit for resistance is ohms, given the symbol (Ω). Note The symbol for the unit is Ω, for ohms, but the symbol for the physical quantity is R, for resistance. Resistance is measured by using a rheostat (otherwise known as a variable resistor), with a voltmeter and ammeter. A V/I graph is then generated to calculate the resistance of the unknown resistor. title: Ohm's Law
body: Ohm's Law Ohm's Law states that the current, I, flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference, V, across the same conductor, provided physical conditions (such as temperature) remain constant. In other words, it can be given in the equation: If temperature is kept constant: I ∝ V , so V = kI (V constant → V/I constant → R constant if temperature remains constant). Conductors which obey Ohm's Law are known as Ohmic conductors. However, at higher temperatures, Ohmic conductors tend to begin to not obey Ohm's Law. The reasoning for this is the same reasoning for why other conductors do not obey Ohm's Law: Temperature increases (current tends to increase temperature) → vibrations of the atoms in the conductor become more vigorous → increased obstruction to flow of electrons in the conductor → resistance of conductor increases. Analogy: Imagine a situation where you are trying to run through a crowd of people. If the crowd of people are moving orderly in their own positions, it is easy for you to run through. However, if the crowd of people are moving more vigorously and are rapidly moving around, it is difficult for you to run through. V/I Characteristics We know that the formula for resistance is R = V/I, which means that a V/I graph would be able to help us obtain the resistance of a component. Evidently, the gradient of a V/I graph cannot simply be taken to be the resistance of the component. Resistance is NOT EQUAL to the gradient of the V/I graph! Although resistance is not equal to the gradient of the V/I graph, the gradient of the graph does affect resistance. It is like how the increase in temperature in a thermometer is not equal to the temperature of the atmosphere, but an increase in the temperature affects the temperature of the atmosphere. From this, we can see that as the gradient increases, the ratio of V/I increases, and since R = V/I, R increases. (Note: it is important to include the link that the "ratio of V/I increases", as otherwise it would imply that gradient = resistance, which is not the case. With the link, it implies accurately that gradient = V/I = resistance.) title: Resistivity
body: Resistivity There are a few properties of a conductor that affect its resistance. Going back to the analogy of the wire being a pipe, logically, the cross-sectional area of the pipe will affect the rate of the flow of water. If the pipe is thin, it is difficult for a large volume of water to pass through it quickly, but if the pipe is wide, then it is easier for a large volume of water to pass through it quickly. Similarly, if the cross-sectional area affected by the radius/diameter of the wire is smaller, the resistance of the wire will be higher. Hence: R ∝ 1/A — Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area of the wire. The length of the wire also matters: R ∝ l — Resistance is directly proportional to length of the wire. Combining both equations: R ∝ l/A — Resistance is directly proportional to length of the wire divided by the cross-sectional area of the wire. In order to remove the proportional sign and make it an equal sign, we have to introduce resistivity: R = ρl/A Resistance is equal to the resistivity of the material of the wire multiplied by the length of the wire divided by the cross-sectional area of the wire. Note: The cross-sectional area always refers to the cross-sectional area of the surface that the current is first flowing through. The symbol for resistivity is ρ, which happens to be the same symbol used for density, but in this context we are referring to resistivity. This occurs multiple times in the topic of Current Electricity, so it is important to be careful. Symbol Alternative quantity What we are referring to in this topic Q Heat (Q = mcΔΘ) — incorrect here Charge — correct here ρ Density (hρg) — incorrect here Resistivity — correct here The same materials will have the same resistivity. How does cross-sectional area (A) of a wire affect resistance? Resistance is inversely proportional to cross-sectional area: R ∝ 1/A. How does length (l) of a wire affect resistance? Resistance is directly proportional to length: R ∝ l. Combine the effects of length and cross-sectional area on resistance. R ∝ l/A. What is the full equation for resistance including resistivity? R = ρl/A, where ρ is resistivity. What is the symbol for resistivity? ρ (rho). What other quantity uses the same symbol ρ, and how is it different here? Density uses ρ too, but in resistivity contexts ρ refers to resistivity, not density. What analogy is used to explain cross-sectional area's effect on resistance? title: D.C. Circuits: Series and Parallel Circuits
body: D.C. Circuits Circuit Symbols (Standard circuit symbols are used to represent components in circuit diagrams.) Series Circuits and Parallel Circuits Note: Do not assume simply because a diagram looks like a series or parallel circuit that it actually is one — it is only a series circuit or a parallel circuit if the defining conditions are met. Current and Potential Difference In a series circuit, the same current flows through all components, but the potential difference may be shared unevenly between components (V1 and V2 may not be equal). Since components are in series and the same current flows through both, the dependent factor is the resistance of the resistors. Example (Series): V = IR; V1 = I × 6Ω; V2 = I × 9Ω; V1 + V2 = VT 6I + 9I = 20V 15I = 20V I = 20/15 A V1 = 6I = 6 × (20/15) = 8V V2 = 9I = 9 × (20/15) = 12V In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across both resistors (branches) is the same — the only thing that affects the current flowing through each resistor is the resistance of the resistor, supposing the resistance of the resistor is fixed. Note that R1 and R2 not being equal only affects the current, not the p.d. Example (Parallel): V = IR; V1 = I1 × 10Ω; V2 = I2 × 20Ω I1 × 10Ω = I2 × 20Ω 10ΩI1 = 20ΩI2 I1 = 2I2 …(1) I1 + I2 = 5 …(2) Substituting (1) into (2): 2I2 + I2 = 5, so I2 = 1.67 A, and I1 = 2I2 = 3.33 A As we can see, I1 is larger than I2 as it has a smaller resistance. Imagine it to be like an immigration checkpoint: more people (larger current) would go towards the immigration checkpoint that is faster (smaller resistance). Bulbs in the Circuits In series: When one of the bulbs blows, the other bulb does not work either, as current cannot flow due to the fact that the circuit is open with the blown bulb. In parallel: When one of the bulbs blows, the other bulb remains lit, as current is still able to flow through the other wire and the circuit is still closed. This is why parallel circuits are used in most homes. Resistors in the Circuits When resistors are connected in series, the total resistance will be bigger than the individual resistors. Think of it as adding more obstructions to the flow of current, hence the resistance will be bigger. When resistors are connected in parallel, the total resistance will be smaller than the resistance of even the smallest resistor. title: Potential Dividers
body: Potential Dividers A potential divider is a number of resistors connected in series. It is used to tap a fraction of the voltage of a source to be used for a load or for another circuit. To determine the portion of the voltage that is tapped, otherwise known as V2, a formula can be used. Since the resistors are in series, the same current flows through the circuit, hence: V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2, and V1 + V2 = VE → VE = IR1 + IR2 → VE = I(R1 + R2) → I = VE / (R1 + R2) → V2 = [VE / (R1 + R2)] × R2 → V2 = [R2 / (R1 + R2)] × VE From this formula, the factors that will increase V2 can be defined as these two factors: Reducing R1 while keeping R2 constant. By reducing R1, the value of [R2 / (R1 + R2)] is increased as the denominator is made smaller, meaning a larger fraction, and hence a larger V2. When R1 is reduced, and the same current flows through, V1 will decrease. Since V1 + V2 = VE, if V1 is smaller, V2 will increase. Increasing R2 while keeping R1 constant. By increasing R2, the numerator is made larger, meaning a larger fraction, and hence a larger V2. When R2 is increased, and the same current flows through, V2 will increase. To vary these values of R1 and R2, we either use a variable resistor or a potentiometer with a jockey. Variable Resistor: R1 set to minimum, V2 maximum, and vice versa. Variable potential dividers are often used in dimmer switches. Potentiometer: RAB set to maximum, V2 maximum, and vice versa. What is a potential divider? A number of resistors connected in series, used to tap a fraction of the voltage of a source for a load or another circuit. What is the formula for V2 (the tapped voltage) in a potential divider with R1 and R2 in series? V2 = [R2 / (R1 + R2)] × VE. How can V2 be increased by adjusting R1? By reducing R1 while keeping R2 constant, which increases the fraction R2/(R1+R2), increasing V2. How can V2 be increased by adjusting R2? By increasing R2 while keeping R1 constant, which increases the fraction R2/(R1+R2), increasing V2. What two devices can be used to vary R1 and R2 in a potential divider? In a potentiometer setup, what happens to V2 when RAB is set to maximum? V2 is maximum (and vice versa). Where are variable potential dividers commonly used? In dimmer switches. title: Input Transducers
body: Input Transducers Input transducers are devices that convert non-electrical signals to electrical signals, and vice versa. There are input transducers that convert non-electrical signals to electrical signals, as well as output transducers that convert electrical signals to non-electrical signals. Two examples of input transducers: Thermistors Light-dependent Resistors (LDRs) Summary Light-dependent Resistor (LDR) Thermistor As it gets dimmer (light intensity decreases), R(LDR) increases and V(AB) increases. This can be used for a lighting device that automatically turns on when it gets dark. As it gets bright (light intensity increases), R(LDR) decreases and V(AB) decreases, and thus R increases, and V(BC) increases. This can be used for a burglar alarm that is triggered by an increase in light intensity as the burglar shines a bright torch. As it gets cooler (temperature decreases), R(TH) decreases and V(AB) decreases, and thus R increases and V(BC) increases. This can be used for a heating device that produces heat when it gets cold. As it gets warmer (temperature increases), R(TH) increases and V(AB) increases. This can be used for a cooling device that produces heat when it gets hot. What is an input transducer? title: Practical Electricity: Uses of Electricity
body: Practical Electricity Uses of Electricity 1. Heating Elements Electricity is used when electrical energy is converted to thermal energy via heating elements in appliances such as electric kettles, electric radiators, electric irons, and electric hotplates. 2. Electric Heating Most household heating appliances use heating elements made of nichrome. Nichrome is used because it can withstand high temperatures, and an electric current passing through nichrome wire generates heat rapidly due to the high resistivity of nichrome (100 × 10 -8 Ωm) as compared to copper (1.68 × 10 -8 Ωm). However, in a filament lamp, which converts electrical energy to light energy, the filament in the lamp is a tungsten wire, which is heated to about 2500°C when an electric current flows through it, generating light due to the intense heating effect. Copper Nichrome Tungsten Resistivity 1.68 × 10 -8 Ωm 100 × 10 -8 Ωm 5.6 × 10 -8 Ωm Melting point 1084.62°C 1400°C 3400°C Evidently, while resistivity affecting heat plays a role in the selection of wires, the melting point of the materials is clearly more significant. Despite tungsten having a lower resistivity than nichrome, which may result in it generating less heat or generating heat slower, it has a higher melting point and is hence able to withstand higher heat without melting and causing the bulb to blow easily. What energy conversion occurs in heating elements like kettles, irons, and hotplates? Electrical energy is converted to thermal energy. What material are most household heating elements made of? Nichrome. Why is nichrome used in heating elements? It can withstand high temperatures, and its high resistivity causes it to generate heat rapidly when current flows through it. What is the resistivity of nichrome compared to copper? Nichrome: 100×10⁻⁸ Ωm; Copper: 1.68×10⁻⁸ Ωm — nichrome has much higher resistivity. What material is the filament in a filament lamp made of? Tungsten. To what temperature is a tungsten filament heated in a lamp? About 2500°C. What energy conversion occurs in a filament lamp? Electrical energy is converted to light energy. What is the resistivity of tungsten? 5.6×10⁻⁸ Ωm. Why is tungsten chosen for filaments despite having lower resistivity than nichrome? title: Measuring Electrical Energy
body: Measuring Electrical Energy Since V = W/Q, then W = VQ. Substituting into P = W/t: P = VQ/t Substituting I = Q/t into P = VQ/t: P = VI Substituting V = IR into P = VI: P = I²R Substituting V = IR into P = VI (rearranged): P = V²/R Often, both equations are used depending on which value you are trying to find or know. Most of the time, in home appliances, the value of V is the same, and hence we use the equation P = V²/R more frequently, whereby a smaller resistance means a larger power, as compared to the equation P = I²R, whereby a smaller resistance means a smaller power. Besides the three equations above, power is also defined as the rate of energy conversion, through the equation: P = E/t Rearranging this equation, we get equations to find the electrical energy, E, used in time, t: E = Pt , or E = VIt , or E = I²Rt , or E = (V²/R)t . In units: J = W × s (Energy in Joules is equal to power in watts times time in seconds). The SI unit of energy is joule (J). Using the above, the cost of electricity consumption in the real world is often calculated based on the number of kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electrical energy consumed. 1 kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the energy consumed by a 1 kW device in 1 hour. Worked Examples Example 1: If a 20W bulb operates for 10s, how much energy is consumed? Energy consumed = P × t = 20 W × 10 s = 200 J Example 2: The bulb in the circuit is rated as 60 W, 240 V. What is the current flowing through the bulb, if the circuit supplies 120 V? Rated as 60 W, 240 V simply indicates the voltage the appliance requires to function and the voltage that is too excessive and will damage the appliance. In this case, the appliance will not work if less than 240 V is supplied, and the bulb will blow if more than 240 V is supplied. Solution 1 (wrong): P = VI; 60 W = 120 V × I; I = 0.5 A. This solution is wrong, as when 120 V is supplied, the power output will be less than 60 W, and hence wrong values are being used. Solution 2 (wrong): P = VI; 60 W = 240 V × I; I = 0.25 A. While the values used are matching (rated values), the circuit shows that only 120 V is being supplied, not 240 V, and hence the value of current obtained is wrong. Solution 3 (correct): Using P = V²/R with rated values: 60 W = 240²/R, so R = 960 Ω. Then using the actual supply voltage: V = IR; 120 V = I × 960 Ω; I = 0.125 A. This is correct. title: Sources of Electrical Energy
body: Sources of Electrical Energy Non-Renewable and Renewable Energy Non-renewable energy Renewable energy Defined as energy from natural sources that cannot be replenished at a sustainable rate. Examples: Fossil fuels and nuclear energy. Defined as energy from sources that can be replenished naturally. Examples: Solar, wind, and hydro-electric energy. In Singapore, the majority of the electrical energy consumed is produced by burning fossil fuels. Fossil fuels are a non-renewable source of energy. Efficiency, Cost, and Environmental Impact of Different Kinds of Energy 1. Solar Power (Light energy → Electrical energy) Efficiency: Higher efficiency when there is daylight and minimal cloud cover. Excess energy generated can be stored or fed back to the power grid. Cost: High costs involved in manufacturing solar panels, but the cost of fuel (which is sunlight) is free. Positive impacts: Clean energy (no pollution). Negative impacts: Requires large areas to be cleared for solar panel installation. 2. Hydroelectric Power (Gravitational potential energy → Electrical energy) Efficiency: Most efficient source of energy, as the water flow is concentrated and can be easily controlled. Cost: High costs involved in constructing the dam and power plant. Costs also involved in maintenance, as silt may build up behind the dam and block the water flow. Positive impacts: Clean energy (no pollution). Negative impacts: Dams can cause flooding and disrupt ecosystems. 3. Wind Power (Kinetic energy → Electrical energy) Efficiency: Efficiency varies, depending on wind direction and speed. Cost: Cost of wind power is falling with improvement in technology. Wind energy is free, therefore cost mainly goes towards maintenance. Positive impacts: Clean energy (no pollution). Negative impacts: Requires large open areas unobstructed by high-rise buildings, and possible noise pollution. 4. Nuclear Power (Nuclear energy → Heat energy → Electrical energy) Efficiency: High efficiency, as a small amount of uranium is sufficient to generate a large quantity of energy. Cost: Compared to other sources of energy, additional cost is involved in the disposal of radioactive waste. Negative impacts: Radioactive wastes can contaminate groundwater and sources of surface water. Examples of the dangers of nuclear accidents: Chernobyl and Fukushima. 5. Fossil Fuel (Chemical potential energy → Heat energy → Electrical energy) Efficiency: Most countries have well-established technology and energy distribution

title: Dangers of Electricity
body: Dangers of Electricity 1. Damaged Insulation When the insulating material covering the conducting wires gets worn or damaged, the conducting wires may be exposed. Exposed conducting wires can cause electric shocks if touched. It can also cause short-circuits. 2. Overheating of Cables Overheated cables can lead to fires. Two common causes of overheated cables include overloaded power sockets and use of inappropriate wires. When a power socket is overloaded, an unusually large current flows through the wires, and as temperature increases with increasing current, this risks overheating cables and presents a danger of electricity. Similarly, appliances that require high power to function need thicker wires to prevent overheating of cables. 3. Damp Environments Water in contact with exposed electrical wires provides a conducting path for current. This can lead to electric shocks. Electrical appliances hence should be kept in dry places and handled with dry hands. What danger arises from damaged insulation on wires? title: Safety Features in Home Circuitries
body: Safety Features in Home Circuitries 1. Three-Pin Plugs The fused plug used in Singapore is a three-pin plug. Safety features of the three-pin plug include: A fuse , which protects the appliance when there is an electrical fault. An earth wire , which protects the user from electric shocks if an electrical fault causes the appliance to be live. The cord grip , which prevents the wires from being accidentally pulled out of their connectors. 2. Switches Switches are used to break or complete an electrical circuit, and must be fitted to the live wire of the appliance. If an electrical fault suddenly causes the casing of the appliance to be at a high voltage, a switch can disconnect the voltage supplied to the metal casing: If connected to the live wire If connected to the neutral wire The metal casing is disconnected from the live wire when the switch is open, and the metal casing will return to a low voltage, such that no current flows through the person touching the casing. The metal casing is still connected to the live wire when the switch is open, and the casing will remain live (with a high voltage), causing a large current to flow through the person to the earth, resulting in the person receiving an electric shock. 3. Fuses A fuse is a safety device added to an electrical circuit to prevent excessive current flow. It has the same function as a circuit breaker. However, a fuse must be replaced after it blows, whereas a circuit breaker can be reset after it trips. A fuse consists of a short, thin piece of wire. The wire is made thin so that when an excessive current that is too large flows through it, it heats up and melts. When a fuse blows, a gap is created in the circuit and the circuit is open, so that current stops and cannot flow through the circuit. All fuses also have a rated value. This value indicates the maximum current that can flow through a fuse before it blows. In general, fuses with thicker wires can conduct larger currents before blowing, and therefore have higher rated values. Typical household fuses are rated at 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and 13 A. When selecting a fuse to be used, the fuse closest to the current flowing through the circuit should be used, as if a too small fuse is used, the fuse will blow easily and the appliance will not work, but if a too large fuse is used, then excessive current will be able to flow through the appliance and cause damage. Fuses must also be connected to the live wire, as it isolates the appliance fro

title: Magnetism: Properties of Magnets
body: Properties of Magnets 1. Magnets Attract Magnetic Materials Magnetic materials are materials that can be attracted to a magnet. Acronym: SINC (Singapore Is Not Cold) — Steel, Iron, Nickel, Cobalt. (Not all metals are magnetic materials; be careful not to mistake cobalt for copper.) Non-magnetic materials are materials that cannot be attracted to a magnet, such as Aluminium, Brass, Copper, and non-metals (e.g. wood, plastic, glass). (Note that copper is non-magnetic.) 2. Magnets Have Two Poles. The Magnetic Effect Is Strongest at the Poles. The most iron filings are found at the poles because the magnetic effect is strongest at the poles. 3. A Freely Suspended Magnet Comes to Rest in the North-South Direction. The end of the bar magnet that points to the geographic North pole of the Earth is called the North-seeking pole and is typically coloured and represented in red, while the opposite end, which points to the geographic South pole of the Earth, is called the South-seeking pole. This property allows magnets to be used as compasses. 4. Like Poles Repel and Unlike Poles Attract Interactions Between Magnets and Magnetic Materials Magnets and magnetic materials Magnets and magnets Attraction always takes place; repulsion will not take place. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. The only test for magnetism is repulsion between two magnets. What acronym helps remember magnetic materials, and what does it stand for? SINC — Steel, Iron, Nickel, Cobalt. Name examples of non-magnetic materials. Aluminium, Brass, Copper, and non-metals (e.g., wood, plastic, glass). Where is the magnetic effect of a magnet strongest? At the poles. In which direction does a freely suspended magnet come to rest? The North-South direction. What is the North-seeking pole of a magnet, and how is it typically represented? The end that points to the geographic North pole of the Earth; typically coloured/represented in red. What practical device relies on the north-south alignment property of magnets? A compass. State the rule for interaction between two magnetic poles. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. How do magnets interact with magnetic materials (not other magnets)? Attraction always takes place; repulsion will not take place. What is the only true test for magnetism? Repulsion between two magnets. Is copper a magnetic material? No, copper is non-magnetic. title: Magnetic Induction, Magnetisation and Demagnetisation
body: Magnetic Induction Magnetic induction is the process whereby an object made of magnetic material becomes a magnet when it is near or in contact with a magnet. Theory of Magnetism and Magnetic Domains The Theory of Magnetism states that if a bar magnet is cut up into three smaller pieces, each piece becomes a magnet itself, with a North and South pole. Thus, if the bar magnet is cut into even smaller pieces, each resulting piece will still be a magnet with two poles. This concludes that the bar magnet is made up of many such "tiny magnets", known as magnetic domains. Magnets, like all matter, are made of atoms. Magnetic domains are hence defined as a group of atomic magnets pointing in the same direction. Magnetising Unmagnetised Bars / Magnetising Magnetic Materials The idea of magnetising magnets is to have all the magnetic domains point in the same direction. Stroking Electrical method using a direct current Determining the Poles of a Magnet: Right Hand Grip Rule By gripping the solenoid using the right hand and curling the fingers in the direction of the current flow, the thumb will point in the direction of the North pole. In an image or diagram provided, there will always be the front and the back of the magnet. Imagine the front of the magnet is facing you. In the diagram, the flow of current shown is the flow of current on the front of the magnet, and the flow of current not shown is the flow of current on the back of the magnet. Up the front, down the back Down the front, up the back Arrows showing current pointing towards the right Arrows showing current pointing towards the left North pole is on the right North pole is on the left Demagnetising Magnets The idea of demagnetising magnets is to have all the magnetic domains not point in the same direction. Heating: Strongly heating a magnet and letting it cool in an east-west orientation will cause the magnet to lose its magnetism. The atoms of the magnet vibrate vigorously when heated, causing the magnetic domains to lose their alignment. Hammering: Hammering a magnet placed in the east-west direction alters the alignment of the magnetic domains, causing the magnet to lose its magnetism. Electrical method using an alternating current: Note that it must be an alternating current, which is an electric current that varies its direction of conventional current flow many times per second. title: Magnetic Fields
body: Magnetic Fields A magnetic field is the region surrounding a magnet, in which a body of magnetic material experiences a magnetic force. When something is placed in a magnetic field, that object experiences a force due to the magnetic field. This field can be visualised as magnetic lines of force, and a group of magnetic lines of force forms a magnetic field pattern. The direction of a magnetic field is defined as the direction of the magnetic force acting on a tiny North-pole magnet. Drawing and Identifying Magnetic Field Patterns To identify magnetic field patterns, there are two methods: Sprinkling iron filings around a magnet. Note that this only helps to identify a magnetic field pattern and show it, but unlike the second method, it does not help to show the direction of the magnetic field. Plotting the magnetic field pattern with a compass. There are also several principles for drawing magnetic field patterns: Magnetic field lines are directed outwards from the North pole of the magnet towards the South pole of the magnet. Magnetic field lines do not touch or cross one another. Field lines are drawn closer together to represent stronger fields and vice versa. Magnetic Field Patterns Between Magnets Unlike poles Like poles Magnetic Shielding Magnetic fields may affect the proper functioning of equipment like magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) equipment and computer hard drives. To prevent surrounding magnetic fields from reaching the sensitive areas of this equipment, we use a technique known as magnetic shielding. In magnetic shielding, thin sheets of soft magnetic materials like iron or MuMetal (a nickel-iron alloy) are used to divert the magnetic fields that are present. They are able to do this because magnetic field lines tend to pass within them. Note that magnetic fields work through non-magnetic materials. Magnetic Keepers Over time, magnets tend to become weaker if not stored properly. This is because the free poles at the ends of the magnet repel one another. Hence, the use of keepers helps to ensure that the magnetic domains remain aligned in the same direction, by placing the poles of these atomic magnets between keepers to ensure constant attraction to the induced poles of the keepers, such that the free poles at the ends of the magnets are always aligned in the same direction and will not repel each other to disrupt the alignment and weaken the magnet. Earth's Magnetic Field The Earth behaves as if it has an imaginary bar magnet within it.

title: Magnetic Field Pattern Around a Straight Wire
body: Magnetic Field Pattern Around a Straight Wire Prior to the topic of Electromagnetism, we had known that a coil of wire is able to generate a magnetic field when current passes through it. Oersted's experiment then demonstrated that a current-carrying conductor also produces a magnetic field around it. Consider a straight, current-carrying wire placed vertically through a sheet of cardboard. The magnetic field of a straight, current-carrying wire consists of concentric circles . The magnetic field is stronger closer to the wire , and this is indicated by a higher number of circles per unit area. Now imagine you are looking at the cardboard from above and the current should be travelling towards you. Evidently, if I 2 shows a higher number of circles per unit area as compared to I 1 , then I 2 > I 1 . Note that a higher number of circles per unit area indicates a stronger current which then indicates a stronger magnetic field. However, more closely packed circles may not necessarily indicate that there is a stronger current, though it indicates a stronger magnetic field. The strength of the magnetic field of a current-carrying wire increases when the current is increased. Right Hand Grip Rule To determine the direction of the magnetic field (i.e. if the circle is in an anticlockwise or clockwise direction), we can use the right hand grip rule . This is used by gripping the wire with your thumb pointing in the direction of the current flow, and the direction in which your fingers curl is the direction of the magnetic field. For example, if the current is going upwards, the thumb points upwards as well, and the fingers curl towards the left. The direction of the magnetic field is also the direction in which a compass needle will point if placed in that magnetic field or near the straight, current-carrying wire. The right hand grip rule only finds the magnetic field, while the Right or Left Hand Rule mainly relates current, force and magnetic field, but can also be used to find magnetic field. Straight Wire — Fingers curl in the direction of magnetic field, thumb is pointing in the direction of current. Solenoid/Coil of wire — Fingers curl in the direction of current, thumb is pointing to the North Pole (magnetic field). From above, it is clear to see that the direction of the magnetic field of a current-carrying wire reverses when the direction of the current is reversed. title: Magnetic Field Pattern Around a Flat Coil
body: Magnetic Field Pattern Around a Flat Coil The magnetic field pattern produced by a flat coil is essentially the same as that of two straight wires travelling in opposite directions placed side by side. Imagine a flat coil to be a coil of wire that has been so compressed such that all its turns and coils have been compressed to look flat. Now imagine the situation at points 1 and 2 differently, such that each scenario is considered like the magnetic field pattern of a straight wire. Recall that every time you are identifying magnetic field patterns, it is to be looked at, always, from the top. Looking from the top, at 1, the current is travelling away from us, and hence using the right hand grip rule, the thumb points downwards and the fingers curl towards the right. At 2, the current is travelling towards us, and using the right hand grip rule once again, the thumb points upwards and the fingers curl towards the left. Increasing the Magnetic Field Strength of a Flat Coil The magnetic field strength of a flat coil can be increased by: Increasing the current Increasing the number of turns in the coils Not the number of coils! Increasing the number of coils simply increases the number of different magnetic fields, and does not increase the strength of a single magnetic field. Instead, increasing the number of turns in the coils will cause the lines representing the magnetic field to be closer, resulting in a stronger magnetic field. How can a flat coil's magnetic field pattern be understood? As the same as two straight wires travelling in opposite directions placed side by side. How should magnetic field patterns always be viewed? From the top. At a point where current travels away from the viewer in a flat coil, what direction does the right hand grip rule give (thumb and fingers)? Thumb points downwards, fingers curl towards the right. At a point where current travels towards the viewer in a flat coil, what direction does the right hand grip rule give? Thumb points upwards, fingers curl towards the left. What two factors increase the magnetic field strength of a flat coil? Increasing the current, and increasing the number of turns in the coils. Does increasing the number of coils increase magnetic field strength? No — it only increases the number of different magnetic fields, not the strength of a single field. title: Magnetic Field Pattern of a Solenoid
body: Magnetic Field Pattern of a Solenoid Previously, we have learnt that a solenoid can be used to produce an electromagnet. This is only possible if there is a magnetic field produced by the solenoid. The solenoid's magnetic field pattern is essentially extremely similar to that of a bar magnet. However, in this case, we take into account the magnetic field inside the solenoid. Since the solenoid is used to produce an electromagnet, recall that it induces poles, and previously we used the right hand grip rule to determine the polarity of the electromagnet produced by a solenoid. Similarly, we can predict the direction of the magnetic field of the solenoid using the right hand grip rule: pointing the thumb in the direction of current, and looking at the direction in which the fingers curl, we can predict the direction of the magnetic field of the solenoid. Increasing the Magnetic Field Strength of a Solenoid The magnetic field strength of a solenoid can be increased by: Increasing the current. Increasing the number of turns per unit length of the solenoid. Recall that with a flat coil, increasing the number of turns in the coils will cause the lines representing the magnetic field to be closer, resulting in a stronger magnetic field. Similarly, increasing the number of turns per unit length of the solenoid will increase the strength of the magnetic field produced by the solenoid. However, it is key to remember the use of "per unit length": comparing two springs (representing solenoids), although the spring on the right may have more or an equal number of turns, the spring on the left has more turns per unit length, meaning the turns of the coil are more closely packed, and only then will the lines representing the magnetic field be more compressed, resulting in a stronger magnetic field. Placing a soft iron core within the solenoid. Recall from the topic of Magnetism that with the use of magnetic shielding, magnetic field lines tend to concentrate and travel through magnetic materials rather than air. Since the space in between the turns on the solenoid is air, and magnetic field lines are present in that space, placing a soft iron core within the solenoid will result in the magnetic field lines in that area being more compressed, resulting in a stronger magnetic field. title: Circuit Breakers
body: Circuit Breakers Previously, under the topic of Practical Electricity, we were introduced to the safety feature of a circuit breaker. Recall that a circuit breaker is a safety device that switches off the electrical supply when there is excessive current flow. Notably, circuit breakers are an application of electromagnetism, with one of the core components of the circuit breaker being the electromagnet. Design of a Circuit Breaker, Under Normal Conditions The switch is closed. If the current flowing from the live wire is below the limit, the magnetic field produced by the solenoid is weak. Hence, the soft iron latch is not strongly attracted to the solenoid. As a result, the safety bar stays in position and the interrupt point remains closed. Current flows normally. However, when a short circuit or an overloading of current occurs and there is a sudden surge in current, the magnetic field produced by the solenoid is very strong. This results in the soft iron latch being strongly attracted to the solenoid. As the soft iron latch is strongly attracted, it tilts downwards, releasing the safety bar, which is pushed outwards by the spring. The switch is similarly pushed outwards into the "off" position. Thus, the interrupt point is finally open, the circuit is open, and excessive current no longer flows. Summary Large current → Electromagnet attracts → Circuit open → No flow → Must reset. What is a circuit breaker? A safety device that switches off the electrical supply when there is excessive current flow. What is one core component of a circuit breaker that relates it to electromagnetism? The electromagnet (solenoid). Under normal conditions, when current is below the limit, what happens to the soft iron latch? It is not strongly attracted to the solenoid, since the magnetic field is weak. What happens to the safety bar and interrupt point under normal current conditions? The safety bar stays in position and the interrupt point remains closed, so current flows normally. What triggers a strong magnetic field in the solenoid of a circuit breaker? A short circuit or overloading of current causing a sudden surge in current. What happens to the soft iron latch when there is a surge in current? It is strongly attracted to the solenoid. What happens after the soft iron latch tilts downwards due to strong attraction? It releases the safety bar, which is pushed outwards by the spring, and the switch moves to the 'off' position, opening the interrupt point. Summarize t

title: Motor Effect and Fleming's Left Hand Rule
body: Force on Current-Carrying Conductor and Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field (Motor Effect) When a current flows in the loop ABCD, the wire swings outwards. Evidently, we can conclude that when a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, the conductor experiences a force, known as the motor effect . When the current flows from A to B to C to D, the wire swings outwards, away from the magnet. When current is reversed and flows from D to C to B to A, the wire swings inwards. Evidently, we can also conclude that the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor is reversed when we reverse the direction of (i) the current or (ii) the magnetic field. To explain the motor effect, consider the magnetic field of a current-carrying wire placed in the magnetic field of a magnet. When the two magnetic fields of a current-carrying wire and a magnet are combined, both magnetic fields overlap each other, and the resultant magnetic field is stronger on one side (magnetic field lines are more concentrated on one side) while the other side is weaker. The resultant force will be in the direction of the weaker side (in this case, towards the right). Replacing the current with a beam of charged particles, using Fleming's left hand rule, due to the resultant force, the charge will experience a deflection. The direction of the force on a beam of charged particles is reversed when (i) we reverse the direction of the magnetic field, or (ii) the direction of the beam of charged particles is reversed. Note that the beam of particles must be travelling; similarly, current must be flowing. A wire that does not carry current will not produce a magnetic field, and a charged particle stationary in a magnetic field will merely produce an electric field and will not produce a magnetic field. An electric field does not interfere with a magnetic field. Fleming's Left Hand Rule To determine the direction of the force (motor effect), one can use Fleming's left hand rule: place your fingers at right angles to each other, with your thumb pointing in the direction of the force, your index finger (second) pointing in the direction of the magnetic field, and your middle finger (third) pointing in the direction of current. Note that current refers to conventional current at all times. title: Turning Effect on a Current-Carrying Coil in a Magnetic Field
body: Turning Effect on a Current-Carrying Coil in a Magnetic Field Coil ABCD will experience a turning effect about the axis PQ. Just as we can increase the magnetic field strength of a magnetic field produced by a straight wire or a solenoid, we can similarly increase the turning effect of the current-carrying coil in a magnetic field. Increasing the turning effect is about increasing the moment produced about the pivot, in this case axis PQ. Since moments are equal to force times distance, increasing the force or the perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot can increase the turning effect. This can be done by: Increasing the number of turns on the wire coil — this will result in the lines representing the magnetic field produced by the current-carrying wire being closer together and more compressed, indicating a stronger magnetic field and a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot. Increasing the current in the wire coil — this increases the strength of the magnetic field, resulting in a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot. Placing a soft iron core in the coil — magnetic field lines tend to concentrate and travel through a magnetic material like a soft iron core rather than air. Since the area between the wire coils is air, placing a soft iron core in the coil will help to concentrate the magnetic field, resulting in a stronger magnetic field, which indicates a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot. Increasing the strength of the external magnetic field — this will increase the strength of the force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot. Increasing the distance of the points (A, B, C or D) from the pivot (size of the coil) — besides increasing the strength of the force, one can also increase the distance, which can increase and produce a larger moment about the pivot. What does coil ABCD experience when placed in a magnetic field with current flowing? A turning effect (torque) about the axis PQ. What is the formula relationship used to explain the turning effect increasing? Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot. List the five ways to increase the turning effect of a current-carrying coil. Increasing number of turns on the coil; increasing current in the coil; placing a soft iron core in the coil; increasing strength of external magnetic field; increasing the distance of points from the pivot (size of coil). title: D.C. Motor
body: D.C. Motor The D.C. Motor is an electric motor, and a key application of the turning effect of a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field. It converts electrical energy to mechanical energy, and is commonly used in appliances such as battery operated toys and DVD players. Previously, we had seen the coil rotate around the axis PQ. However, consider what happens when the coil rotates 180° and the wires are now on an opposite pole than they were before — consider the moments produced. Notice that originally, when the wire AB is on the side of the North pole, the force produced is a clockwise moment. However, when the wire AB is now on the side of the South pole, the force produced is an anti-clockwise moment. This means that every time the coil rotates and places the wire at a different pole than it was before, the direction of rotation of the coil will change, and continuous rotation of the coil in one direction is not possible. It will only be possible if the flow of current in CD and AB changes with the rotation of the coil as well. In order to do this, the D.C. motor utilises a split ring commutator and two carbon brushes . The function of the split ring commutator is to reverse the direction of the current in the coil when it passes the vertical position, as this ensures that the moments produced remain in the same direction and the coil continues to rotate in the same direction. The function of the carbon brushes is to allow the coil to turn without entangling the wire in the external circuit. (Carbon brushes have fine hairs that maintain contact with the split ring commutator whilst allowing free rotation of the rings.) The split ring commutator is essentially wielded to the wires such that every time a rotation occurs, the direction of the flow of current changes with each rotation. For example, for wire AB, on the left current is flowing from A to B; 180 degrees later, on the right, current is flowing from B to A, ensuring a change in the direction of current flow along with the rotation of the coil to ensure continuous rotation of the coil in one direction. This change in the direction of current flow occurs when the coil is in a vertical position, where the rings do not have any contact with the carbon brushes. Increasing the Turning Effect of a D.C. title: Electromagnetic Induction
body: Electromagnetic Induction Previously, electromagnetism studies how electricity can induce magnetism. Electromagnetic induction studies how magnetism can induce electricity. This was first discovered by Faraday's Solenoid Experiment in 1831. During this experiment, he observed that: When a magnet was inserted into a solenoid, the galvanometer needle was deflected in one direction. When the magnet was withdrawn from the solenoid, the galvanometer needle was deflected in the other direction. When the magnet was stationary in the solenoid, the galvanometer needle was not deflected. Note: It is not important to note which direction the deflection is in. What is important is only that the direction of deflection when inserted is opposite to the direction of deflection when withdrawn. Magnetic Flux and Flux Linkage Magnetic flux refers to the lines that make up the magnetic field of a magnet. Magnetic flux linkage refers to how closely linked the magnetic field lines are with the solenoid. Note: High flux linkage does not equal a strong magnetic field. The strength of the magnetic field is related to flux density, which is the number of lines and how close they are. Induced E.M.F. Faraday's Solenoid Experiment concluded that an e.m.f. (difference in potential) is induced, producing a current, when there is a change in flux linkage , be it an increase or decrease in flux linkage due to the magnet moving towards or away from the coil. A change in flux linkage must occur; flux linkage on its own cannot induce an e.m.f. Points to note: Momentary deflection — since only a change in flux linkage induces an e.m.f., unless the change is sustained and flux linkage continues to change, deflection in the galvanometer as a result of electromagnetic induction is often momentary. Which moves does not matter — the change in flux linkage often occurs through movement, such as the movement of a magnet closer to or further away from a conductor. The opposite case, whereby a conductor moves closer to or further away from a magnet, also induces an e.m.f. Only if there is a complete circuit will an induced current flow. Magnitude of Induced E.M.F. Since an e.m.f. can only be induced by a change in flux linkage, the magnitude of induced e.m.f. can thus only be affected by the rate of change of flux linkage . This can be done by directly increasing the speed of the movement, or alternatively by increasing the amount of magnetic flux and surface area in contact with magnetic flux, such

title: Straight Conductor and Fleming's Right Hand Rule
body: Straight Conductor Besides a coil of wire and the change in flux linkage between two coils or a coil and a magnet, electromagnetic induction can occur in straight conductors too. Coil of Wire Straight Conductor (Rate of) Change in flux linkage → (Magnitude of) Induced e.m.f. (Rate of) Cutting of magnetic flux → (Magnitude of) Induced e.m.f. Cutting of magnetic flux induces an e.m.f. as follows: when the conductor moves upwards and cuts the magnetic field lines, the electrons in the conductor also move upwards. Using Fleming's Left Hand Rule, since the magnetic field is travelling into the screen, and the movement of the electron is upwards, meaning conventional current is downwards, the electrons will experience a force to the right, resulting in conventional current to the left. For coils in a generator, instead of explaining how the electrons move, simply put: as the coil rotates, the conductor/coil cuts the magnetic field lines, thus inducing an e.m.f. Fleming's Right Hand Rule To determine the direction of the induced current in the conductor, besides the method above, one can also use Fleming's Right Hand Rule: First 3 fingers at right angles to each other. Thumb points in the direction of the movement of the conductor. Index finger (second) points in the direction of the magnetic field the conductor is cutting. Middle finger (third) will point in the direction of the induced current. Note that current refers to conventional current at all times. Left Hand Rule Right Hand Rule Most of the time used to determine direction of force acting on a conductor in a magnetic field. Used when there is already a current flowing in a conductor (battery is present) in a magnetic field, resulting in a force acting on the conductor. (Results in force — Motor rule) Most of the time used to determine direction of induced current in a conductor cutting a magnetic field. Used when a conductor is moving through a magnetic field (no current originally, no power source, but conductor is moved), and cutting magnetic field lines results in an induced e.m.f./current. (Results in current — Generator rule) What causes an e.m.f. to be induced in a straight conductor, as opposed to a coil? The (rate of) cutting of magnetic flux, as opposed to a change in flux linkage for a coil. When a conductor moves upward through a magnetic field going into the screen, in which direction do the electrons move? Upwards (with the conductor). title: Alternating Current Generator
body: Alternating Current Generator Function of an Alternating Current Generator The alternating current generator makes use of electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical energy into useful electrical energy. Comparison: D.C. Motor vs A.C. Generator D.C. Motor A.C. Generator Electrical energy to mechanical energy Mechanical energy to electrical energy Split-ring commutators and carbon brushes Slip rings: solely for the purpose of connecting the coil to the external circuit via the carbon brushes. (Slip rings do NOT ensure the induced current reverses direction every half cycle — that is not their function, unlike the split ring.) Carbon brushes: allow the coil to turn without entangling the wire in the external circuit. Carbon brushes have fine hairs that maintain contact with the slip rings whilst allowing free rotation of the rings. Current in a conductor → produces a magnetic field → overlaps with existing magnetic field, interacts → results in motion. Motion of the conductor also cuts magnetic field lines, producing an induced e.m.f. in the conductor known as back e.m.f. , which opposes the original current due to Lenz's Law. (Lenz's Law: induced current always opposes the change causing it. Since the change causing it is the turning of the coil, and what starts the turning is the current, ultimately the induced e.m.f. will oppose the change — the turning — which is ultimately created by the current, thus opposing the current. Fleming's rules are not used here because they only identify relationships and direction, and do not explain why.) Motion → change in magnetic flux linkage or cutting of magnetic field lines → produces current. No back e.m.f. Though, motion can be sustained by the induced current producing a magnetic field that overlaps and interacts with the existing magnetic field, producing motion that will not be opposite, but will rather sustain the current motion in the same direction. How an A.C. Generator Produces Alternating Current At position 1, the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field, and the coil is rotated in the clockwise direction. As the coil rotates, it cuts the magnetic field lines and an e.m.f. is induced in the coil. By applying Fleming's Right Hand Rule on AD, the induced current will flow in the coil from A to D. At position 2, the plane of the coil is now perpendicular to the magnetic field, hence the rate of cutting is lowest, and there is no induced e.m.f.
