title: Transformers
body: Transformers Structure and Function of a Transformer A transformer is a device that can change a high alternating voltage to a low alternating voltage, or vice versa. This change can either be an increase, in the case of a step-up transformer , or a decrease, in the case of a step-down transformer . A transformer consists of thin sheets of soft iron insulated from one another, with a primary coil connected to an A.C. supply and a secondary coil connected to a device. Principle of a Transformer When an A.C. supply is supplied to the primary coil, it sets up an alternating current. Since a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic effect, a fluctuating magnetic field with fluctuating magnetic flux linkage is set up. Due to the constant change in magnetic flux linkage, the continuous change results in a continuous induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil. The magnitude of this induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil can be calculated through the formula V S /V P = N S /N P , where: V S = magnitude of the induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil V P = magnitude of the input voltage of the A.C. supply connected to the primary coil N S = number of turns in the secondary coil N P = number of turns in the primary coil Step-up Transformer Step-down Transformer N S > N P ; V S > V P N P > N S ; V P > V S Power in a Transformer In a transformer, electrical energy is transferred from the primary coil to the secondary coil. Ideally, power loss in this process should be kept to a minimum, and this can be done by: The use of insulated iron sheets to reduce energy loss, as iron sheets concentrate magnetic flux, reducing energy loss. Soft iron is used because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised. This also reduces energy loss. Besides calculating the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil, it is also important to be able to calculate the power loss in a transformer. To do this, we often need to identify the amount of current flowing through the coils first. Ideal Transformer Non-ideal Transformer In an ideal transformer, by the Principle of the Conservation of Energy, input power must be equal to output power. Therefore, since P = VI: V P I P = V S I S , which can also be written as V S /V P = I P /I S , where I S = current in the secondary coil and I P = current in the primary coil. title: Cathode Ray Oscilloscopes
body: Cathode Ray Oscilloscopes A Cathode Ray Oscilloscope, also known as a CRO, is a device whereby an electron beam is projected onto a fluorescent screen. The display produced can vary depending on the deflection of the electron beam horizontally, vertically and over time. The cathode releases the electrons, while the grid is used to focus the electrons into a single beam, which is then deflected using the X and Y plates that are connected to an input voltage. Interpreting CRO Displays CRO displays show the deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal and vertical direction, occasionally over time. When interpreting CRO displays, there are three things to note: Vertical (voltage) Input voltage (e.g. 5.0 V) Y gain (e.g. 1.0 V/div) — amplifies the deflection of the electron beam in the vertical direction Horizontal (time) Timebase (e.g. 20 ms/div) — controls the speed of the deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction. When the timebase is off, the speed of deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction is 0, meaning there is no deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction, and the display will not show any deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction. D.C. Supply A.C. Supply Voltage is constant with the timebase off Voltage changes with the timebase off Uses of a CRO 1. Measuring voltage. To do so, switch off the timebase and adjust the trace (dot) so that it is vertically in the middle of the screen. Then, connect the voltage to be measured to the Y-plates terminal, and a vertical trace (for an A.C. supply) or a displaced dot (for a D.C. supply) will be shown. To increase the sensitivity of the CRO in measuring voltage, the Y-gain can be adjusted to adjust the height of the trace, such that even a small voltage can be read off the screen easily. Note: When measuring the voltage of an A.C. supply, the peak voltage is half of the voltage displayed [i.e., the displayed trace height corresponds to twice the peak voltage, peak-to-peak]. 2. title: Temperature
body: Definition Temperature is defined as the degree of hotness and coldness of a place. It is affected by latitude , altitude and ocean currents . How does Latitude affect Temperature? As latitude increases, temperature decreases. Big idea: curvature of the Earth – due to the curvature of the Earth, the sun's rays strike at different angles to different parts of the Earth. This must be the key sentence present when answering a question about how latitude affects temperature. Based on this big idea, latitude affects temperature through: Angle of incidence Layer of atmosphere How does Altitude affect Temperature? As altitude increases, temperature decreases. This is due to two main reasons: how the Earth is heated, and gravity and density of air. How the Earth is heated Temperature decreases with altitude mainly because the atmosphere is not directly heated by shortwave radiation from the sun's rays. Instead, when the Earth's surface warms up, it absorbs heat energy (in the form of shortwave radiation) from the sun and reflects it in the form of longwave radiation to heat the air around it. As the heat is reflected in the form of longwave radiation, it diffuses into and warms the atmosphere, transferring some of the heat to the upper layers of the atmosphere in turn. This illustrates a concept known as the heat balance of Earth. Layers of atmosphere closest to Earth's surface (low altitude areas) are typically warmer than layers of atmosphere at higher-altitude areas because: As altitude increases, the distance between Earth's surface and the air increases. More longwave radiation reflected by the Earth's surface is absorbed by the rest of the atmosphere (e.g. clouds) and by greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Less longwave radiation heats the air at a higher altitude, and more of the sun's solar energy is trapped at a lower altitude. This results in a lower intensity of heating at a higher altitude, as air at higher altitudes absorbs less heat from longwave radiation than air nearer to the Earth's surface. This results in a lower temperature. Gravity and Density of Air Altitude also affects temperature through the gravity and density of air. How do Ocean Currents affect Temperature? Ocean currents help to regulate temperatures across the world. title: Relative Humidity
body: Definitions Term Definition Water vapour Gaseous state of water produced from evaporation/boiling of water or sublimation of ice Evaporation Change of state of water from liquid state to gaseous state Condensation Change of state of water from gaseous state to liquid state Saturation Maximum amount of water vapour that air can hold → takes place at dew point Dew point The temperature to which air must be cooled to become saturated with water vapour Humidity Amount of water vapour (moisture) in the air Absolute humidity Measure of water vapour (moisture) in the air, regardless of temperature Relative humidity Ratio between the actual amount of water vapour present in a mass of air (g/m³) and the maximum amount of water vapour (moisture) the air could hold at a given temperature, expressed as a percentage. (If relative humidity is high → near saturation point → going to rain) Relative humidity (%) = (actual amount of water vapour present in a mass of air, g/m³) ÷ (maximum amount of water vapour/moisture the air could hold at a given temperature, g/m³) × 100 Relationship between Temperature and Relative Humidity As temperature increases, relative humidity decreases. This is an inverse relationship. A place with fluctuating temperatures will have fluctuating relative humidity. The amount of water vapour capacity the air can hold increases as air temperature rises and decreases as it cools. Note on answering technique: When stating relationships, it is first important to state what kind of relationship it is. However, more importantly, you must elaborate on what this relationship is. e.g. "Inverse relationship" (good but not good enough) e.g. "Inverse relationship, whereby as temperature increases, relative humidity decreases." title: Precipitation
body: Definition Precipitation is defined as water falling from the atmosphere onto the Earth's surface in any form (rain, hail, snow, sleet, etc.). Precipitation typically occurs in the tropics, and rainfall can be classified as follows: Areas with >1500mm of rainfall – experience high rainfall (e.g. Singapore) Areas with <250mm of rainfall – experience very low rainfall Formation of Rain Ideas generally associated with the formation of rain include: Bodies of water (e.g. oceans, lakes, rivers) and forms of water (e.g. water vapour, rain, clouds) Evaporation, condensation, precipitation Heating from the sun's rays Continuous process Looking at the various ways rain is formed, there are often categories such as: Concept of processes – evaporation, condensation, precipitation Concept of relationships and interaction – relief rain is impacted by moisture in the air (relative humidity) and wind; convectional rain is impacted by temperature (sun's rays); similarities exist in the relationships between elevation and temperature Concept of place – different places have different conditions resulting in different types of rain formed in different areas Source of water vapour – relief rain gains water vapour through warm wind and moisture from the ocean; convectional rain gains water vapour through evaporation and transpiration However, from all this, there is only ONE BIG IDEA: for rain to form, air must be forced to rise. Regardless of the type of rain, air must first be forced to rise. How air is forced to rise differs for different types of rain, though after air is forced to rise, the processes that follow are rather similar. Convectional Rain vs Relief Rain Convectional Rain Occurs when the earth's surface is heated intensely (air is forced to rise due to intense heating of the Earth's surface) Produced by strong convection currents in the atmosphere Common in the tropics, which receive a great amount of sunlight, or during summer in temperate countries (due to latitude), occurring typically in the afternoon (the hottest period of the day) While common in the tropics, convectional rain can still occur in other areas outside the tropics, but will typically only occur in these other areas when they are experiencing summer, as during summer, due to the rotation of the earth, these areas receive a greater amount of sunlight than usual, allowing for intense heating of the Earth's surface and the formation of convectional rain Often associated with lightning and thunder

title: Pressure
body: Definition Pressure is defined as the force exerted on a unit area of the Earth's surface by the weight of a column of air above it. Relationship between Altitude and Pressure As altitude increases, pressure decreases (inverse relationship). Chain of reasoning: As altitude increases → the distance between Earth's surface and the air increases → gravity's pull on the air molecules decreases → molecules are less dense and are more spread out → weight of air decreases and air becomes thinner → pressure decreases due to less weight being above it. Relationship between Temperature and Pressure As temperature increases, pressure decreases (inverse relationship). Chain of reasoning: As temperature increases → warmer air molecules have more energy to move and collide with one another, and move faster as well → this causes warm air to expand → as warm air expands, the air molecules are spaced further apart and air becomes less dense → there is less weight of air per unit area, and air becomes lighter/thinner → there is less force per unit area due to less weight, and hence less pressure. Special case – mountain top: At a mountain top, due to a lower temperature, pressure should logically be higher, as pressure decreases as temperature increases. However, pressure should also be lower as pressure decreases as altitude increases. So which do we follow? Reasoning it out: at a higher altitude there are lower temperatures, but gravity's pull on the molecules is also lower and the air molecules are more spaced out. Hence, we take the air at the mountain top to be of low pressure. Relationship between Density and Pressure As density decreases, pressure decreases (direct relationship). Chain of reasoning: As density decreases → there is less weight of air per unit area, and air becomes lighter/thinner → there is less force per unit area due to less weight, and hence less pressure. Note: The relationship between density and pressure is also related to temperature and altitude, so it is important to pick up on these links. title: Winds
body: Definition Wind is defined as the horizontal movement of air from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure. The greater the difference in air pressure, the faster the wind speed. Wind is a result of: Air moving from a region of higher pressure to a region of lower pressure, and The differential heating capacity of land and water – land heats and cools faster than water, which heats and cools more slowly Winds can be classified by scale, time, location and magnitude: Type Time Location/Magnitude Land Breeze (small scale) Occurs on a daily basis, for a short period of time Affects specific areas, typically only coastal areas Sea Breeze (small scale) Occurs on a daily basis, for a short period of time Affects specific areas, typically only coastal areas Monsoon Winds (large scale) Occurs seasonally Affects large regions and areas Cyclones/Typhoons (large scale) Typically occur in summer Generated over the sea and near coastal areas; affect large areas to a large extent Small Scale Winds (Local Winds) Small scale winds mainly refer to land breeze and sea breeze. They occur on a daily basis and for a short period of time, and affect specific areas, typically only coastal areas. Land Breeze – a local wind that takes place during the night. Sea Breeze – a local wind that takes place during the day. Large Scale Winds (Regional Winds) Large scale winds mainly refer to monsoon winds, and more specifically the Southwest Monsoon and the Northeast Monsoon. Monsoon winds are defined as the seasonal reversal of winds across the earth, as the Northern and Southern Hemispheres experience different seasons. They are caused by the formation, overland, of intense high pressure in winter and low pressure in summer (due to different temperatures in different hemispheres). They occur seasonally and affect large regions and areas. Monsoon winds are affected by the Coriolis effect – a force produced by the Earth's rotation that causes the bending or deflection of winds: Northern Hemisphere → winds are deflected to the right Southern Hemisphere → winds are deflected to the left The naming of the monsoon depends on the region. It is called the Southwest/Northeast Monsoon in the Northern Hemisphere because the wind appears to be coming from the Southwest/Northeast. In the Southern Hemisphere, it is called the Southeast/Northwest Monsoon because the wind appears to be coming from the Southeast/Northwest. title: El Nino and La Nina
body: El Nino and La Nina are a global climate phenomenon caused by cyclical shifts in the water temperature of the Pacific Ocean. While focused on a small section of the Pacific near the Equator, these shifts have global ramifications. These changes are due to natural interactions between the ocean and atmosphere: sea surface temperature, rainfall, air pressure, and atmospheric and ocean circulation all influence each other. Each El Nino or La Nina event lasts between 9–12 months, and, on average, occurs every 2–7 years. How do El Nino and La Nina Impact Humans? Rainfall is not simply influenced by one or two factors, but rather, all elements of the weather are affected by a multitude of factors. In this case, rainfall patterns are affected not just by winds, pressure, temperature or monsoons, but also El Nino and La Nina. El Nino, La Nina, and the normal condition all produce important consequences for people and ecosystems across the globe. The interactions between the ocean and atmosphere alter weather around the world, and can result in severe storms or mild weather, drought or flooding. Beyond influencing the weather, these changes can produce secondary results that influence food supplies and prices, as well as forest fires. Food production is particularly impacted by El Nino and La Nina conditions. Changes in ocean temperatures and currents during El Nino can impact marine life, which in turn impacts individuals who fish for a living and consumers who depend on certain fish for food. Agriculture is very dependent on climate and weather; hence, as a result of changes in La Nina and El Nino conditions, rainfall and temperature patterns may change, which has important consequences for food production and availability. Famines and political strife can result from these environmental conditions. For example, in the southern United States, from autumn to spring, El Nino usually causes increased rainfall and sometimes destructive flooding. La Nina, however, usually causes drier weather in the south, but the northwest tends to be colder and wetter than average. Even though El Nino occurs in the Pacific Ocean, it often reduces the number of hurricanes that form in the Atlantic Ocean. Conversely, La Nina events tend to be related to an increase in the number of Atlantic hurricanes. title: What is Climate Change?
body: Questions to consider: Is climate change the same as global warming? How is it different from global warming? Is it extreme weather events? Are natural disasters part of climate change? Climate change is NOT global warming, and it does not directly include natural disasters or extreme weather events. Global Warming vs Climate Change (not equal) Global Warming Is the long-term heating of Earth's climate system observed since the pre-industrial period (between 1850 and 1900), due to human activities, primarily fossil fuel burning, which increases heat-trapping greenhouse gas levels in Earth's atmosphere Refers to a rise in global temperatures (focuses only on temperature) Climate Change Is a long-term change in the average weather patterns that have come to define Earth's local, regional and global climates; these changes have a broad range of observed effects that are synonymous with the term Refers to the increasing changes in weather patterns (rain patterns, wind patterns, temperature patterns) of a climate (looks at all the elements of weather in general) Global warming is part of climate change. Evidence of Global Climate Change Global climate change is real and is evident in the global warming (global rise in temperatures) and global cooling (global decrease in temperatures) experienced in past years. As the Earth moved out of ice ages over the past million years, the global temperature rose a total of 4°C to 7°C over approximately 5,000 years. In the past century alone, the temperature has climbed 0.7°C, roughly ten times faster than the average rate of ice-age-recovery warming. Mean global temperatures rose faster between 1980 and 2000, increasing by about 0.4°C in 20 years. There has been a 1.18°C temperature increase since the late 19th century. Increasing impacts and examples of global warming: Increase in extreme weather events Increasing loss of Arctic sea ice – Arctic sea ice is declining at a rate of 13.1% per decade Increasing rise in sea level – global sea level rose about 8 inches (20 centimetres) over the last century; the rate in the last two decades is nearly double that of the last century, and accelerating slightly every year Increase in carbon emissions – a 250 times increase from human sources compared to natural sources The Greenhouse Effect The greenhouse effect is a natural process that occurs when gases in the Earth's atmosphere trap the sun's heat. Chain of reasoning: Earth receives shortwave radiation in the form of visible lig

title: Causes of Climate Change
body: Natural Causes Due to the sheer duration (tens of thousands of years) required for natural causes to have a large impact on the climate and result in large-scale climate change, the effect that natural causes have on climate change is small, though these causes do still cause minor changes every day. Variations in Solar Output The sun does not always shine at perpetually the same level of brightness; it brightens and dims slightly, taking approximately 11 years to complete one solar cycle. The sun undergoes various changes in its activity and appearance during each cycle: levels of solar radiation go up or down, as does the amount of material the sun ejects into space, and the size and number of sunspots and solar flares. This results in high and low global temperatures, as well as warmer and colder periods on Earth. Such changes also have a variety of effects in space, in Earth's atmosphere, and on Earth's surface, eventually leading to climate changes. Sunspots are darker areas on the sun's surface. The sun emits slightly more radiation during active periods of sunspots, contributing to a warmer global climate in these active periods. 300 years ago, the Little Ice Age was caused by a period of reduced solar activity. At the start of a solar cycle, there is a solar minimum, when the sun has the least sunspots. The middle of the solar cycle is the solar maximum, when the sun has the most sunspots. The more sunspots there are, the more heat is suppressed, so more heat flows to surrounding areas, causing these regions to be brighter than normal and radiate more heat towards the Earth. Plate Tectonics and Volcanic Eruptions Erupting volcanoes emit sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere. Sulfur dioxide is much more effective than ash particles at cooling the climate. The sulfur dioxide moves into the stratosphere and combines with water to form sulfuric acid aerosols; together with dust and ash, these particles reflect solar energy back into space, resulting in a cooling influence on the Earth's surface. The cooling effect can last for months to years, depending on the characteristics of the eruption. title: Impacts of Climate Change
body: Positive Impacts of Climate Change 1. Lengthening of Growing Seasons in Some Regions Due to climate change, there is a global rise in temperature. With this, higher temperatures result in longer growing seasons in some regions. Some colder regions may experience the early onset of spring and the delay in the onset of autumn or winter frost. This creates a longer warm season for growing, which could allow for more crops to be grown, increasing global food production and food supply (especially for impoverished countries), as well as allow plants to grow for a longer period during each growing season and absorb more CO2 as a result. Due to climate change, there is also an increasing amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Increased carbon dioxide can allow for more photosynthesis to occur, which causes crops to grow faster, leading to increased crop yields. Due to climate change, certain areas are also able to grow different crops. All the above result in increased food supply, but also provide a variety of food, as well as perhaps even greater economic revenue from the increased surplus of food products that can be sold. The longer growing period, as a result of higher temperatures due to climate change, also creates an extended summer season in some landscapes, which allows for increased revenue from tourist activities requiring good weather in the country. 2. More Habitable Places and New Growth in Areas Due to climate change, there is a global rise in temperature. Hence, colder and previously inhabitable areas can become more habitable with warmer temperatures, with a likely increase in food production in these areas. More animals and plants can also now be grown in areas due to higher temperatures. Hence, these previously frozen and inhabitable regions of Earth can now experience more plant growth (can grow crops) and milder climates, allowing more people to live there without worrying too much about the harsh conditions (e.g. Siberia, Arctic, Antarctica and other frozen regions of the Earth). 3. More Efficient Shipping Routes As global warming melts sea ice across the Arctic, it clears the way for ships to sail through, opening more possible shipping routes (including routes directly over the North Pole), making transport faster, easier, more efficient and cheaper in areas with glaciers. 4. title: Responses to Climate Change: Mitigation and Adaptation
body: There are various risks and challenges brought about by the negative impacts of climate change. Hence, in order to respond to such challenges posed by climatological hazards, coordinated responses are required, from different levels. Responding to climate change can be categorised into two possible approaches: mitigation and adaptation, which are not equal. Mitigation Mitigation involves reducing the amount and flow of heat-trapping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere and stabilising the levels of heat-trapping greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, either by reducing the sources and amount of these gases (for example, the burning of fossil fuels for electricity, heat or transport) or enhancing the "sinks" that accumulate and store these gases (such as the oceans, forests and soil). The goal of mitigation is to avoid significant human interference with the climate system. Adaptation Adaptation involves anticipating the adverse effects of climate change and taking appropriate action to adjust systems and societies to actual or predicted future climate and change, in order to better withstand the impacts of climate change and prevent or minimise the damage from various impacts of climate change. What is the goal of mitigation? To avoid significant human interference with the climate system. Define adaptation. title: Climate Change: Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies (Examples)
body: Mitigation vs Adaptation Mitigation involves reducing or preventing the emission of greenhouse gases. Adaptation includes making the most of any potential beneficial opportunities associated with climate change (for example, longer growing seasons or increased yields in some regions). The goal of adaptation is to reduce humans' vulnerability to the harmful effects of climate change (such as sea-level encroachment, more intense extreme weather events, or food insecurity). Examples of Mitigation 1. Retrofitting Buildings for Efficiency Refers to increasing the heating and cooling efficiency of buildings to help save energy and cut greenhouse gases. New York's Empire State Building is one example, and was recently retrofitted for energy efficiency, reducing the building's expected energy use by 38%. 2. Changing Lifestyles Refers to policies that can help individuals and communities reduce their carbon footprints by making low-emission development and modes of transportation more convenient. For example, enhanced public transportation, bike paths, and walkability can promote smart growth while reducing urban sprawl and traffic congestion. 3. Researching New Fuels Refers to using new fuels to provide needed energy while reducing greenhouse gas emissions. For example, scientists are studying how to generate biofuel from non-edible plant material such as switchgrass and algae. It is important to study both the benefits and the potential unintended consequences of these innovations. 4. Implementing Small-Scale Innovations Refers to small-scale innovations that can make a big difference by producing energy from sources other than burning fossil fuels, thus reducing carbon emissions and greenhouse gases. For example, compact biogas plants produce usable energy from materials such as manure or garbage, offering an affordable, sustainable, and reliable renewable fuel source that can be implemented locally. Another example is using food waste for energy, and another is windmills in the Netherlands. This is a mitigation as it reduces the burning of fossil fuels and reduces carbon emissions by generating energy in other ways. 5. Streamlining Industrial Processes Refers to ways industries can optimise their use of energy to reduce the need to burn more fossil fuels to generate more energy and produce more greenhouse gases, and instead reduce the amount of carbon emissions and greenhouse gases. title: International Responses to Climate Change: The Kyoto Protocol
body: Background The human enhancement of global warming leading to climate change is seen as a worldwide problem. Policy responses have been led by international negotiation with the aim of reducing carbon dioxide emissions. The principal forum for international climate change action has been the United Nations, which has led to the Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and the Kyoto Protocol. In December 2015, the Paris Agreement consolidated years of negotiations with agreement among 188 countries to limit carbon dioxide emissions. What is the Kyoto Protocol? The Kyoto Protocol was adopted on 11 December 1997. Owing to a complex ratification process, it entered into force on 16 February 2005. Currently, there are 192 Parties to the Kyoto Protocol. The Kyoto Protocol in short is an agreement linked to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), which is an international convention set up with the goal of reducing the levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere. On top of the UNFCCC, which only asks countries to adopt policies and measures on mitigation and to report periodically, the Kyoto Protocol operationalises the UNFCCC by committing industrialized countries, economies in transition, and its parties to setting internationally binding emission reduction targets to limit and reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions in accordance with agreed individual targets. The main objective of the Kyoto Protocol is to reduce the amount of harmful chemicals pumped into the atmosphere. It does this through the annex-based structure of the protocol, which establishes a structure of rolling emission reduction commitment periods for its members to abide by. The Kyoto Protocol sets specific commitments and binding emission reduction targets for 37 individual industrialised, developed countries and economies in transition and the European Union, to reduce emissions overall by an average of 5.2% below 1990 levels by the five-year period 2008-2012 (the first commitment period). These specific commitments would also be reckoned on a net basis, considering sinks as well as sources, and each country must credibly measure its contribution and meet its commitment. Greater responsibility to reduce greenhouse gas emissions was placed on the 37 developed countries and the European countries. A heavier burden was placed on these developed countries as the protocol enacts a stricter policy on them under the principle of "common but differentiated responsib

title: International Responses to Climate Change: The Paris Agreement
body: What is the Paris Agreement? The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change, signed at the Paris Climate Conference in December 2015. It was adopted by 196 Parties at COP 21 in Paris on 12 December 2015 and entered into force on 4 November 2016. By signing this agreement, countries committed to tackle climate change by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and taking measures to adapt to the unavoidable impacts of climate change. The Paris Agreement is a landmark in the multilateral climate change process and the most significant global climate agreement to date, being the first universal and global action plan to bring all nations into a common cause to undertake ambitious efforts to combat climate change and adapt to its effects. The agreement aims to tackle climate change by limiting global warming and keeping the global average temperature from rising well below 2°C, preferably to 1.5°C, compared to pre-industrial levels. The Paris Agreement also aims to reach global net-zero emissions – where the amount of greenhouse gases emitted equals the amount removed from the atmosphere – in the second half of this century (also known as being climate neutral or carbon neutral). To achieve this long-term temperature goal, countries aim to reach global peaking of greenhouse gas emissions as soon as possible to achieve a climate-neutral world by mid-century. Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) The Paris Agreement requires all countries to set emissions-reduction pledges. Governments set targets known as nationally determined contributions (NDCs). In their NDCs, countries communicate actions they will take to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions in order to reach the goals of the Paris Agreement. Countries also communicate in their NDCs the actions they will take to build resilience and adapt to the impacts of rising temperatures. This may include information on adaptation and finance flows. To better frame efforts towards the long-term goal, the Paris Agreement invites countries to formulate and submit, by 2020, long-term low greenhouse gas emission development strategies (LT-LEDS), which provide the long-term horizon to the NDCs. Unlike NDCs, these are not mandatory. Nevertheless, they place the NDCs into the context of countries' long-term planning and development priorities, providing a vision and direction for future development. title: National-Level Responses: Singapore's Climate Policies
body: Why National-Level Responses Matter Although climate change agreements emphasising carbon emission reduction have been reached through international approaches, the policy measures to meet the obligations and objectives set by such agreements have to be implemented at the national or regional level. The Paris Agreement especially requires all countries to present their best efforts through nationally determined contributions (NDCs) that set out emission reduction contributions and adaptation plans and actions. These efforts have to be progressively strengthened in the coming years and include all societal actors within each country, including businesses. The Agreement commits countries to report regularly on their emissions and implementation efforts, and to communicate their NDCs every 5 years. These NDCs provide a clear direction for businesses and investors in the countries they operate in or plan to enter, and also highlight potential future opportunities. Thus, responses at the national level are crucial and essential for meeting the targets set by international agreements. As a relatively low-lying and densely populated island, Singapore is vulnerable to climate change. The measures taken by Singapore are an example of how countries can work towards addressing potential climate change impacts as well as fulfilling the targets and goals set by international agreements. 1. Singapore Green Plan 2012 Launched by the then Ministry of the Environment (now renamed the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment) in 2002, the Green Plan aimed to generate 60% of Singapore's energy needs using natural gas by 2021. (Natural gas is a cleaner form of energy compared to coal because it does not produce smoke.) Successes: As early as 2010, about 79% of Singapore's electricity was being generated from natural gas. This exceeded the Ministry's target ahead of schedule. Limitations: Natural gas requires complex treatment plants to process and pipelines to transport. These pipelines have high maintenance costs because they need to be laid underground and have to be checked regularly for leakage. 2. Singapore Green Plan 2030 The Singapore Green Plan 2030 ("the Green Plan") was launched on 10 February 2021. title: Changing Interactions Between Land and Water: The Hydrological Cycle
body: Rivers, Coasts and the Hydrological Cycle Rivers and coasts are a large part of the hydrological cycle, and through the power of water, the constant movement of water has the power and ability to influence the shape of the land, by carving and shaping the land on which it interacts. The Hydrological Cycle The hydrological cycle is a continuous circulation of the Earth's water. It is a system, and like all systems, its components include inputs, outputs and processes (transfers and storage). Category Term Definition Input Precipitation Fall of water from the atmosphere in the form of rain, snow, hail, etc. The intensity, duration, frequency and type of precipitation will all have an effect on the amount of water in the system. Output (Drainage) River channel Eventually the water from overland flow, stream flow, throughflow and groundwater flow collects in the channel, and the final release of water from a drainage basin or river system is known as its output. Typically, the main output of a drainage basin will be the river channel or the sea. Output (Drainage) Evaporation / Evapotranspiration Outputs also include the various ways moisture from the drainage basin escapes or is removed, including evaporation from the land and oceans as well as transpiration from vegetation (plants and trees). All together, this is known as evapotranspiration. Transfer (Processes) Interception Some of the falling rainwater is intercepted by trees and does not reach the ground. Transfer (Processes) Infiltration / Percolation Some of the falling rainwater infiltrates into the subsurface of the soil (infiltration is when water enters the soil layer from the surface). This water that infiltrates into the ground forms the groundwater flow and throughflow. The process of water infiltrating deeper into the groundwater is known as percolation (percolation is when water goes deeper down through the layers and reaches groundwater to be stored). Transfer (Processes) Surface runoff / Overland flow Water that does not infiltrate the soil or ground instead flows over the surface of the drainage basin, forming surface runoff or overland flow. Surface runoff typically occurs when the soil is too [saturated or impermeable to absorb further water – continued in the next section]. title: Water Transfer and Storage Processes (Throughflow, Groundwater Flow, Storage)
body: Throughflow The transfer and flow of water beneath the surface of the ground is known as throughflow, which is also the lateral movement of water through the layers of the soil towards the river channel and towards the groundwater. Throughflow is typically slower than surface runoff (overland flow) but quicker than groundwater flow. Groundwater Flow Groundwater flow is the slowest. When water eventually reaches the deep soil, the flow of water deep beneath the surface is known as groundwater flow. The groundwater flow eventually reaches the surface again and together with the surface runoff, they form tributaries and rivers. The water in the rivers in turn enters lakes, seas and oceans. Note: Overland flow (surface runoff) occurs when the ground is saturated, so rainwater cannot infiltrate the soil and instead flows over the surface of the drainage basin. This also occurs when the surface is urbanised, such as concrete and tarmac. Storage Storage refers to somewhere that water stays for a period of time (e.g. groundwater, surface water or in the ice caps). Storage type Description River channel / Drainage basin Water is stored in lakes or rivers. Groundwater When water is stored beneath the ground as water infiltrates the soil, water is stored as groundwater. Soil Through the processes of infiltration and percolation, water can also be stored in the soil or rock, depending on the porosity of the soil and the permeability of the rock. Vegetation (Interception) Water can also be temporarily stored during interception by vegetation, when water is stored on the stems of leaves and plants. What is throughflow? The transfer and lateral movement of water through the layers of soil beneath the surface, moving towards the river channel and towards groundwater. How does the speed of throughflow compare to surface runoff and groundwater flow? Throughflow is slower than surface runoff (overland flow) but quicker than groundwater flow. What is groundwater flow? The slowest flow of water, occurring deep beneath the surface after water eventually reaches the deep soil; it eventually resurfaces and joins surface runoff to form tributaries and rivers. When does overland flow (surface runoff) occur? When the ground is saturated so rainwater cannot infiltrate the soil, or when the surface is urbanised (e.g. concrete and tarmac), causing water to flow over the surface instead. title: The Drainage Basin and River System
body: Features of a drainage basin and the river system River drainage basins and river systems are a key part of the hydrological cycle and are also a system. They are local open systems with inputs, outputs and processes. Being an open system means that inputs and outputs can move to another system, and the input of one drainage basin could be the output of another. (For example, an input would refer to a tributary, and one tributary could actually be an input for multiple river systems.) Term Definition River A body of flowing water in a natural channel. It is part of the hydrological (water) cycle. River system A major stream or river with all its tributaries. Drainage basin The land area where precipitation collects and is drained by a river and its tributaries. Also known as the catchment area. Watershed The boundary of a drainage basin, between one drainage basin and another (separates the various drainage basins/river systems and is an imaginary line or boundary that is not visible). Source The place at which a river begins, usually found in mountainous areas or highlands. It is the beginning of the river, where water begins to flow down and form a river (e.g. could be at ice caps or glaciers where ice melts). At this point, the river is very small and its discharge is extremely small. Tributary A smaller stream, river or flow of water which joins a larger main river (tributaries add more water to the river, causing it to be wider). Tributaries are usually found nearer to the source of the river. Confluence The point at which a tributary joins the main river, and the point where two rivers meet. Distributary A channel diverging from the main river and flowing into the sea or a lake (e.g. when a river enters a delta, it branches from the main river into channels known as distributaries). Distributaries are usually found at the lower course, closer to the end of the river, where the water distributes and branches out. River mouth The place where a river ends its flow — the end point where the river joins and meets the sea/ocean/lake, and the river discharge goes into the sea/ocean/lake. River course The path taken by a river from its source to its mouth. Also known as the long profile of the river course. It can be split into three sections: the upper course (near the source, usually in the highlands), the middle course (where the river begins to meander more), and the lower course (close to the mouth). Different processes occur at each course. Meanders Tu

title: Drainage Patterns
body: Drainage patterns refer to the patterns formed by the streams, rivers, and lakes in a particular drainage basin. They are determined by the topography (shape) of the land, geology of the land (hard or soft rocks), and the gradient (steepness) of the land. Drainage patterns also refer to spatial relationships among streams or rivers, and these patterns are created by stream erosion over time that reveals characteristics of the kind of rocks and geologic structures in a landscape region drained by streams. There are four main types of drainage patterns: Parallel : A drainage pattern commonly found on newly uplifted land, where rivers and tributaries flow downhill more or less parallel to each other. Dendritic : A tree-like drainage pattern with tributaries converging on the main river channel. Common in areas dominated by one rock type. Radial : Commonly found in areas dominated by dome-shaped mountains or volcanic cones. Rivers flow outwards from a central point like the spokes in a wheel. Trellis/Irregular : A drainage pattern that develops in areas dominated by alternating harder, more resistant rocks and softer, less resistant rock. What factors determine drainage patterns? The topography (shape) of the land, the geology of the land (hard or soft rocks), and the gradient (steepness) of the land. What do drainage patterns reveal? Spatial relationships among streams/rivers created by stream erosion over time, revealing characteristics of rocks and geologic structures in the drained landscape. What is a parallel drainage pattern? A pattern commonly found on newly uplifted land, where rivers and tributaries flow downhill more or less parallel to each other. What is a dendritic drainage pattern? A tree-like drainage pattern with tributaries converging on the main river channel, common in areas dominated by one rock type. What is a radial drainage pattern? A pattern commonly found in areas dominated by dome-shaped mountains or volcanic cones, where rivers flow outward from a central point like spokes in a wheel. What is a trellis/irregular drainage pattern? A pattern that develops in areas dominated by alternating harder, more resistant rocks and softer, less resistant rock. Name the four main types of drainage patterns. Parallel, dendritic, radial, and trellis/irregular. Which drainage pattern is associated with volcanic cones? Radial drainage pattern. Which drainage pattern is tree-like, with tributaries converging on a main river channel? A radial drainage

title: River Processes: Energy, Velocity and Volume
body: Overview Along the river, various processes take place. There are three main courses of the river: the upper course, the middle course and the lower course. At these various courses, all the various processes take place at one time, though at different courses of the river some processes may be more prominent than others. These processes include erosion, transportation and deposition, and they are all closely related. They also have the ability to produce several landforms or features, and are dependent on the energy of the river. River Energy All flowing rivers have energy. Much of the energy is used to overcome friction with the river bed and sides as the river flows along. The rest of the energy is used to erode and transport materials. When a river runs out of energy, deposition takes place. A river's energy is determined by two factors: the speed of flow (velocity) and the volume of the river (river volume). The most powerful rivers are those with a high volume of flow as well as a high speed of flow. River Velocity River velocity, otherwise known as the speed of the river, refers to the speed of the flow of water in the river, or how fast the discharge and flow of water in the river is. Factors affecting river velocity 1. Gradient of channel — Rivers flow downhill from a high altitude due to gravity. The speed at which it does so depends on the steepness of the channel (the gradient). If the gradient is steep, the river will flow quickly; if the gradient is gentle, the river will tend to flow more slowly. At the highest point of the river, near the source, there is a steeper slope and the gravitational pull is stronger, resulting in higher velocity and faster flow (this explains why erosion is more dominant at the upper course). At the lowest point of the river, near the delta, there is a gentler slope and weaker gravitational pull, resulting in lower velocity and slower flow (this explains why erosion is less dominant at the lower course). Thinking point: Why is the average speed of the river in the mountains about the same as in the plains, despite the steep gradient? The high speed generated by the steep gradient at the upper course is hampered by the large amount of friction generated by large boulders and rocks there. At the lower course, there are fewer large boulders and rocks, but despite the lack of obstruction, the speed is hampered by the gentle gradient. 2. Roughness of channel — A river flowing within a smooth channel tends to flow faste

title: River Erosion Processes
body: There are four main erosional processes of a river. Erosion is the wearing and destruction of land caused by the power of water. 1. Abrasion (Corrasion) The process whereby the river uses its load, such as rock fragments, to grind, rub and scrape against the sides and bed of the channel, dislodging materials and carrying them away. This process widens the channel through lateral erosion (sideward erosion), and wears down the channel's walls and bed like sandpapering, deepening it through vertical erosion (downward erosion). Most effective during floods when huge rock fragments grind against the river bed, forming potholes and deepening existing plunge pools. 2. Hydraulic Action The process whereby the force and pressure of fast-flowing river water surges and forces air and water into lines of weakness of the river channel, such as joints and cracks. Continuous action enlarges the cracks and weakens the rock; its sheer force breaks and loosens materials and sweeps them away. A good example of hydraulic action is the formation of a plunge pool at the foot of a waterfall. 3. Attrition The process whereby rock fragments being transported downstream constantly grind, smash and collide against one another. As a result, large rock fragments become smaller, smoother and more rounded. The rounded shape of a river's load (e.g. pebbles) is evidence of attrition. Rock fragments carried by the water smash into each other, leading to fragments breaking into even smaller pieces. 4. Solution (Corrosion) The process whereby the solvent action of the water dissolves soluble minerals and reacts chemically with minerals in rocks, forming a solution which is carried away. For example, calcium carbonate in limestone regions is dissolved and carried away in solution (common in limestone areas). What is abrasion (corrasion)? The process whereby the river uses its load to grind, rub and scrape against the sides and bed of the channel, dislodging and carrying away materials, widening and deepening the channel. What is hydraulic action? The process whereby the force and pressure of fast-flowing water surges and forces air and water into cracks and joints, weakening and breaking rock which is then swept away. What is attrition? The process whereby transported rock fragments grind, smash and collide against one another, becoming smaller, smoother and more rounded. What is solution (corrosion)? title: River Transportation Processes
body: There are four main types of river transportation. Transportation is the downstream movement of eroded materials (the river's load) from one place to another. The greater the energy the river has, the more load it can carry. 1. Traction The process by which the largest and heaviest rock fragments (e.g. bigger pebbles and boulders) are transported downstream. The material (bed load) is moved by rolling and gliding along the river bed. They move only if there is adequate velocity; some are so heavy they can only be rolled along during heavy flooding. Large boulders are too heavy to be lifted by the water, so they roll and slide along the river bed. 2. Saltation The process by which smaller and lighter particles, like coarse sand and small rock fragments (e.g. gravel, pebbles, sand), are transported downstream. The material is moved by the water through hopping and bouncing along in a series of jumps along the river bed. Larger rock particles are too heavy to be suspended in the water all the time, so the river can pick them up and drop them repeatedly, causing them to bounce or hop along the river bed. 3. Suspension The process by which fine particles like silt and clay are held up in suspension and carried along in the upper levels of water. The suspension load forms the largest part of the river's load. The muddy appearance of rivers during a flood or heavy rain is due to a large suspended load. Suspended materials are fine particles kept from settling on the river bed due to turbulent flow, so they float in the river, making the water look cloudy downstream. 4. Solution The process by which soluble minerals in rocks, such as calcium and sodium, are dissolved in the river and transported downstream. Very clear water may in fact be carrying a large load of materials in solution, since the dissolved load may be invisible. Only if the water evaporates does the material become visible, as crystals begin to form. Solution occurs even when the speed and volume of the river are low. Soluble rocks like limestone are dissolved in water and carried downstream. What is traction? The transportation of the largest and heaviest rock fragments (e.g. boulders) by rolling and gliding along the river bed. What is saltation? The transportation of smaller, lighter particles (e.g. gravel, pebbles, sand) by hopping and bouncing along the river bed in a series of jumps. What is suspension? title: River Deposition and Characteristics of the Three Courses
body: Deposition Eroded material of various sizes is carried by the running water in the river. Deposition may take place at any point along a river's course. A river begins to drop its load when the energy of the river decreases, and the river no longer has enough energy to transport its load, so it begins to deposit. This can be due to a decrease in volume and speed (velocity) of the river. The size of the load deposited by the river is not the same throughout the course of the river. Generally, the river load is sorted as it is transported and deposited downstream — a river drops heavier and coarser materials first and finer materials last (e.g. upper course: more boulders and larger rocks; middle course: more stones and pebbles; lower course: more mud and silt). Characteristics of the three courses of a typical river Characteristic Upper Course Middle Course Lower Course Gradient Steep Gentle Very gentle to flat Velocity of flow Low — energy is consumed during vertical erosion and overcoming friction caused by rugged river beds Moderate — energy is consumed during lateral erosion and transportation of load High — large water volume and smooth river bed may cause less friction Volume of flow Small — the number of tributaries is small; fewer tributaries join the main river; small size of channel Moderate — the number of tributaries is moderate; more tributaries join the main river; moderate size of channel Greatest — the number of tributaries is largest as the river receives water from the upper and middle courses; wide channel Amount of river load Small Moderate Greatest Key processes Mainly erosional processes Erosional and depositional processes Mainly depositional processes Type of transportation Mainly traction and saltation Mainly saltation and suspension Mainly suspension and solution Amount of deposition Little deposition (more boulders and larger rocks) Some deposition (more stones and pebbles) Large amount of deposition (more mud and silt) When does a river begin to deposit its load? When the energy of the river decreases and it no longer has enough energy to transport its load, often due to decreased volume and velocity. How is a river's load sorted as it is deposited downstream? Heavier and coarser materials are dropped first, and finer materials are deposited last. What type of load characterises the upper course? title: River Landforms: Floodplains, Levees and Deltas
body: Floodplains A floodplain is a wide and gently sloping plain of alluvium (a deposit of clay, silt, and sand left by flowing flood water in a river valley or delta, typically producing fertile soil). Formation of floodplains In the lower course, the gradient is gentle and flat. The river carries large quantities of sediments brought down from the upper and middle courses. Since flooding is common in the lower course due to large quantities of sediments and the largest volume of water from tributaries, flood water which overflows the river banks when the river level rises during floods often carries the sediments/load to the adjacent lands. When the flood water subsides, these sediments are deposited, and over time, with repeated flooding, there is a build-up of extensive layers of alluvium (layers of sediment like silt, sand and clay deposited), resulting in a floodplain. On floodplains, features such as levees, ox-bow lakes and meandering rivers are also commonly found. Examples of floodplains: Ganges Plain (India), North China Plain (China), Chao Phraya Plain (Thailand) and Mississippi Plain (USA). Levees Levees are raised embankments built up along the banks of the river, rising above the level of the surrounding floodplain. Formation of levees Levees occur in the lower course of a river, where the valley floor is gentle and flat. When the river floods, the water level rises and overflows its banks, causing the flood water carrying sediments/river's load to flow over to the adjacent lands/floodplain. As the flood water carries sediments/river's load over the adjacent lands/floodplains, the lighter, smaller and finer materials like silt are spread further away to build up a floodplain, while the heavier, larger and coarser materials are deposited close to the banks, forming ridges which are higher than the surrounding plain, known as levees. Deltas A delta is a flat depositional plain formed at the mouth of the river. It is a continuation of the river's floodplain. Formation of deltas When a river is about to enter a body of quiet water such as a lake or a sea, the river's energy decreases as a result of the decrease in volume and speed of the river (due to the generally flat gradient at the lower course near the river's mouth, as well as the many distributaries which direct water away from the main channel and decrease the volume of flow). When this occurs, the river begins to deposit its load. Larger, heavier and coarser sediments like sand and gravel ar

title: Storm Hydrograph
body: A hydrograph is a graph that shows the variation in river discharge at a particular point in a river over a certain period of time. It is also used to show how long a river takes to flood. Term Definition Baseflow Portion of the streamflow that is sustained between precipitation events. Originates from groundwater supply and stormflow. Before the storm, the water in the river comes from the base flow. Baseflow responds slower to the storm (depends on the rate of infiltration and percolation): groundwater flow is slowly released into the channel, continually maintaining river flow during periods of low precipitation. Baseflow is more significant over a longer period of time than an individual storm. Stormflow — Rising Limb Consists of the rising limb and the falling limb. The steeply rising limb represents the increasing rise in river discharge due to the initial surface runoff and throughflow of the storm eventually reaching the river — this explains the concave shape of the rising limb, as water reaches the channel more quickly (when the storm reaches its peak). When the storm first starts, the river water does not rise immediately because some rain enters the river directly while much of it falls elsewhere in the drainage basin. Stormflow — Falling/Recession Limb Represents the decreasing river discharge as the storm subsides. The falling limb is not as steep as the rising limb (also known as the recession limb) because water does not decrease rapidly, due to throughflow still flowing into the river. When the storm subsides and rain has ended, throughflow is released relatively slowly into the channel and all water brought by the storm drains away; eventually, the river's water is once again maintained by the baseflow. The steeper the rising limb, the faster the response to rainfall. Peak Flow Represents and shows the highest discharge. Occurs after the most intense rainfall has ceased. A storm hydrograph may have more than one peak if there are several consecutive heavy downpours. Lag time The time difference between the heaviest rainfall in the storm and the peak of the river discharge. Its length varies from one river basin to another and from one storm to another. A short lag time means water has got into the river quickly and it is more likely to flood. Bankfull discharge The maximum discharge that a particular river channel is capable of carrying without flooding. Any increase above the bankfull discharge will cause flooding. title: Coasts: Definition of Terms and Factors Affecting Coastal Environments
body: Coasts — Definition of terms Term Description Offshore Refers to the area off the coasts, off the beach, away from shore, typically referring to the sea or the ocean. This is the area of deeper water beyond the point at which waves begin to break (foamy waters; waves breaking). Nearshore Refers to the area of shallow water that extends seaward beyond the low tide mark, and the zone in which waves affect the seabed as friction between the shallow seabed and waves distorts the wave sufficiently to cause it to break (breaker zone). Foreshore Refers to the area closest to the shore, bounded between the high tide shoreline mark and low tide shoreline mark. Also known as the inter-tidal or surf zone. Backshore Refers to the upper part, lying behind the beach, furthest away from the sea and the coastline. Often dominated by berms (little humps) and without much vegetation. This is the area above the high tide mark, and part of the shore which is dry under normal conditions, affected by wave action only during major storm events (tsunami, typhoon, hurricane etc.). Beach A narrow, gently sloping strip of land that lies along the edge of an ocean, lake, or river — the zone of unconsolidated materials such as sand, pebbles, rocks, and seashell fragments that extend from the low water line to the line of permanent vegetation (the effective limit of storm events). Factors affecting coastal environments Waves Tides and Sea Level Changes Currents — Large-scale, continuous movements of water in seas and oceans. Responsible for distributing sediments and regulating temperatures. Carry large amounts of energy. Geology — The arrangement and composition of rock found in an area affect the rate of change of environment (arrangement/layering, composition). Types of ecosystem — Interaction of communities of plants and animals and the environment. Example: mangroves — the deep roots of mangroves hold on to the soil and prevent it from eroding away. Human Activities — A natural coastline would look different from one where the coastline has been straightened artificially. When describing coasts or coastal features, always pay attention to four things: 1) slope/gradient (steep, gentle), 2) profile (sandy, rocky), 3) types of material (fine sediment, large sediment), 4) types of beach (wide, narrow). title: Waves: Definitions, Factors and Types
body: As a wave approaches a shore, its shape changes. Towards the land, the orbital motion of water particles in the waves encounters friction with the shallow seabed, making the waves slow down. As the wave speed decreases, it is pushed by the wave behind it. This causes the wavelength to decrease and wave height to increase. The wave crest is thrown forward as the wave breaks, trapping air and developing a white turbulent water mass. Term Description Wave A disturbance on the surface of the sea or ocean, in the form of a moving ridge or swell. As wind blows over the surface of the sea, it causes friction, making the water surface rise and fall — this rising and falling forms the waves. Hence waves are formed when wind blows across the surface of the sea. Crest The highest part of a wave. Trough The lowest part of a wave. Wave height Vertical distance between the crest and the trough. Wave length Distance between two consecutive crests or two consecutive troughs. Factors affecting wave energy The size and energy of waves depend on three factors: Fetch of the wave — the distance a wave travels / how far the wind has travelled / the expanse of water surface over which the wind is blowing. Speed of the wind blowing over the water surface (strength of the wind). Duration of the wind — how long the wind has been blowing for. The greater the speed of the wind, the longer the duration, and the longer the fetch, the larger and more powerful the waves. Longer fetch, stronger wind, and longer duration all lead to higher wave energy. Types of waves Waves are categorised as either constructive waves or destructive waves. Feature Constructive Waves Destructive Waves General effect Build beach; deposit material Take away, destroy, erode, remove sediments from the beach Wave length Long wavelength and low wave height, resulting in small, low, gentle waves Short wavelength with high and steep wave height Wave height Low wave height in proportion to wavelength High wave height in proportion to wavelength Breakers Spilling breakers (spilling over when breaking) Plunging and surging breakers that break downwards with great force Swash and Backwash Weak backwash, strong swash — the strong swash brings more sediment onto the beach, and weak backwash means what is brought up is not taken back into the ocean Strong backwash, weak swash — the weak swash brings less sediment onto the beach, and strong backwash takes it back into the ocean Wave energy Low wave energy, due to low gradie

title: Wave Erosion, Transportation and Deposition
body: Wave Erosion Waves can erode via four different coastal erosion processes: Hydraulic action: The weight of waves crashing repeatedly against the coast can weaken and loosen rocks so that ultimately they break off. Water also surges into cracks, joints and faults in rocks and compresses the air inside tightly. The compressed air exerts pressure on these lines of weakness. When the water retreats, there is a release of pressure and the trapped air expands. This action, repeated many times, widens and weakens these lines of weakness, ultimately breaking the rocks up. Abrasion / Corrasion: As waves break, they carry rock fragments such as cobbles, pebbles and gravel. When these fragments are hurled against the coast, they act like chiselling tools, knocking and scraping against coastal cliffs, eventually cutting up, weakening and breaking the rocks forming the coast. Over time, the impact from abrasion is powerful enough to undercut a cliff. Attrition: When rock particles carried by waves are thrown, rubbed or hit against one another, they gradually break down into smaller, smoother and more rounded pieces over time. Solution / Corrosion: Soluble minerals in coastal rocks are dissolved in and removed by seawater. For example, calcium carbonate in limestone rocks reacts chemically and is easily eroded by carbonic acid in seawater, changing into soluble calcium hydrogen carbonate. When solution of minerals occurs, the rocks are weakened and eventually disintegrate. Factors affecting rate of marine erosion Wave size — The bigger the waves, the more energy they have to erode the coast. The longer the fetch, the larger and more powerful the waves. Larger waves have a more powerful backwash than smaller waves, plunging over when breaking and eroding material from the coast faster. Rock composition and structure — Where there are resistant and less resistant rocks at the coast, the less resistant rocks (such as sand and clay) will be eroded faster than resistant rocks (such as limestone). The structure of rocks also affects the rate of marine erosion — if rocks have lines of weakness such as joints and bedding planes, they will be attacked more easily by waves. Position of coast — If the coast is exposed to strong prevailing onshore winds, it will be susceptible to erosion. A sheltered coast, such as one enclosing a bay between two headlands, is subject to more deposition than erosion. Climate — When there are strong prevailing onshore winds, marine erosion intensifi

title: Coastal Features: Headlands and Bays
body: Coastal features can be broadly divided into erosional and depositional features: Erosional features Depositional features Headlands and bays; Wave-cut platforms; Sea cliffs; Sea caves, arches, stacks and stumps; Blowholes Beaches; Spits; Bars; Tombolos; Mudflats Headlands and Bays The coast is made of alternating bands of resistant rocks (e.g. limestone and granite) and less resistant rocks (e.g. sand, chalk and clay) with different resistance to erosion. Thus, headlands and bays are most likely to develop in these areas. When waves crash against the rocks, the continual erosion of rocks of different resistance occurs — it is more difficult for waves to erode rocks that are more resistant to erosion, so the wave will erode away rocks that are less resistant, causing the coast to be eroded unevenly. This is known as differential erosion, caused by hydraulic action and abrasion, which is more effective on less resistant rocks. Over time, with repeated and continuous erosion, the less resistant rock is eroded much more than the more resistant rock, causing the area of more resistant rock to protrude out, forming headlands, while the area of less resistant rock caves in, forming wide indented curves known as bays. This results in an uneven coastline, as wave action on rocks of different resistance causes the coast to be eroded unevenly, thus changing the slope of the coast. Example of an area of headlands and bays resulting from differential erosion: the Dorset Coast, England. Wave refraction (after the formation of headlands and bays) Eventually, wave refraction will straighten the coast, and the coast will return to a straight coastline, as the coast is dynamic. Wave refraction is defined as the process by which waves change direction as they approach the coast. What is differential erosion? The uneven erosion of a coast due to rocks of different resistance, caused mainly by hydraulic action and abrasion, which is more effective on less resistant rocks. title: Wave Refraction: Headlands and Bays
body: Wave Refraction: Headlands and Bays Coastlines with protruding headlands and inward-curving bays cause wave refraction: the headlands that protrude out act as an obstruction to the waves and disrupt the parallel pattern of the incoming waves, causing the waves to bend. The obstruction posed by the headlands is the shallow water that the waves reach first, which causes the waves to slow down. Since one part of the wave is slowed down before the other part, the wave front becomes curved. This is called wave refraction. (Applies to sheltered coasts — a peninsula slows waves and protects bays or sheltered coasts, versus straight coasts, which have a long fetch and stronger erosion.) When waves converge on the headlands, the wave energy is also more concentrated, giving rise to increased wave height and greater erosive energy at the headlands, forming notches, caves, wave-cut platforms and many other coastal landforms. When the waves then go past the headlands and approach the bays, they approach the bay in a curved pattern, and as they diverge, the wave energy is also distributed and spread out, resulting in decreased wave height and reduced erosive energy, indicating more deposition, which often leads to the formation of beaches at the bay area. With more erosion occurring at the headlands and more deposition occurring at the bay area, this eventually shortens the headlands and enlarges the bay. Over time, as the process of erosion and deposition repeatedly occurs, more erosion happens at the headlands due to the waves converging (resulting in higher wave energy), and more deposition happens at the bay area due to the waves dissipating (resulting in lower wave energy). This causes the headlands to protrude out less and the bay to not curve inwards as much. Eventually, wave refraction ultimately results in the straightening of the coastline as the bay area becomes broader and bigger due to more deposition, and the headlands get shorter. What causes wave refraction at coastlines with headlands and bays? Headlands protrude out and act as an obstruction to waves, disrupting the parallel wave pattern and causing the waves to bend. Why do waves slow down first at headlands? Headlands are surrounded by shallow water, which the waves reach first, causing that part of the wave to slow down before the rest, curving the wave front. title: Wave-Cut Platform (Caves and Notches)
body: Wave-Cut Platform (+ Caves and Notches) When destructive waves crash against the rock face between its high and low tide, the base of the cliff is eroded through hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution, concentrated at the cracks and lines of weaknesses at the base. As a result, the base of the cliff will gradually erode, and over time, with the repetition of this process enlarging the crack and weakening the base, a notch (or wave-cut notch) is formed. As erosion proceeds over a longer period of time, as the waves continually crash against the rock face between its high and low tide, the wave-cut notch is deeply undercut and enlarged to form an overhang — the piece of rock above the notch — and subsequently a cave. Over time, when further erosion causes the notch to become deeper and the overhang along with the cave to be larger, due to gravity, the roof of the cave loses support, it collapses, and a cliff is formed. Further undercutting at the base of the cliff forms an overhanging portion which eventually collapses as well. As the steep cliff retreats landwards, a gently sloping rocky platform between the base of the cliff and low tide level is formed, called a wave-cut platform. Example: A wave-cut platform is found at Flamborough Head in Yorkshire, England. Over time, an extended wave-cut platform can form as cliff profiles vary greatly, depending on: 1) rate of coastal erosion (cliff retreat), 2) strength of the rock, 3) presence of joints and bedding planes. The wave-cut platform is covered with rock fragments from the receding cliff. Rocks being carried forward and backward by breakers smoothen the wave-cut platform by abrasion. As the wave-cut platform lengthens, wave attack at the base of the cliff is reduced. Weathering and mass wasting (downhill movement of loosened and broken materials owing to gravity) become more important than marine erosion. What processes erode the base of a cliff at high and low tide? Hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution, concentrated at cracks and lines of weakness. What is a notch (wave-cut notch)? A gradually eroded indentation at the base of a cliff formed as cracks are enlarged and weakened over time. How does a cave form from a notch? Continued erosion deeply undercuts and enlarges the notch, forming an overhang and then a cave. Why does a cliff eventually collapse? Further erosion deepens the notch and enlarges the overhang/cave until the roof loses support due to gravity and collapses. Wh

title: River and Coastal Protection Measures: Overview
body: River and Coastal Protection Measures As a result of erosion and the effects of processes along the river and the coast, there is a need for river and/or coastal protection measures. These measures have their pros and cons and can be classified into two categories: soft and hard engineering measures. Hard engineering measures are defined as short term, more expensive, less sustainable measures with a greater impact on the river landscape and surrounding environment. They require more extensive alterations to the river to try to stop flooding. Soft engineering measures are defined as long term, less expensive, more sustainable and ecologically sensitive measures with a low impact on the environment, aiming to protect the coasts from physical processes while still allowing them to take place. They attempt to manage the flood rather than prevent it. Why are river and coastal protection measures needed? As a result of erosion and the effects of processes along rivers and coasts, protection is needed to manage impacts. Into what two categories can protection measures be classified? Soft engineering measures and hard engineering measures. What defines hard engineering measures? Short term, more expensive, less sustainable measures with a greater impact on the landscape and environment, requiring extensive alterations. What defines soft engineering measures? Long term, less expensive, more sustainable and ecologically sensitive measures with low environmental impact. Do soft engineering measures stop physical processes from occurring? No, they aim to protect the coasts while still allowing physical processes to take place. What is the aim of soft engineering measures regarding flooding? They attempt to manage the flood rather than prevent it. What is the aim of hard engineering measures regarding flooding? They try to stop flooding through extensive alterations to the river/coast. Which type of measure generally has a lower cost? Soft engineering measures. Which type of measure is generally less sustainable? Hard engineering measures.
