title: Soft Coastal Protection Measures
body: Soft Coastal Protection Measures 1. Beach Nourishment Beach nourishment is a soft engineering measure which builds up the beach by replenishing beach material, particularly at the base of a structure, to provide a "natural" solution to absorbing wave energy. The process involves continually replacing lost beach material (like sand lost by coastal erosion or longshore drift) from a natural store either offshore (beach rebuilding) or from downshore along a stretch of longshore drift (beach recycling). Examples: Vale do Lobo Beach, Portugal; Cancún, Mexico; Gold Coast, Australia. Advantages Disadvantages Does not disrupt the beach's physical appearance (blends in with existing beach); aesthetically better solution (natural looking — difficult to tell that management is taking place) Beach does not shrink in size, allowing tourists to continue to use the beach (larger beaches appeal to tourists) Provides most "natural" solution Sand may erode Can be expensive to keep transporting large amounts of sand (sediment will be moved by longshore drift so it will need frequent replenishment unless other defences are used) and has to be repeated periodically (may accumulate high costs over time) Beach is inaccessible during nourishment 2. Sand Dune Stabilisation Sand dunes are a natural feature and are ridges of sand along the coast. Sand dune stabilisation involves the use of vegetation, like the growth of spinifex and marram grass, or sand fencing to trap sand and stabilise the sand dune, preventing the dunes from shifting along the coast and preventing erosion of sand dunes. Examples: Bei Men Coast; Bondi Beach, Australia; Dune de Pyla, Southwestern Coast of France; Francois Peron Natural Park, Australia. Advantages Disadvantages Creates new habitats for wildlife Creates opportunities for nature studies Blends in with the natural surrounding, maintaining a natural looking coastline Prevents flooding of inland areas and the coast Relatively cheap Sand dunes protect coastal deposition and human features like houses and roads against coastal erosion Reduces area of the beach accessible to the public (may take away tourism from the beach) Can be damaged by storm waves Sand dunes can migrate landwards and destroy property and roads Vegetation on dunes can be destroyed by human activities — hiking, recreational activities 3. title: Hard Coastal Protection Measures
body: Hard Coastal Protection Measures 1. Seawall A seawall is a concrete wall, curved on the seaward side to deflect the power of the waves. They block the waves and reflect the energy back into the sea, preventing flooding of the land and structures behind it, and protecting areas of human habitation, conservation, and tourism or leisure activities from wave or tidal action. Examples: Stanley Park, Vancouver; Ventnor on the Isle of Wight, England; Urangan, Queensland; Paravur near Kollam City in India; Galveston Island, Texas; Omaha Beach, New Zealand. Advantages Disadvantages Protects the base of cliffs and protects beaches and coasts from erosion Prevents coastal flooding Reduces the energy and impact of the waves greatly and is very effective in protecting the coast from erosion Sea walls reflect rather than absorb wave energy, meaning it is one of the most effective means of preventing erosion Most expensive to build and maintain (up to 2.5 billion pounds/km), average lifespan of only 75 years before they must be replaced Unattractive, affecting the landscape of the coast, and may also cause ecological damage as it intrudes into the coast Curved sea walls merely reflect the energy of the waves back to the sea and do not necessarily reduce the energy of the waves in all cases Deflected waves often scour the base, undermining the wall (may eventually collapse) 2. Revetments Revetments are wooden or steel structures which break the force of the waves and trap beach material behind them. They prevent existing beaches from getting washed away and may contribute to beach building, by reducing wave action at the boundary between the sea and land. Examples: Dynamic revetment at Cape Lookout State Park, Oregon; Colhugh Beach, Llantwit Major, Wales; Norfolk, UK. Advantages Disadvantages Much cheaper than a sea wall and most hard engineering measures, and effective for many years Absorbs wave energy through the slats Can be made permeable or impermeable, resulting in increased effectiveness of dissipating the force of waves Rather effective at breaking the force of the waves Expensive (approximately 1000 pounds per metre) and may simply displace erosion to other non-protected, downdrift areas Less durable than a sea wall, hence may need regular maintenance many times, and is not effective in stormy conditions; does not give total protection to the base of the cliff Requires large space Environmentally ugly, unattractive 3. title: Soft River Protection Measures
body: Soft River Protection Measures 1. Planting Vegetation Increasing the number of trees planted around the river valley, like replanting forests or planting new forests, allows for more infiltration and interception, reducing surface runoff and lowering the risks of floods. Examples: Boscastle, Cornwall, UK; Afon Tywi, Carmarthenshire; Green Belt Movement (Kenya). Advantages Disadvantages Economic benefits (forestry) Provides new ecosystems, benefits environment Relatively low cost option, which enhances environmental quality of the drainage basin Less water gets to the river, reducing the discharge The ecosystem of the area is protected Very effective method for reducing discharge, while keeping the environment protected Cannot fully prevent flooding, only reduces the likelihood Reduces farmland Difficult to plant forests in urban areas Takes time for the flood prevention to be successful 2. Sustainable Drainage Filter strips and permeable paving allow for more infiltration into the ground. Sustainable drainage results in a lower amount of water that would directly flow into the river channel, as there is more throughflow and groundwater flow, which is much slower compared to surface runoff (which carries only a low amount of water). However, it has disadvantages such as the high cost of the measure, as engineers have to factor in creating impermeable pathways to increase surface runoff. Older buildings might also not be able to have this function. Example: UK Flood Act of 2010. 3. Washlands Washlands involve setting aside areas of land of lower importance where water can wash during a flood, to be flooded when river levels get too high, usually at the lower course of the river. Flood gates can let water flood this area easily, diverting it away from more densely populated and more important areas. Examples: Yangtze River, China, Jingjiang Basin; The Ouse Washes of Cambridgeshire. Advantages Disadvantages Easy to construct; only requires sluice gates Land is often available for use most of the time as an empty lot and can be used for other purposes (farming, residential); water is only allowed in when major floods are imminent Easily manages and controls floods with less need to construct hard engineering Cheap and rather effective May become silted due to farming, causing them to become unsuitable for use (if not maintained properly) People living in washlands have to be evacuated during major floods Hard to find such an available place 4. title: Hard River Protection Measures
body: Hard River Protection Measures 1. Flood Barriers Flood barriers act as gates in the river that can be activated to prevent a large surge in river discharge during a storm, preventing floods from occurring. They can be used to raise the height of the river bank to a level where the river will not burst its banks. Examples: Maeslant Barrier in the Netherlands; River Thames in London; Delta Works in the Netherlands; St. Petersburg Dam in Finland; glass barriers in use in Keswick, Cumbria. Advantages Disadvantages Can be activated only when necessary, meaning it can be temporary and non-obstructive most of the time Can be a permanent feature or a feature incorporated into the design of an area (does not look unnatural or unattractive, does not largely affect the appearance of the landscape) Expensive with high cost and requires advanced technology Consumes/requires large space May have an environmental impact on river wildlife 2. Dredging As deposition occurs, silt builds up on the river bed over time. During heavy rain, due to this accumulation of silt, river discharge spills over its banks and floods the surrounding area. Using excavators or pumps to remove this silt allows for larger river capacity and faster flow downstream, reducing the risk of floods. Dredging the bottom of the river for sediment means the river is deeper and can hold more water. Examples: River Tone and Parrett in Somerset, UK; Netherlands. Advantages Disadvantages River can hold more water, reducing flood risk in the built-up area Allows river to be used as a shipping route Easy method to reduce flooding in built-up areas Has to be done frequently to ensure effectiveness (expensive and may accumulate high costs over time) Increases river velocity, which may lead to flooding at the lower course Can change the ecosystem in the river 3. Levees/Embankments Levees are concrete or wooden walls that hold back the river from the banks. They raise the banks of a river and prevent water from spilling over, containing the discharge during a storm, thus reducing the risk of flooding. Examples: Yangtze River in Hubei, China; Moskva River in Moscow; Delta Works in the Netherlands. Advantages Disadvantages Allows for more flood water to be contained within the river, reducing flood risk in the built-up area Cheaper as it is only a one-time construction/one-off cost Lower environmental impact; may 'blend in' to the environmental landscape; doesn't destroy animal habitats More water can pass through Ba

title: Evaluation of Hard and Soft Engineering Measures
body: Evaluation Both hard and soft engineering measures are equally important. However, their importance and effectiveness vary and can be looked at from different concepts. Place — Different places have different coastlines and rivers, shaped differently, some with steeper gradients and some with gentler gradients, with different kinds of landscapes, landforms and uses. This influences the ability for engineering measures to be implemented, considering their different disadvantages. For example, why does Hong Kong implement tetrapods at their coast whereas Singapore uses breakwaters? This could be due to the fact that tetrapods are too massive and large for Singapore's coastlines and pose a risk to beach goers. Power and Place — All these measures cost money, and just like with other measures (e.g. earthquake measures), the ability to implement such measures and the choice of measures ultimately depend on the government and the resources they have. For less economically developed countries, it may be harder to implement hard measures due to a lack of resources, whereas more economically developed countries, with expertise, technology and financial resources, find it much easier. This is similar to mitigation and adaptation: mitigation is like hard engineering measures, while adaptation is like soft engineering measures. Just as less economically developed countries are unable to mitigate and have to adapt, they are unable to implement hard engineering measures and have to adopt soft ones instead. Ultimately, it would be ideal for hard engineering measures to be implemented first, and then for soft engineering measures to be implemented to sustain it in the long run, since both are equally important. It is also important to weigh both of them in different circumstances alongside their limitations. Hard engineering measures are more drastic and have a larger impact, though they are hard to implement, facing limitations such as cost, unsightliness and the risks they pose. title: Globalisation and Development
body: Global Forces of Change (Globalisation) Globalisation and Development At a glance, globalisation and development may largely seem like the same thing. However, there are vast differences between the two. For example, globalisation cannot occur within a single country and requires the interdependence of multiple countries, in contrast to development, which can occur within a single country. Development refers to the process by which a country sees an improvement in their quality of life and standard of living, associated with increased living costs and political, social and economic reforms within a country. Globalisation instead refers to: the growing interaction, interconnectivity and interdependence of countries worldwide, among the people, companies, and governments the global integration of economies, politics, products, ideas and other aspects of culture through the: aid of more rapid and widespread diffusion of information technology driving force of increasing volume and variety of cross-border transactions in goods and services, and international capital flows (trade and investments) which has led to: the free movement of people companies becoming multinational an increase in international trade Can globalisation occur within a single country? No, globalisation requires the interdependence of multiple countries, unlike development. What is development? The process by which a country sees an improvement in quality of life and standard of living, associated with increased living costs and political, social and economic reforms. What is globalisation? The growing interaction, interconnectivity and interdependence of countries worldwide among people, companies and governments, and the global integration of economies, politics, products, ideas and culture. What technological factor aids globalisation's diffusion of information? More rapid and widespread diffusion of information technology. What economic driving force is behind globalisation? Increasing volume and variety of cross-border transactions in goods and services, and international capital flows (trade and investments). What are three outcomes globalisation has led to? title: Driving Forces and Aspects of Globalisation and Development
body: Driving Forces and Aspects of Globalisation The aspects of globalisation are often seen as the driving forces of globalisation too, and vice versa. For example, the rapid and widespread diffusion of information technology has driven globalisation by allowing for increase in and ease of cross-border communications, but is also an aspect of globalisation, as a globalised country often has a strong technological network to connect itself to other countries. However, this is not so for development — besides the key differences in the definitions of globalisation and development, there are also key differences in what the two terms entail, in their aspects and driving forces. Aspects of Development A developed country contains aspects such as: Quality education (e.g. high literacy rate) Good and affordable housing (e.g. warm and dry housing) Good healthcare and medical services with higher life expectancy and decreased infant mortality Clean and better food and water supply, along with proper sanitation Secure employment with low unemployment rate Good working conditions Security in old age (financial, medical and social) Good transport infrastructure and network Higher GDP and GNP per capita Freedom of speech Gender/racial equality Provision of quality recreational/entertainment services Development is also often measured using the Human Development Index (HDI). Driving Forces of Development Social — The population, educational and health facilities play a key role in driving development. Strong educational and health facilities help to contribute to development and globalisation. Infrastructure — Transport and technological infrastructure is critical to development. Good transport infrastructure ensures accessibility and ease of movement of goods and services for development and globalisation. Natural Endowment — The presence of abundant and accessible natural resources and raw materials, with the infrastructure to appropriately utilise such resources, makes a country attractive for, and aids it in, development and globalisation. The presence of smooth terrain can have a similar effect, while physical factors play a key role in development and globalisation, as hilly mountains, for example, make it difficult for development. Political — Power plays a key role in globalisation and development, and lies in the hands of the government. Poor leadership and governance can hinder globalisation and development. title: Role of Transport and Technology in Globalisation
body: Role of Transport and Technology in Globalisation Besides the aspects and driving forces of globalisation mentioned above, improvements in transport and information technology have played a key role in globalisation, and continue to be key aspects of it. Improvements in transport technology and transportation networks have made the transportation of goods, services and people further, cheaper and quicker. Improvements in Transportation Made the movement of people, goods and services further, cheaper and quicker (easier, more efficient) → increased interactions between countries (globalisation). Further Goods and Services: From 1993 to 2002, the average shipping distance increased by 40%. People: In the 1950s, most commercial planes would fly short distances, with a range of about 2400 km. In contrast, the invention of jet aircraft like the Airbus A380 gives planes a range of up to 15700 km, more than 4 times the original distance. Cheaper, Quicker (More time and cost efficient) Goods and Services: As a result of the invention of jet aircraft, containerisation, and improvements in technology leading to mechanised loading, the movement of goods and services is now much faster. Currently, due to containerisation, the use of Standard Twenty Foot Equivalent Shipping Containers allows for up to 6000 pairs of shoes to be transported in one container. Improvements in shipping technology led to innovations such as the Maersk Triple E Shipping Tanker, which can carry up to 2500 more containers and has a 16% increase in capacity compared to other ships. The Maersk Triple E also reduces fuel consumption by 37%. In 1956, it took up to 1 week to load a single ship. In contrast, with improvements in technology such as mechanised loading, loading times are now (2015) reduced to 5 hours. The invention of jet aircraft has provided a variety of transport options. Cargo planes are faster and more time efficient than trains and ships. Jet aircraft like the A350 are also 25 to 30% more fuel efficient. These have led to reduced shipping and loading times and reduced the need for multiple trips, making the movement of goods and services more time and cost efficient. People: The invention of jet aircraft reduced travel time for passengers to hours, rather than days, replacing steam ships. title: Transnational Corporations (TNCs) and Globalisation
body: TNCs and Globalisation Economic liberalisation, including removing capital controls and legal restrictions, and creating Special Economic Zones (SEZs) , has enabled the growth of transnational corporations (TNCs). TNCs influence every aspect of our lives, from the socio-cultural aspects of what we eat, wear, use and see, to the economic aspects. These firms tend to be global brands that sell in multiple countries. They often have factories in countries that are less economically developed (LEDCs) due to a variety of reasons, while their main offices are situated in more economically developed countries (MEDCs). Examples of TNCs (MNCs) McDonald's, Coca-Cola and Apple. Wal-Mart Stores had a 2016 turnover of $482 billion (equivalent to Poland's GDP) and 2,300,000 employees. Nike : global headquarters in Beaverton, Oregon, USA. Employs more than 700,000 contract workers in over 700 factories worldwide, including 124 plants in China, 73 in Thailand, 35 in South Korea and 34 in Vietnam. More than 75% of the workforce is based in Asia. Nike has 542 factories situated across 42 countries. Placing factories in other countries relies on the economic processes of outsourcing and offshoring . Process Offshoring Outsourcing Definition Getting work done in a different country by moving part of one's company to another area — an extension of your own company in a different country Employing another company to help with, or farming out, a particular aspect of the operation to another company or external organisation on the basis of a contract Benefits Cheaper operational costs due to cheaper labour/land in another area, and faster working times due to a global talent pool; better availability of skilled people, taking advantage of expertise in that area so work can be done faster through a global talent pool Same benefits: cheaper operational costs and faster working times/access to skilled global talent Risks Risk of employment issues and constant criticism of transferring jobs to other countries; geopolitical risks, language differences and poor communication, etc. Risk of misaligned interests of clients and vendors; increased reliance on third parties (if third parties are at risk, the company is too); risk of lack of in-house knowledge and oversight of critical (though not necessarily core) business operations, etc. What is a Transnational Corporation (TNC)? title: Global Industrial Shift
body: Global Industrial Shift Despite the risks of offshoring/outsourcing, TNCs continue to place factories in LEDCs, resulting in global industrial shift — a trend where there is a global shift in the location of large-scale manufacturing plants. It is an effect of the role of TNCs in driving globalisation and increasing foreign direct investment in: Newly industrialising countries (NICs) – countries that started industrialising in the 1960s, e.g. the 4 Asian Tigers: South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Hong Kong. Recently industrialising countries (RICs) – countries that started industrialising in the 1980s, e.g. the Philippines, Indonesia and Cambodia. Reasons manufacturing shifted from MEDCs to LEDCs Attractiveness of LEDCs as areas of lower cost of production due to cheap and flexible labour and lower transportation costs — reduces manufacturing cost and increases profit. High labour costs in MEDCs. Larger consumer market in LEDCs due to larger population. Development in transportation encouraging companies to set up factories worldwide. Incentives from LEDC governments (tax incentives, tax deductions, tax-free zones) so TNCs pay less tax and gain more profit. Presence of cheap raw materials, land and natural resources. Few/no barriers in LEDCs – fewer trade barriers and laws not enforced by government: Labour laws – no labour unions, workers have no rights, easy to exploit and cheaper; workers are overworked and underpaid with longer hours, increasing yield and profit. Health and safety regulations – fewer regulations due to lack of education, often not enforced, reducing costly management needs and lowering manufacturing costs. Land laws – companies can exploit and evict locals/farmers to use land without paying for it. Environmental laws – companies can pollute land and water without resistance, saving on waste management costs. Advantages for LEDCs Employment Setting up factories requires workers, generating more jobs and better/new job opportunities with better income. Better income increases purchase of goods and services, widening the customer base; local businesses benefit, expand and create more jobs, generating more revenue and wealth ( multiplier effect ). Education and Training TNCs invest in training and skills development to improve workforce productivity; some skills are transferable to other industries, increasing skills and expertise for LEDC workers. title: Food and Globalisation
body: Food Globalisation affects the nature of the food supply chain, altering the quantity, type, cost and desirability of foods available for consumption. Large corporations (TNCs) are usually engaged in agribusiness , which affects the food supply chain — the majority of resources from agriculture are produced by these commercial food businesses. Currently, TNCs like Walmart, and especially the Big 10 (Associated British Foods (ABF), Coca-Cola, Danone, General Mills, Kellogg, Mars, Mondelez, Nestlé, PepsiCo and Unilever), control 80% of food exports. Increasing Demand Food Consumption Patterns in LEDCs Food Consumption Patterns in MEDCs Large increase in consumption of meat, eggs and fish in LEDCs such as China due to increase in wealth. Demand for livestock (cows, pigs, sheep, chickens) has increased since the 1960s due to rising income. People in MEDCs such as the USA consume a higher amount of meat, eggs and fish, but the rate of increase is smaller. People in MEDCs are consuming less red meat as this has been linked to health problems such as obesity and heart disease. Consumption of fruits and vegetables has increased for both MEDCs and LEDCs, due to rising incomes in LEDCs and efforts of international organisations such as the World Health Organization and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN promoting their consumption. A significant amount of fruit and vegetables in a diet is believed to reduce the risk of diseases such as heart disease, cancer and diabetes. Reasons for changing consumption Rising incomes give people access to foods that were previously unaffordable. Western diets are seen as more modern and fashionable, so eating meat and fast food becomes aspirational for upwardly mobile people. As economic development occurs, trade links develop and a greater range of western and other foreign foods becomes available. Rising farm productivity makes some foods more affordable, widening access to a growing middle class: Technological changes have increased mechanisation on farms — machinery lets farmers plough and harvest much more quickly. Purchased inputs such as pesticides and chemical fertilisers increase yields by removing competing plants/insects and boosting nutrients. Improved spatial integration through construction of roads and railways enables farmers to transport produce cheaply to more markets, increasing sales and profits. title: Managing Food Shortage
body: Managing Food Shortage GM (Genetically Modified) Crops Food derived from crops with genetic make-up modified to create desired qualities (e.g. more resistance), by taking desirable genetic traits from other organisms and transplanting them into plants/animals. Common GM foods include potatoes, corn, soya beans and tomatoes. Strengths: Some GM crops produce higher output than non-GM crops (e.g. Super Rice, a type of GM rice, produces double the output of normal rice); farmers can earn more income selling excess produce to overseas markets. GM crops more resistant to pests, e.g. Bt corn — a bacterium (Bt), a natural pesticide, is inserted into the corn plant so it suffers less insect damage, increasing farmer output. Some GM crops stay fresh longer, letting farmers sell to markets further away and earn more money to invest in their farms. GM food can withstand greater variations in weather/climate and tolerate more saline water, allowing cultivation on land once thought unsuitable for farming, producing more food for the world. Improved nutritional value of food. Limitations: Fear of potential health risks/unknown consequences of consuming unnatural GM food, including allergies; the EU bans import/cultivation of most GM crops, and countries like Zambia reject GM food imports fearing health impacts. (e.g. lectin, a protein from beans, used in potatoes to prevent aphid attacks, but some people are allergic to lectin.) GM crops are limited in availability and affordability; generally only farmers in MEDCs or richer LEDC farmers have the means and capital to grow them, unlike poor farmers. Green Revolution The application of science and modern agricultural techniques to increase agricultural productivity, including breeding high-yield varieties (HYVs) of grains, effective use of pesticides, and improved fertilisation, irrigation, mechanisation and soil conservation techniques. Strengths: High Yielding Varieties (HYVs) – crops specially bred/selected through cross-breeding to produce higher output than natural species. HYV IR8 rice was produced in India in the 1960s, significantly reducing food shortage as it was more resistant to drought and disease, had a shorter growing period, doubling/tripling crop yield per year. Other innovations: central pivot irrigation (mechanised irrigation with pipes/overhead sprinklers on wheeled towers moving around a central point), and combined harvesters, weeders and ploughs (farm mechanisation). title: Water and Globalisation
body: Water Globally, water consumption is not equal. This imbalance in demand and supply, along with growing demand, results in the issue of water shortage. Reasons for unequal water consumption MEDC consumption > LEDC consumption: MEDC LEDC >1600 cubic metres of water a year (average person in North America); up to 800 litres per person per day <200 cubic metres a year (average person in sub-Saharan Africa); only 10 litres per person per day Temporal and seasonal differences: In India, most renewable water resources arrive during the three-month monsoon period, when 70–95% of annual precipitation occurs. Large differences in precipitation between continents, regions, countries, and within countries. Regionally, South and Central America with the Caribbean is the wettest continent, averaging more than 1600mm/year, compared to North America (637mm/year), Africa (677mm/year) and Europe (545mm/year). Locally, Egypt has the lowest precipitation worldwide at only 51mm/year, but the Nile brings large amounts of freshwater from neighbouring countries to the south; renewable freshwater resources per person are 1900 litres/day in Egypt, much higher than in Libya (300 litres/day). Increasing Demand Demand for freshwater has tripled over the last 50 years as the world's population grows, increasing by 64 billion cubic metres a year. Demand grows not only for domestic water, but also from industry as countries develop, and from agriculture as irrigated farmland area increases. On a global scale, agriculture uses the largest amount of freshwater, representing about 70% of all water withdrawal worldwide (with regional variation). The productivity of irrigated land is roughly three times greater than rain-fed land, and global food production is expected to increase by 60% from 2000 to 2030, creating a 14% increase in water demand for irrigation. Our water footprint and virtual water footprint are also growing. The water footprint measures humanity's appropriation of freshwater in volumes consumed and/or polluted, including: Amount of water used to produce each good/service we use. Amount of water used for fuel. Amount of water used for every process (e.g. growing rice). Amount of water used for a product (e.g. a pair of jeans). Everything we use, wear, buy, sell and eat takes water to make. title: Managing Water Shortage
body: Managing Water Shortage Solution Advantages Disadvantages Rivers, lakes and other natural bodies of water – includes restoration of damaged rivers, lakes and wetlands so they can play their full and proper part in the hydrological cycle Water is naturally available and easy to access/distribute to users; dams and reservoirs can be built to further increase storage. In LEDCs these sources can become easily polluted, and if untreated can carry diseases such as cholera. Wells and boreholes Water is naturally purified by filtration through bedrock and can exist in arid areas with limited surface water (e.g. Great Artesian Basin in Australia). Constructing wells costs money, as does extracting water through pumps; usually limited in quantity and cannot sustain large populations or agriculture. Desalination plants / filtration technology Supply is virtually unlimited (sea water). Extremely expensive and uses a lot of energy (contributing to global warming). Rainwater harvesting – (LEDC) people collect rain falling on roofs and store it in buckets for domestic purposes (flushing toilets, watering gardens); (MEDC) water collected in large catchment areas and reservoirs Water is usually very pure and can be consumed with limited treatment. Rain is unpredictable and storage can be difficult — not reliable and requires large catchment space. Water condensing Water is very pure and does not require treatment; technology is inexpensive and simple. Can only provide small quantities of water. Solutions to reduce agricultural water demand Smart irrigation – traditional sprinklers and surface flow systems replaced by modern automated spray technology and advanced drip irrigation systems. Hydroponics – growing crops in greenhouses that are carbon dioxide and temperature controlled, in shallow trays where they are drip-fed nutrients and water; no soil used. Recycling of greywater – a low-cost option producing water for agricultural use, but not human consumption. What are advantages of using rivers, lakes and other natural water bodies? title: Energy and Globalisation
body: Energy Due to globalisation, global energy demand is expected to grow by 30% before 2035, driven by increasing prosperity in developing countries. Traditional centres of demand are being overtaken by fast-growing emerging markets such as India and China. Energy powers the world, allowing economies and societies to function, making it critical for life to go on. At the same time, energy moves around the world. The energy crisis is the concern that the rate of consumption overwhelms the rate of replenishment/production of energy, making our current overreliance on fossil fuels unsustainable. If this continues, the world would eventually run out of fossil fuels, creating a shortage of energy worldwide. The energy crisis stems from the issue of fossil fuels: more than ¾ of the world's energy supply in 2018 was from fossil fuels, meaning the world is too dependent on these sources. While fossil fuels provide effective amounts of energy, they are limited in supply and take thousands of years to replenish. They are also found almost exclusively in OPEC countries, so regional issues may cause a worldwide energy shortage. They also cause major land, air and water pollution, contributing greatly to climate change. The supply of fossil fuels continues to dwindle, and there is an overall lack in renewable energy production, so supply of energy is unable to match growing demand, which is increasing because of: Entertainment requires energy – in developed/globalised economies, besides commuting to work, people travel to see friends, enjoy pastimes and go on holidays. Increasing use of labour-saving devices – devices like vacuum cleaners and washing machines make life easier and free up time for leisure, but require energy. Increasing desire for car ownership grows continuously worldwide. Increasing world population. Globalisation and developing industries which require even more energy to function. Poor infrastructure and wastage also leads to energy being used less effectively. Globalisation plays a key role in this imbalance: on one hand it increases the use of technology and the production/exchange of goods and services, increasing energy demand. On the other hand, it increases interactions between countries and the possibilities of sharing ideas and resources for renewable energy, and leads to improvements in technology that could reduce demand for energy via cleaner and more efficient forms of energy or production, requiring less consumption of conventional energy.

title: Managing Energy Shortage
body: Managing Energy Shortage 1. Demand Reduction Reduction in demand for fossil fuel energy and for energy services, both contributing to reducing carbon emissions from energy use. Demand reduction helps make energy supplies more sustainable, as supply should be able to match demand into the future. 2. Increased Energy Efficiency Reducing energy needed to perform tasks and eliminating wastage during consumption. This makes energy supply more sustainable by conserving as much energy as possible, offering a more immediate method to reduce fossil fuel use. By reducing overall energy use, fewer resources are used up and environmental effects (e.g. greenhouse gas emissions) are limited. Homes, workplaces and transport can be designed to conserve energy: Buildings can be made more sustainable, reducing energy needed for heating and lighting by installing double glazing, draught-proofing, loft insulation and cavity wall insulation to reduce heat loss, as well as features that absorb/retain the sun's energy (e.g. large south-facing windows) to provide heat and light. Energy-efficient appliances , like energy-efficient boilers where a greater proportion of heat energy is used to heat water and less is lost to surroundings; use energy-saving appliances wherever possible (e.g. energy-saving light bulbs). Using computers, printers and faxes that turn themselves off after a period of time instead of staying on (stand-by mode can consume nearly as much energy as being turned on permanently). Changing to vehicles that need no fuel, with incentives (e.g. bicycles – employers receive tax exemptions for loaning or selling bicycles as part of the Cycle to Work scheme), and designing cars to need less fuel to run. Establishing out-of-town park-and-ride schemes, investing in public transport, and introducing congestion charges – reduces fuel consumption by reducing the number of vehicles on the road (e.g. London, Singapore, Rome and Stockholm). 3. Renewable Energy Increasingly using energy produced by renewable sources like the sun, wind or rivers. Since these can be replenished much faster than fossil fuels and produce little carbon emissions, they are a sustainable source that will never run out. Increasing renewable energy use decreases reliance on fossil fuels and increases clean energy supply. Disadvantages include high costs, inconsistency due to changing weather/climate, and producing less energy than fossil fuels — though future scientific and technological advancements ma

title: Challenges of Globalisation: Pros and Cons
body: Challenges of Globalisation Globalisation continues to face challenges despite its various positive benefits. Below are the pros and cons across different dimensions. Economic Pros: Ease of trade and exchange of goods and services, leading to economic growth and strengthening of economies through increased interdependence of countries (e.g. specialised nations can work together to create cheaper goods). The US relies on India for half of its computer service imports; India's computer service exports rose from $11 billion in 1995 to almost $110 billion in 2015, with economic growth in India averaging 6.5% a year during that time (strengthening of each other's economies). LEDCs like Zambia are able to develop by reducing debt through World Bank's help. Access to newer, larger markets brings better availability of products/services, increased customer base, wider market and increased profit, strengthening the economy (less chance of shortage). Cons: Increased vulnerability and reliance of LEDC countries – they become too dependent on wealthier countries to invest in them and are unable to function without this support system. Socio-Economic Pros: Increased job opportunities – Social: increase in employment/job opportunities and education (reduces unemployment), upskilling of LEDC population, providing stable and better jobs/income for a decent standard of living. Economic: more people working increases GDP and GDP per capita. E.g. TNCs provide access to a larger market and, by offshoring factories in LEDCs, provide jobs and better income for the LEDC population (reducing poverty and unemployment). Alleviation of poverty – globalisation significantly increases capital mobility; remittances (people working in MEDCs sending money to their hometown in LEDCs) have become increasingly popular, leading to improved conditions, sanitation and education over time, helping locals break the poverty cycle. E.g. $2,600,000,000 USD sent to the Philippines annually (9.7% of 2020 GDP) according to the World Bank. More efficient shipping and transportation – Social: increased ease of travel, increased access to goods/services (cheaper, faster). Economic: increased movement of people means a greater number/variety of customers and increased access to goods/services. E.g. the Boeing 747 (introduced in the 1960s) lowered the cost of international air travel, increasing tourism and business travel and reducing travel time from days to hours, replacing steam ships. title: Summary of Globalisation
body: Summary of Globalisation Globalisation is the growing interdependence of countries worldwide through the increasing volume and variety of cross-border transactions in goods and services and of international capital flows, and through the more rapid and widespread diffusion of technology. With growing interdependence between countries, they would not be as adversely affected by adverse processes, since they can receive support and information from other countries to combat these impacts. Globalisation benefits everyone, whether equally or not, over time and varying in scale from place to place. This is not to say that LEDCs do not benefit at all from globalisation and become more vulnerable as a result. While it may not benefit LEDCs in the short term, due to issues such as labour abuse and exploitation of natural resources, globalisation does benefit LEDCs in the long term. For example, they can grow their economy and improve relations with MEDCs as they gain access to new information and improve their own country through aspects such as public awareness, stabilising their economy and socio-political relations. With a larger influence of globalisation over many countries, there is more reliance between MEDCs and LEDCs, which can help elevate less developed countries. There is also unison in movements and actions, such as the Paris Agreement and the Kyoto Protocol, which help with mitigation and adaptation to negative impacts that globalisation might bring. As a result, weighing the benefits and problems of globalisation, in the long term its benefits help to stabilise the state of countries in economic, social, political and environmental aspects. How is globalisation defined in the summary? The growing interdependence of countries worldwide through increasing volume and variety of cross-border transactions in goods and services and international capital flows, and more rapid/widespread diffusion of technology. What benefit does growing interdependence bring to countries facing adverse processes? Countries are not as adversely affected since they can receive support and information from other countries to combat these impacts. Does globalisation benefit all countries equally? title: General Points to Note (Exam Technique)
body: 1. Always do some preparation before writing your answer Read the question and its "provenance" — the text above the question or the data given may prove useful in helping you understand the question and answer it better. Plan the points you intend to write in your answer, taking note of the pointers below as you plan. Always read the question itself carefully. For example, if the question says "using the sequence identified in the diagram", then you must use that sequence. So besides being alert to understand the question, you must also respect the question context and answer it accurately. 2. Always pay attention to mark allocation to know how much to write [4] and [6] mark questions can also be known as [2+2] and [3+3] questions respectively. When marks are allocated as such, refer to the table below: [2+2] questions [3+3] questions 2 points 3 points 2 explanations 3 explanations Knowing this, you then know you are not to write too much or too little — bearing in mind that the above only applies when marks are allocated as [2+2] or [3+3]. In all other cases, where marks are allocated as [4] or [6], 4 or 6 points respectively with explanations are required. Exception: when [4] marks are awarded, there are typically 4 points required to be attained (usually), but in some abnormal cases where only 3 points can be found, it is best to explain as thoroughly as possible so as to avoid the loss of the 4th mark. 3. Always give a variety of answers Whenever you answer a question involving the keywords below, always remember to give a diversity of answers, because you do not want a situation where, for a push and pull factor question, you simply write "less traffic congestion in MEDC, but more traffic congestion in LEDC". This only warrants 1 mark because you are simply repeating the same point in a different way. Offering a diversity of answers also shows your understanding and may help you attain marks for not-so-complete answers. Keyword How to answer Compare / Compare and Contrast Give both similarities and differences. Also look generally and not too specifically, because a very narrow comparison shows a lack of understanding. Contrast Differences only. Impacts / Benefits Positive and Negative; use ESPN (Economic, Social, Political, Natural/environmental). Factors / Reasons For factor questions, always try to give push and pull factors. title: Data Response Questions (Command Words)
body: Command word How to answer Points to note Marks awarded State / Identify / Give a reason Just give the reason or state; no need for explanation, but occasionally requires data from the question. NIL [1–2] Calculate / Define Just calculate or define; no need for data or explanation. NIL [1–2] Describe / Suggest State what you see and give data from the question. Be careful not to start comparing or to start simply stating when you see the word "describe". For example, in a question asking to "describe the growth of cities in the LEDCs and MEDCs", be careful not to compare LEDC and MEDC growth together — instead describe each. Describing is not comparing, but it is also not simply stating: describing something is to use what you see to make an inference (e.g. if a photo of a squatter settlement is given, you cannot just say there is "poor infrastructure" — you must state that "due to the presence of housing made of zinc roofs and iron sheets standing on wood stilts, it shows that there are poor housing structures/poor infrastructure"). When the question asks you to "describe the changes" and provides data, it is important not just to state the data as evidence but to interpret the data. To process data is to give an analysis of the data instead of simply stating it, such as giving percentages to show a rate of change (taken from two extremes, A and B → (B−A)/A × 100% = rate of change in %), as well as using adjectives to describe change (e.g. slight increase, exponential growth, etc.). Should a diagram or data representation (e.g. table, graph, values, photos) be given, the answer must always make reference to it. You must give specific, accurate and relevant data to support your answer. Descriptions/explanations should always be complete, and must always begin with a general statement that directs the answer or directly answers the question. They must also end with a concluding statement that links back to the question. title: Diagram Sketching
body: There are many diagrams you need to be able to sketch, and you need to be able to differentiate between the various types of questions asking you to sketch a diagram. Types of possible questions There are three main types of questions they can ask: A well-labelled diagram An annotated diagram "With the aid of a well-labelled diagram, explain the…" (e.g. formation of volcanic island arcs) Approach to diagram sketching questions Identify the diagram you need to sketch and then proceed to sketch it. A well-labelled diagram only requires a sketch and simple labelling, so just label the parts of your sketch. An annotated diagram requires a sketch and a short description for each label/part in the sketch. Unless provided with the case below, you do not need to write a paragraph — simply annotate on your sketch and provide a short description of the features. If asked, "With the aid of a well-labelled diagram, account for the formation of stratovolcanoes," you should label a sketched diagram with numbers and then write the process corresponding to the numbers in a paragraph below your sketched and numbered diagram. Check that you have included all important details in your sketch and drawing. For example, if the question already gives you certain information like the names of places, you must draw and label the plates or include these names of places. Fundamentally, if you are given any information to sketch a diagram, your sketch must show details of the information given to you. Types of diagrams you need to know how to sketch Relief rain formation Convectional rain formation Monsoon diagrams What are the three main types of diagram sketching questions? A well-labelled diagram, an annotated diagram, and 'With the aid of a well-labelled diagram, explain the...' questions. What is required for a 'well-labelled diagram' question? Only a sketch with simple labelling of the parts. What is required for an 'annotated diagram' question? A sketch plus a short description for each label/part (annotation), not a full paragraph unless otherwise specified. body: This section will be worth 10 marks, and can ask a range of questions under this section, by simply providing an infographic. title: Essay Writing
body: Unpacking the question Look at the question and identify the issue. If you see the phrase "To what extent" or "How far", you must: Take a stand (your thoughts or opinion on the issue and where you stand. Note that your stand can either be to agree to a large extent or a small extent, but not to totally agree or fully disagree). Consider the merits and perspectives of the argument or concept and discuss/show perspectives (since you cannot totally agree or fully disagree, you must take into account different perspectives — most of the time, 2 perspectives on an issue). After looking at the question, look at the statement and identify keywords. Understand and define these keywords and identify the extreme word, which will tell you where this statement stands or what it is saying on the issue. Example Question: To what extent is climate change a threat? Issue: Climate change Identify keywords: "To what extent" and "threat" Define keywords: (i) "To what extent" means we must take a stand and show perspectives. (ii) "Threat" means we are looking at the negative effects — the threats, challenges and risks of climate change. Essay preparation: (i) The given factor is: climate change is a threat. (ii) The perspectives we can discuss are: climate change is a threat, and climate change is not a threat. Format Introduction Begin with a general statement — a broad stroke of what the topic is about (e.g. Migration — across the years, people have been moving across international boundaries in search of a higher standard of living and quality of life). After the general statement, state your scope. Stating your scope is similar to defining terms, but instead of defining the words (e.g. "benefit refers to…"), you are setting boundaries to the keywords (e.g. "Migration has both positive and negative impacts in different aspects, both to the country from where people move from and to where people go to"). Be careful to scope the question correctly (e.g. should the word "today" be used in a question about climate change, it should be narrowed down to global warming). Scoping is a way of narrowing a broad term like climate change and placing it in the right context, not simply defining it. After stating your scope, proceed to the most important part of your introduction — stating your stand. When stating your stand, maintain a more academic perspective and avoid saying "I feel" or "I agree", but rather follow something like: "This statement can be agreed to a small/large exten

title: Geographical Concepts
body: Strong essay responses are able to: Synthesise three or more concepts in a well-structured way and utilise case studies in body paragraphs to aid explanation of a focused geographical concept (note that as much as concepts are important, evidence is equally important too). Offer a critical evaluation of the statement. Introduce and discuss the issue from different perspectives. Provide new insights and a different perspective that "wows" the examiner. Key idea: discuss how there are multiple perspectives to a certain issue under a broad geographical concept. For example, under the geographical concept of space, the impacts of climate change can be discussed — how does space result in positive and negative impacts in certain regions? E.g. positive impacts: food can now be grown in cooler highlands, with a longer growing season; negative impacts: more extreme weather events resulting in lower crop yield, and some crops can no longer be grown in certain regions. Concept of Place Using this concept, we can understand how a more economically developed country (MEDC) is better able to adopt measures and responses compared to a less economically developed country (LEDC). This is because the MEDC has more resources, both financially and in terms of technology and manpower, and is thus more able to implement them compared to an LEDC, which lacks all these. The advancement of communication networks, which is also a limitation due to economic constraints, is also related to the concept of place. In different countries, especially between MEDCs and LEDCs, the economic and social context varies. For example, if a country's economic and social context is good, the country will have the money to prepare well, and its people will be able to understand preparedness measures (especially emergency drills) since they are literate and educated, compared to a country with a poor economic and social context, where the government cannot fund high-level preparedness measures and the less-educated people would not be able to understand them. Think of places in terms of geographical, political, and economic places. Places can be compared according to cultural or physical diversity, or disparities in wealth or resource endowment — for example, MEDCs and LEDCs. How do places fit into your argument? title: Causes of Climate Change (Natural and Anthropogenic)
body: Natural Causes In 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted, releasing an estimated 20 million tonnes of sulfur dioxide and ash particles more than 20 km up into the atmosphere. The sulphur-based particles reflected solar energy back into space and lowered temperatures in the northern hemisphere by as much as 0.6°C. Over the past century, Earth's average temperature has increased by approximately 0.6 degrees Celsius. Solar heating accounts for about 0.15°C, or 25%, of this change, according to computer modelling results published by NASA. Solar variations are expected to continue to modulate both warming and cooling trends at the level of 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius over many years. Anthropogenic Causes The world's usage of fossil fuels has increased in recent years. Billions of tonnes of carbon dioxide are released into the atmosphere each year. Carbon emissions from fossil fuels grew 1.5% in 2017, 0.89% in 2018, and were expected to reach 36.81 billion tonnes in 2019. Globally, trash released nearly 800 million metric tons (882 million tons) of CO2 equivalent in 2010 — about 11 percent of all methane generated by humans. At the landfill, the food and yard waste that trash contains is decomposing and releasing methane, a greenhouse gas that's 28 times more potent than carbon dioxide. According to the best current estimate, 11 percent of all global greenhouse gas emissions were caused by deforestation, amounting to 284 km² — an area 83 times the size of New York's Central Park — in January 2020 alone, with 10 million km² of forest estimated to have been lost since the beginning of the 20th century. What natural event in 1991 released sulfur dioxide and ash affecting global temperature? The eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines. How much sulfur dioxide and ash did Mount Pinatubo release, and to what altitude? An estimated 20 million tonnes, released more than 20 km up into the atmosphere. By how much did Mount Pinatubo's eruption lower northern hemisphere temperatures? By as much as 0.6°C. How much of Earth's temperature increase over the past century is attributed to solar heating, according to NASA modelling? Approximately 0.15°C, or about 25% of the 0.6°C increase. How much can solar variations modulate warming/cooling trends over many years? Between 0.1 to 0.2 degrees Celsius. title: Impacts of Climate Change (Positive and Negative)
body: Positive Impacts In the long term, shipping commerce will benefit from the opening of the Northwest Passage through Canada's formerly icy north for longer periods of the year, due to the loss of Arctic sea ice, as trade is made easier and cheaper. Shorter travel distances of up to 40% between Asia and Europe are possible, with around 5% of the world's trade potentially shipped through the Northern Sea Route (NSR) in the Arctic alone under year-round and unhampered navigability, generating additional income for many European and East Asian countries. In 2019, there were increases in temperature of 3.4°C to 9.1°C in mid-winter and increases of 1.9°C to 5.7°C in mid-summer in Siberia, making the temperature warmer and more habitable for people. In the UK, new crops such as blackberries, citrus fruits and maize can now be cultivated. The 1961–1990 average UK growing season was 252 days, but the average for the first years of the 21st century increased to up to 270 days. Negative Impacts According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), 33% of coastal land and wetland habitats are likely to be lost in the next hundred years if sea levels continue to rise at current rates. In Cuddalore district in Tamil Nadu, sea level rise turned large tracts of agricultural land in the village into wasteland. According to the IPCC, the rise in temperatures, along with projected increases in population, could put 5 to 6 billion people at risk of contracting dengue fever in the 2080s. What positive shipping impact could result from Arctic sea ice loss? The opening of the Northwest Passage through Canada's north for longer periods, making trade easier and cheaper, with shorter travel distances of up to 40% between Asia and Europe possible via the Northern Sea Route. title: Responses to Climate Change (SG Green Plan, Kyoto Protocol, Paris Agreement)
body: Singapore Green Plan The Singapore Green Plan 2012 aimed to generate 60% of Singapore's energy needs using natural gas by 2021, but as early as 2010, about 79% of Singapore's electricity was already being generated from natural gas — exceeding the Ministry's target ahead of schedule. (However, natural gas requires complex treatment plants to process and pipelines to transport. These pipelines have high maintenance costs because they need to be laid underground and checked regularly for leakage.) The Building Construction Authority (BCA) Green Mark Scheme aimed to encourage developers and owners to build and maintain greener buildings and achieve a 28% energy efficiency improvement from 2005 building codes. Major retrofitting works, like open-sided building concepts and fitting high-performance glass, help buildings achieve energy savings of between 20% and 40%. The National Library Building and the Park Royal Hotel on Pickering reported energy savings of 15% to 35% compared to conventional buildings. (Limitation: more expensive to build due to expensive material costs, so this is less popular with developers.) New registrations of diesel cars and taxis to cease from 2025. 8 EV-ready towns with chargers at all HDB carparks by 2025. All new car and taxi registrations to be of cleaner-energy models from 2030. 60,000 charging points nationwide, including 40,000 in public carparks and 20,000 in private premises, by 2030. Expand cycling network to 1,320 km by 2030. Increase rail network to 360 km by early 2030s. Increase share of trips taken on mass public transport to 75% by 2030. (Making public transport more appealing by increasing frequency and access, and by making car ownership more expensive. Limitation: due to the rising standard of living and wealth of Singaporeans, many are still prepared to buy cars.) Kyoto Protocol 10 years into the Kyoto Protocol, in 2015 the UNFCCC showed that many countries with targets under the Protocol collectively met or exceeded their targets by over 20 percent, due to constant monitoring and reporting by countries for self- and peer-assessment. Between 1990 and 2012, the original Kyoto Protocol parties reduced their CO2 emissions by 12.5%, well beyond the 2012 target of 4.7% (CO2 only, rather than all greenhouse gases, and including Canada). The Kyoto Protocol was also successful in encouraging sustainable development through the Clean Development Mechanism, whereby developed countries are encouraged to work with developing

title: Mitigation and Adaptation to Climate Change
body: Mitigation The Empire State Building was recently retrofitted with 6,514 windows and reused 96% of old materials. Until 2008, the Empire State Building used energy equivalent to 40,000 single-family homes in a single day. After retrofitting, the building is more energy efficient and its energy use was reduced by 38%. It saved up to 4,000 metric tons of carbon by 2012, equivalent to the offset provided by 750 acres of pine forests. Promoting public transport use: increased public transport use reduces carbon emissions. US public transport has been found to save 37 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually. Adaptation Netherlands: a storm surge barrier consisting of 13 dams was built near Rotterdam that can protect the city from storm surges 3m higher than normal. They also built floating homes that remain stable despite the water around them rising and falling. This is an example of how a low-lying country has taken measures to adapt to rising sea levels. Bangladesh: spent over 10 billion dollars to combat climate change. For example, they have floating vegetable gardens that rise and fall with the water. During the monsoon season, these also double as shelter for cattle and poultry. title: Coastal Management Measures (Soft and Hard)
body: Soft Coastal Protection Measures Indonesia (East coast of Kalimantan and East coast of Sumatra): according to World Bank data, in an area with 26,705 km² of mangrove area, the area subject to coastal erosion by storm surge was 37,904 km² without mangroves and 27,865 km² with mangroves — a 26.5% decrease. UK, Lincshore: 530,000 m³ of sand were pumped from licensed offshore sites onto 20 km of beach in 2013, protecting 30,000 properties and 35,000 hectares of land from tidal floods. Watching the new beach being created in front of the promenade has actually become a tourist attraction, and on a sunny day there can often be quite a crowd. Annual cost is about £6 million. Kapuhenwala and Wanduruppa , two villages in a lagoon in southern Sri Lanka, show the importance of mangroves in saving lives: Kapuhenwala, surrounded by 200 hectares of dense mangroves and scrub forest, saw the 2004 tsunami kill only two people — the lowest number of tsunami-related fatalities in a Sri Lankan village — versus Wanduruppa, surrounded by degraded mangroves, which was severely affected with 5,000 to 6,000 deaths in the district. Hard Coastal Protection Measures Ishinomaki City: the 2011 Japan tsunami caused severe damage — areas without breakwaters had 87% of buildings swept away, versus areas with breakwaters, which were protected, with only approximately 25% of buildings damaged. Mappleton, UK: in 1990, this popular tourist destination was under threat of losing 30 houses. In 1991, hard engineering measures like revetments and two large rock groynes were built (GBP 2 million). Today, farmlands and tourist sites such as caravan parks and villages remain, despite being under threat over 20 years ago. Pondicherry, India: the city is protected by a seawall which stretches 2 kilometres along its coastline, reaching a height of 27 feet above sea level. When a 24-foot high tsunami caused by the 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake struck Pondicherry, the city centre stayed dry, and casualties were limited to about 600, most of whom were residing in villages outside the protective barrier offered by the seawall. title: River Management Measures (Soft and Hard)
body: Soft River Protection Measures Pickering, Yorkshire: the Slowing the Flow scheme was enacted in 2009, after the town had suffered four serious floods in 10 years, with the flooding in 2007 estimated to have caused about £7 million of damage. According to The Guardian, the 40,000 trees planted in Yorkshire as part of the scheme (reforestation) successfully reduced peak river flow by 20% during a 2016 flood, when 50mm of rain fell in 36 hours, thereby preventing widespread damage to houses and the town museum. UK, Dagenham, Beam Washlands: a £4.5 million capital scheme to make space for water and reduce the risk of flooding to 570 homes, 90 businesses (including the Ford Dagenham plant), major infrastructure (including Barking power station), and strategic development sites. Hard River Protection Measures Mississippi River: raised embankments and artificial levees. Samuel Muñoz, a geoscientist from Northeastern University, compared results across flood records and found that overall flood risk has gone up 20 percent, with 75% of that risk coming from human engineering of the Mississippi for navigation and flood control. In the 2019 flood season, artificial levee breaches along the Mississippi River cost the US government a total of US$1.9 billion to repair. Ebro River Basin, Spain: studies showed that reservoirs were very efficient in reducing peak flows in their neighbouring downstream zones, by as much as 80%. Additionally, the global effect of dams and reservoirs on the mouth of the River Ebro reduced overall peak flows by around 57%. (Dams reduce the risk of flooding.) Enacted in 2009 after four serious floods in 10 years (2007 flood caused ~£7 million damage); involved reforestation (40,000 trees planted). title: Causes of Globalisation
body: Increased movement of people US: in absolute numbers, the United States has a larger immigrant population than any other country, with 47 million immigrants as of 2015. This represents 19.1% of the 244 million international migrants worldwide, and 14.4% of the US population. According to the UN, the estimated number of international migrants worldwide increased between 2000 and 2020, reaching 281 million in 2020 — up from 248 million in 2015, 220 million in 2010, 191 million in 2005 and 173 million in 2000. Increasing migration and tourism make populations more unified and diversified, with more people using, adopting and consuming increasingly similar food, clothes, music and values. Increased capital mobility and increase in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) linking global economies Singapore is an extremely globalised nation that has based its economic development on a proactive strategy to attract FDI using its trade openness. According to UNCTAD's World Investment Report 2020, FDI inflows rose to USD 92 billion in 2019, from USD 79 billion a year earlier. Singapore is the 5th largest recipient of FDI inflows in the world, behind the United States, China, the Netherlands and Hong Kong — all heavily globalised countries. In Singapore, at the HS6 digit level, 4,257 products are exported to 220 countries and 4,307 products are imported from 221 countries. The total value of exports (FOB) is US$390,332 million, while the total value of imports (CIF) is US$358,975 million. Reduced trade barriers and reduced tariffs encouraging trade The North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), signed in 1994, created the world's largest free trade area of 454 million people, effectively linking the economies of the US, Canada and Mexico. According to the US International Trade Commission, between 1993 and 2019, trade between the three members quadrupled from US$290 billion to US$1.23 trillion as a result of NAFTA. Tariff reduction/elimination for 81% of Singapore's exports to India make Singapore-originating products more competitive and allow Singapore exporters to increase their exports to India's large consumer market. Products that benefit include food products, plastics, electronics, pharmaceuticals, and mechanical appliances. Improvements in transportation From 1993 to 2002, the average shipping distance increased by 40%. title: Impacts of Globalisation
body: Increased job opportunities (Socio-economic) Increased job opportunities and a means for rural poverty reduction: with globalisation and the rise of TNCs, more companies are practising offshoring. This provides those in rural areas with a stable income, as despite a relatively low wage of US$2–3 a day, it is still more than most rural incomes. Since 1990, with increasing globalisation, 1 billion people have been lifted out of poverty, with 600 million lifted between 1992 and 2015 in China alone. Breakdown of socio-cultural barriers resulting in increased cultural diversity (Social) Travel around the world is more accessible than ever, facilitating the breakdown of socio-cultural barriers between people and increasing cultural diversity. According to the International Civil Aviation Organisation, the 4.3 billion airline passengers carried in 2018 are expected to grow to about 10 billion by 2040, with the number of departures projected to rise to 90 million in 2040. Singapore: integration of Malay, Indian, Eurasian, Western and Chinese immigrant food, culture, festivals, dressing, and services catered to them, like Chinatown and Little India. Increase in power and dominance of global organisations like the UN (Political) The United Nations (UN) is a global organisation that has significantly contributed to the betterment of the human race. The UN administers the World Food Programme (WFP), an initiative aiming to eradicate hunger and malnutrition globally. The world's largest humanitarian agency, the WFP helps almost 100 million people in approximately 88 countries with assistance every year through food or cash distributions and more. Increased global cooperation leading to unified efforts to combat climate change (Environmental) Examples: Paris Agreement, Kyoto Protocol, United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), Montreal Protocol. Increased exploitation of labour in LEDCs (Socio-economic) Tens of thousands of female migrant workers from Asia and Africa work in the Middle East as domestic workers, where the Kafala "sponsorship system" continues to drive economic growth whilst leaving workers vulnerable to abuse. The system denies migrant workers their right to freedom of movement — the employer controls the mobility of the worker through control over critical documents such as passports and legal control over their ability to change employment or exit the country. Threat to local cultures (Social) Globalisation brings about Westernisat

title: Transnational Corporations (TNCs)
body: Reinvestment into communities and LEDCs (Socio-economic) In 2000, the multinational oil and gas company Shell launched and subsequently provided a US$250 million endowment to the Shell Foundation, a charitable organisation aiming to alleviate poverty in Africa and Asia through increasing communities' access to energy and sustainable mobility. According to official figures from the charity's website, the Shell Foundation has to date reduced 48.15 million tonnes of carbon emissions, supported 584,297 jobs, and improved the livelihoods of 193.7 million people. The Foundation also contributed to the UN Investment Climate Facility for Africa with a US$2.5 million investment over 5 years. Increased employment and wages (Socio-economic) In the Netherlands, foreign-owned transnational companies created over 700,000 full-time equivalent employment positions in 2014. These organisations also contributed another 650,000 FTEs indirectly to other companies within the nation, with most involved in either trade or manufacturing. 20% of all full-time jobs in the Netherlands are created because of the presence of these organisations. TNCs such as Daewoo (Republic of Korea) have been attracted to Bangladesh because of low wage rates compared to other Asian countries, and 'spare' quotas to supply ready-made clothes to the European Union and the US. In 1980, Daewoo signed an agreement with a medium-sized Bangladeshi garment firm (Desh Garment Company). Since then, garment exports have increased dramatically, and by 1992 accounted for 46% of Bangladesh's total export earnings. Daewoo provided training programmes, start-up capital and international marketing expertise. Within the Export Processing Zones (EPZs) in Bangladesh, other Korean TNCs have invested heavily in food processing, electrical machinery and chemical industries. (This shows improvement of the country's economy and workforce, and a multiplier effect.) Siemens, the German engineering and electrical giant, first announced its intention to build a £1.1 billion semiconductor plant in North Tyneside in 1995. After receiving a British government grant of several £million, the factory opened in 1997, creating nearly 800 jobs.
