title: The Cold War: Definition and Outbreak (Ideological Differences)
body: The Cold War The end of the Second World War led to a decisive change in the power balance around the world. Countries that had previously dominated European affairs, such as France, Britain and Germany, were now poorer or less powerful. World history was much more affected by what the leaders of the new 'superpowers' believed and did (USA and USSR). From entering Berlin together and celebrating VE Day, relations between the two superpowers deteriorated in the succeeding years, leading to decades of geopolitical conflict and rivalry known as the Cold War. Definition In a traditional sense, the Cold War is not considered an actual war where direct and actual fighting takes place. Rather, it can be classified as a state of hostility and high tensions where conflict takes the form of non-cooperation , including propaganda from both sides and economic measures . The Cold War can be divided into 3 phases: Outbreak Escalation Manifestation 1. Outbreak of the Cold War How did the Cold War start? How did the USA and USSR turn from allies to enemies? a) Ideological Differences/Conflict Although the USA and USSR were wartime allies, they inherently believed in differing ideologies, political and economic systems. This difference of beliefs laid the basis of all subsequent conflicts during the Cold War. Capitalism (USA) Communism (USSR) Distinct class differences → disparity in wealth Classless system → equitable distribution; everyone is equal Individual enterprises; businesses owned by private individuals. Market economy → production determined by market forces; prices set by competition State-controlled economy; government owns means of production. Command economy → production determined by state government; prices set by state Promotes democratic political freedoms (includes freedom of speech/multi-party system elections) → values freedom Concentrates power into the hands of a select few; one-party rule/authoritarian dictatorship → lack of freedom; does not value freedom → possibly corrupt politicians, party officials and government Healthcare managed by private sector Free healthcare services — One-party state (only the Communist Party allowed to contest elections) As seen from the table above, both systems of governance differ greatly. Communism entailed high levels of government intervention, giving the state a lot of power, while Capitalism believed in individual rights and the value of freedom. This difference led to conflict as both powers attempted to spre

title: Breakdown in Wartime Alliance: The Yalta and Potsdam Conferences
body: b) Breakdown in Wartime Alliance When Germany invaded Russia and was pulled to declare war on the USA by Japan, the USSR and USA found themselves in an unlikely alliance, fighting together against a common enemy. After the defeat of Germany in 1945, both celebrated together; however, the problems brought by the war would soon turn relations sour. In February 1945, as Germany was on the brink of defeat, Allied leaders met at Yalta, Ukraine, to plan what would happen after Germany's defeat. The Yalta Conference went well. Despite their differences, the Big Three — Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill — agreed on some important matters. It seemed that, although they couldn't all agree, they were still able to negotiate and do business with one another. Yalta Conference (February 1945) Agreements Disagreements On Japan: Stalin agreed to enter the war against Japan once Germany surrendered. On Borders: Stalin wanted the border of the USSR to move westward into Poland, much to the disapproval of Roosevelt and Churchill. On the United Nations: The Big Three agreed to the new United Nations, successor of the League of Nations, to keep peace after the war. On Elections: The Declaration of Liberated Europe promised that countries liberated from the German army would be allowed to hold free elections regarding their government. On Germany: The Big Three agreed that Germany would be divided into 4 zones: American, British, French and Soviet. On Poland: A government of 'national security' was to be set up in Poland, comprising both communists and non-communists. Post-Yalta Changes Stalin's armies were occupying most of Eastern Europe: Soviet troops had liberated country after country in Eastern Europe, but instead of withdrawing his troops, Stalin left them there. Refugees were fleeing the country, fearing a communist takeover. Stalin had set up a communist government in Poland, ignoring the wishes of the majority of the Poles. He insisted his control of Eastern Europe was a defensive measure against possible future attacks. America had a new president: President Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945 and was succeeded by his vice president, Harry Truman. Truman was much more anticommunist than Roosevelt and was very suspicious of Stalin; together with his advisors, he saw Soviet actions in Eastern Europe as preparations for a Soviet takeover of the rest of Europe. The Allies had tested an atomic bomb: On 16 July 1945, the Allies successfully tested an atomic bomb at a desert site

title: Mistrust and Suspicion; Post-War Developments (Iron Curtain and Eastern Europe)
body: c) Mistrust and Suspicion Actions which drew suspicion and worsened relations between the West and the USSR: The West USSR 1939 Munich Agreement: When negotiating with Hitler over the fate of the Sudetenland, Russia was not invited to the talks. This expressed the West's fear of communism, indicating to Stalin that they were willing to allow Hitler to destroy Russia before taking action. Giving Hitler the Sudetenland, allowing him to advance East, and refusing Russia a voice only furthered distrust. Communism was also seen as a mutual enemy, which motivated the policy of Appeasement. Perceived delays in opening a second front and delayed action after the invasion of the USSR also caused Stalin to lose faith in the Allies, resulting in his post-war feelings of insecurity. 1917 Russian Revolution: In 1917, communist ideology led to a revolution which overthrew the Duma provisional government. This event caused fear within the West, as they suspected communism would be a threat to their democratic system of governance, with the potential to disrupt the order of society and topple other forms of government. 1939–46 Manhattan Project: Russia feared the power of America's atomic bomb. The success of the first nuclear arms had shocked and angered Stalin, as its development was kept secret from him. This caused feelings of wariness and suspicion in the USSR about the motives of the West. 1939 Nazi-Soviet Pact: In 1939, the USSR signed the Nazi-Soviet Pact (Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact) with Nazi Germany, promising mutual non-aggression and benefit through cooperation. This revealed suspicion between the Allies and the USSR, as they refused to put aside their differences and ally against Hitler, resulting in the USSR deciding the best option was to work with the enemy. It was only after betrayal and dismantling of the pact that the USSR had to align with the Allies for self-preservation. The disagreements at the Potsdam Conference had soured relations between the US and USSR. This was coupled with various suspicious actions by both sides in WW2, which made them wary of each other. Disparities between both countries increased as the US underwent a leadership transition, with a more anti-communist person helming the country. The situation further escalated as Stalin's army was occupying Eastern Europe while the Americans had developed a nuclear bomb. All these events contributed to heightened tensions and hostility between the two superpowers, with violence being a very r

title: Escalation: Greece and Czechoslovakia, the Truman Doctrine, Containment, the Marshall Plan and NATO
body: 2. Escalation How did the West react to Stalin's actions? Greece, 1947 In 1946, a civil war erupted in Greece between the Soviet-backed communists and the British-backed monarchists. Monarchists wanted the return of the king of Greece; communists wanted Greece to be a Soviet Republic. The British could not afford such a war and intended to withdraw their troops, previously sent to Greece to restore order and supervise free elections. Truman intervened: paid for by the Americans, some British troops stayed in Greece and tried to prop up the King's government. By 1950, the royalists were in control of Greece, although they were a very weak government, always in crisis. Czechoslovakia, 1948 Czechoslovakia was ruled by a coalition government which, although it included communists, had been trying to pursue policies independent of Moscow. The communists retaliated by purging anti-Soviet leaders. A pro-American minister, Jan Masaryk, was found dead below his open window. The communists said he had jumped; the Americans suspected he'd been pushed. Truman Doctrine When the Greek Civil War broke out, the Americans were alarmed. Despite the conflict only taking place at a local scale, America viewed it as a threat of communist takeover and subsequent spread. In response, President Truman declared that the United States would provide aid (money, equipment and advice) to any country under the threat of communist takeover. This policy of aid is known as the Truman Doctrine. With it, the Americans exited their isolationist policy and became more involved with European affairs. Containment Policy Communism would be limited only to areas already under Soviet control, and Americans would resist Soviet expansion everywhere else. In the late 1940s, the USSR made attempts to extend her influence, by stationing her army in Eastern Europe and installing satellite communist governments there. The USSR also created Cominform, to coordinate the activity between the communist parties in Europe. This raised grave concerns among Americans, and a policy of containment was adopted to stop the spread of communism into other nations. The manifestation of this policy can be seen through the Truman Doctrine, where Americans promised military and economic aid to any country under threat of communist takeover. Common symbols: Uncle Sam as America; Bear as communism/USSR. Marshall Plan After WW2, Western Europe was in ruins. Truman was worried that weakened Western European nations would be m

title: How Stalin Reacted: Cominform, Comecon and the Warsaw Pact
body: How did Stalin react to the West's actions? Cominform The Cominform (Communist Information Bureau) was created in 1947 to coordinate the activities of Communist Parties in Europe under the direction of the USSR. This was done both in response to Communist leaders in European nations being uncertain of whether they should participate in the Paris Conference on the Marshall Plan, as well as in response to the Marshall Plan itself. It also aimed to tighten Soviet control in Eastern Europe, to build collective heavy industry in those countries, and to create a trade network between Communist countries. It published its own newspaper to spread Communist ideals and held conferences in the Eastern Bloc. Communist leaders also gathered in Moscow to take instruction from Stalin. Comecon (Council for Mutual Economic Assistance) Established in 1949 to facilitate and coordinate the economic development, planning and trade of the Eastern European countries belonging to the Soviet bloc. Warsaw Pact Created in response to the admission of West Germany as a member state of NATO, partly due to the creation of NATO itself. In 1955, after NATO admitted West Germany as a member, the USSR began to feel the threat of the West, with a security alliance that stretched from the Western European coast all the way to the border of Russia's sphere of influence. In order to protect herself and her satellite communist states, the USSR created the Warsaw Pact, a security alliance similar to NATO, involving several satellite states under communist influence. Similar to NATO, an attack on any member state in the Warsaw Pact would have been considered an attack on all Warsaw Pact nations, prompting a response from all member states to defend the nation under attack. The Warsaw Pact was another piece of evidence of the USSR's threat and the threat of communism. In essence, the Warsaw Pact was: (1) a security alliance between the USSR and the communist satellite states; (2) created in response to the growing threat and power of the West, after the creation of NATO. What was Cominform and when was it created? The Communist Information Bureau, created in 1947 to coordinate the activities of Communist Parties in Europe under USSR direction. Why was Cominform created? In response to uncertainty of Communist leaders about the Paris Conference on the Marshall Plan, the Marshall Plan itself, and to tighten Soviet control over Eastern Europe. What is Comecon and when was it established? The Council

title: Division of Germany, Bizonia, and the Berlin Blockade/Airlift
body: Division of Germany, Bizonia and the Berlin Blockade After the war, it was agreed for Germany to be divided into 4 zones. Initially, Truman intended to remove all German industry and make it an agricultural country so it could never wage war again. However, growing concerns over the USSR made Truman decide that a strong Germany might be a useful ally. It was also clear that if German industries were not allowed to recover, millions would starve. In 1947, America and Britain combined their zones into Bizonia, and with the addition of France in 1948, the entity became known as the Trizone (West Germany). Stalin believed Germany should be kept poor and weak, to prevent it from being a threat to European powers again. Stalin also wanted reparations for damage done to the USSR and began to exact this from its zone. 10 million refugees fled from the Soviet zone to other Western-powers-occupied zones, straining resources on the Western powers. In order to help the West German economy recover, the Allies agreed to create a new currency, the Deutsche Mark, replacing the severely inflated old currency. Bizonia began receiving aid under the Marshall Plan, and Western zones began to recover and prosper. Stalin felt he had to show Western leaders that he would fight back if they encroached on the Soviet 'Sphere of Influence'. Afraid that Germany would grow strong and threaten the USSR, Stalin planned to seize control of West Berlin through a blockade, hoping to force the Western powers to leave the city by blocking all supplies of food to West Berlin. West Berlin lay deep in the Soviet zone and was connected to the West via roads, railways and canals which crossed Soviet territory, much to Stalin's resentment. In 1948, Stalin blocked these supply lines, stopping the Western powers from reaching their zones in Berlin. He aimed to starve the people of West Berlin until they surrendered to communist rule. If the USA rammed roadblocks or railway blocks, it would be seen as an act of war. Stalin expected Truman to announce an embarrassing withdrawal from Berlin, giving him Soviet control of the entire city and a propaganda victory. Berlin Airlift The West had three options: (1) break down and ram the blockade, potentially initiating a war with the USSR and being blamed as the aggressor; (2) give in to Stalin's demands and withdraw from Berlin, suffering an embarrassing defeat and paving the way for the entire Germany to fall to the USSR; or (3) find another method to delive

title: Manifestation of the Cold War and the Korean War
body: 3. Manifestation The Cold War had been a race between the two superpowers — the US and USSR — to spread their ideologies and prevent the enemy from doing so. This conflict spilled over into other parts of the world, and proxy wars broke out in Asia where, much like the Iron Curtain, the Bamboo Curtain had formed between communists and non-communists. Proxy War: Armed conflict between two states or non-state actors which act on the instigation or on behalf of other parties that are not directly involved in the hostilities. The Korean War As the Japanese pulled out of the Korean peninsula, the USSR and USA liberated the nation from the North and South respectively. Conflict arose between the leaders of the Communist North and Capitalist South, developing into a Civil War. The war soon transformed into the first major proxy war of the Cold War, as the USSR and China supported their fellow communist counterpart against the US and UN backed South. Belligerents North Korea — Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK); South Korea — Republic of Korea (ROK). Leaders Kim Il Sung (Premier and Dictator of North Korea): Communist leader trained and backed by the USSR (influenced by and supported policies of purges, collectivisation and industrialisation; installed by Stalin). Ran a Soviet-style one-party system; dictatorship, totalitarianism. Wanted to unify Korea by force and impose communism on the whole peninsula. Used a militaristic style of governance — extending military influence into civilian social, political and economic spheres, prioritising and preserving the armed forces. Syngman Rhee (First President of South Korea): Anti-communist dictator. Wanted to unify Korea under the banner of capitalism. Authoritarian and responsible for many massacres. Mass-arrested political opponents. Supporters USSR: Wanted to secure the Korean Peninsula and include it in the communist bloc to maintain its growing power. Due to the successes of communism in the region, Stalin had become determined to increase his influence. China: Due to its geographical proximity to Korea, it could act as a platform to spread communism in the Asia-Pacific region, establishing satellite states. USA: Initially, Korea was not a priority for the US. As communism had succeeded in China and the USSR gained atomic power, the US became increasingly alarmed. China had fallen to communism, and Stalin had been encouraging communists in other countries (Malaya and Vietnam) to rise up against their colo

title: The Vietnam War
body: The Vietnam War Much like Korea, post-WWII Vietnam had been divided into the North and South, communists and capitalists. Vietnam had suffered greatly under the hands of multiple powers, and for many, this was a fight for independence. However, the difference in ideologies and fear of the 'Domino Theory' (that if one country fell to communism, other proximal nations would soon fall too) got the US involved yet again, fighting in the dense jungles of Indochina. The war marked one of the USA's greatest defeats, as many innocent civilians, US soldiers and Viet Cong guerrillas died in both conflicts and massacres. Background 111 BC – 1427 AD: Chinese Rule and Influence — Since ancient times, Vietnam had been under the influence of China, at times under the rule of various Chinese dynasties. For almost 1000 years, China had tried to absorb Vietnam into itself through both conquest and cultural assimilation. This stopped in the 19th century as China faced its own problems with colonisation and Western imperialism. 1887 – 1945: French Occupation — In the 19th century, the French colonial empire took over the regions of Cambodia, Laos and Vietnam collectively under the union of French Indochina. The Vietnamese state had capitulated and been reduced to a puppet administration with no oversight over the country's affairs. French occupiers exploited the region's natural resources and peasant population for self-benefit. Any sign of nationalistic resistance was dealt with by force, evident by decades of failed rebellions and uprisings. Vietnamese peasants grew desperate to escape their French colonisers. 1940 – 1945: Japanese Invasion — Under its expansionist foreign policy, Imperial Japan set her eyes on French Indochina, wanting to create an 'Asia for Asians' under the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, where Western colonists would be driven out of the region. In 1940, Japan annexed Indochina, occupying it for the next 5 years until losing the war in 1945. Under Japanese rule, French colonisers continued Vietnamese administration, instead working for the Japanese (under Vichy France). During the Japanese occupation, a strong anti-Japanese movement (Viet Minh) emerged under the leadership of communist Ho Chi Minh, who inspired the Vietnamese people to resist and fight their Japanese occupiers. In 1945, the Viet Minh entered the northern city of Hanoi and declared Vietnam independent. Bảo Đại Final Emperor of the Nguyen Dynasty, the last ruling family of Vietnam

title: End of the Vietnam War and Impacts
body: End of the War and Impacts America's Withdrawal from Vietnam By 1973, US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger had secured a peace agreement with North Vietnam. Under the agreement, the US had to withdraw all of its troops within 60 days. The South Vietnamese were left alone, although economic aid was still supplied by the US. Without US support, the South eventually fell to the North. Paris Peace Accords At the end of the war, President Johnson eventually lost support from the American people for his poor role and management of the Vietnam War, and was succeeded by President Richard Nixon, who worked towards ending American involvement in Vietnam together with Henry Kissinger. However, no concrete progress was made towards peace until the Paris Peace Accords of January 1973 (both North and South Vietnam had earlier refused to sign agreements proposed by the US-UN). Eventually, the Paris Peace Accords led to the signing of a mutual agreement that ended the war and restored peace among the USA, North Vietnam and South Vietnam. Reunification and Independence of Vietnam North Vietnam refused to hold elections South Vietnam could not hold on to power without US help North Vietnam invaded South Vietnam 1975: North and South Vietnam unified under communism, with the capture of Saigon Who was the US Secretary of State who secured the 1973 peace agreement with North Vietnam? Henry Kissinger. Under the peace agreement, how quickly did the US have to withdraw all its troops? Within 60 days. Did the US completely abandon South Vietnam after withdrawing troops? No — the US withdrew troops but continued to supply South Vietnam with economic aid. What eventually happened to South Vietnam without US military support? It eventually fell to North Vietnam. Which US president succeeded Lyndon Johnson and worked to end American involvement in Vietnam? Richard Nixon. Why did President Johnson lose the support of the American people? His poor role and management of the Vietnam War. What agreement, signed in January 1973, ended the war and restored peace between the USA, North Vietnam and South Vietnam? The Paris Peace Accords. Did North Vietnam and South Vietnam sign earlier US-UN peace proposals before 1973? No, both had earlier refused to sign them. After the Paris Peace Accords, did North Vietnam hold the elections it had promised? No, North Vietnam refused to hold elections. What happened in 1975 that ended the Vietnam War? title: Cuban Missile Crisis: Background and Cuban Revolution
body: Cuban Missile Crisis The Cuban Missile Crisis (CMC) is a key instance of brinkmanship — the practice of trying to achieve an advantageous outcome by pushing dangerous events to the brink of active conflict. The CMC marks a critical point in the Cold War, being the first time the United States was directly threatened by nuclear destruction. The Cuban Missile Crisis lasted 13 days, from 16th to 28th October 1962. Background: Why was Cuba significant to the US? Aspect What was Cuba? Why did it matter to the US? Economic Cuba was a Spanish colony and centre of commerce in the Americas region. It was a major producer of rum, sugar and tobacco, which were in high demand in both Europe and America. Taking Cuba would mean the US could use the island for American business interests, taking advantage of the island's products and benefitting its trade and economy. Geopolitical Cuba was in close proximity to the US, located between the US and the Caribbean islands. The US saw the Americas as its own sphere of influence, and Cuba was its gateway to extending power over the Caribbean. The island would be strategic in the US plan to expand its power and ensure its security. Early American Involvement in Cuba In 1898, Cuba struggled to fight against the Spanish in the Cuban War of Independence. The US intervened, supporting the Cuban independence fighters, and America won the war. Even after withdrawing troops from Cuba in 1902, the US continued its interests in the region. Political: Although the US promised to hand over power to an independent and democratic Cuban government, it had established a pro-US government friendly to American political and economic interests. The Cuban government was not allowed to make alliances with other nations without US approval. America frequently intervened in Cuban politics to maintain US security, installing "puppet presidents" to guard national interests, much to the resentment of Cuban nationalists. Fulgencio Batista — the final "puppet president" of Cuba: Corrupt and dictatorial, oppressing the Cuban people and violently persecuting opponents. Had ties with the mafia, allowing them to control illegal business in Havana and big US corporations in Cuba. Used secret police to remove opponents. The US was nonetheless reluctant to withdraw support, for fear of communism being brought by his opponents into their backyard. Economic: Due to the pro-US government, US companies invested heavily in Cuba and in improving its infrastructure. In

title: Cuban Missile Crisis: Timeline
body: Cuban Missile Crisis Timeline 16th October — After US spy planes discover medium-range ballistic missiles in Cuba, and that the missile bases were for offensive weaponry, Kennedy is informed of the threat and gathers a group of advisors (later known as the Executive Committee/National Security Council) to consider potential measures to diffuse the situation. 17th October — Kennedy spends the day meeting with advisors, discussing various courses of action and their potential consequences, and realises the grave possibility of war. 18th October — The Soviet Union lies to Kennedy, claiming the missile sites were only for defensive purposes, not offensive reasons. This leads Kennedy to order further spy jets over Cuba, which discover seven more missile sites, including medium and long-range missiles (the excessive number of sites and the range of the missiles signalled to the US that they were for offensive purposes). 19th October — The escalating threat leads Kennedy to cancel a campaign stop in Chicago so he can return to Washington. The media is told the President must return due to a "cold"; the real reasons are withheld. 20th October — The US begins to make military preparations as it determines its course of action moving forward, teetering on the strategy of brinkmanship. 21st October — The US notifies its allies of the growing threat in Cuba and the escalating tensions with the USSR. 22nd October — President Kennedy goes live on national television to inform US citizens of the looming danger of nuclear war. 23rd October — Kennedy orders a naval blockade of Cuba, intended to prevent weapons and military equipment from reaching the country. 24th October — At 10am EDT, the blockade goes into effect. It is dubbed a "quarantine", as a blockade is perceived as an act of war under International Law; a 'quarantine' limited the restriction to offensive weapons, which would be more reasonable to the rest of the world, implying the US was not trying to deny Cuba weapons for self-defense or trying to starve the Cuban people. The USSR was shocked and outraged, condemning the blockade as an illegal act of war against Cuba. Khrushchev wrote to Castro assuring continued USSR support and that they would ignore the blockade, but simultaneously ordered recently-departed Soviet ships to return to port to prevent further escalation, while urging ships already en route to Cuba to reach their destination faster. title: Comparing the Korean War, Vietnam War and Cuban Missile Crisis
body: Korean War, Vietnam War and Cuban Missile Crisis Compared Aspect Vietnam War Korean War Cuban Missile Crisis Cause(s) Caused by the power vacuum created after World War II when Japan surrendered. The Viet Minh, led by Ho Chi Minh, saw an opportunity to rise and set up the Democratic Republic of Vietnam (DRV) with Hanoi as its capital. In 1949, the French-backed Bao Dai set up the State of Vietnam with Saigon as its capital. The conflict (First Indochina War) stretched on for several years before it evolved into a proxy war in 1954. Key factors: superpower involvement (Gulf of Tonkin); difference in ideology (Ho Chi Minh vs Diem); protection of allies/geopolitical significance (Domino Theory). Caused by the power vacuum created after World War II when Japan surrendered. Korea was split in two along the 38th parallel after Japan surrendered its colonies. The conflict was caused by two dictators, Syngman Rhee and Kim Il Sung, both wanting to reunite the Korean peninsula under their respective regimes. This evolved into a proxy war after American and Soviet powers provided support for their respective sides. Key factors: superpower involvement (installation of Kim, training of North Korea, cooperation with UN); difference in ideology (Kim vs Rhee); protection of allies/geopolitical significance (Japan, greater Pacific). Caused by the US instituting a puppet pro-US government in Cuba in the form of Batista, who was corrupt, dictatorial, with ties to the mafia. In 1959, Fidel Castro and a group of rebels, with the backing of the Cuban people, overthrew the government in the Cuban Revolution. Cuba then aligned itself with the USSR, leading to the USSR placing ICBMs in Cuba and the thirteen days of crisis. Key factors: superpower involvement (USSR missiles, Bay of Pigs); difference in ideology (Castro vs US); geopolitical significance (Caribbean, US backyard, resources and economic interests). title: The United Nations
body: The United Nations The origins of the United Nations lie in the Second World War. During the war, 26 nations forged a coalition to fight the Axis powers. They agreed not to enter into any separate deals with Nazi Germany and its allies, and adopted a set of principles to underpin their efforts: freedom, human rights and justice for all. The UN embodies these principles and represents the culmination of the Allies' efforts. Founded in 1945, in the aftermath of the war and the horrors of the Holocaust, it was hoped that the UN would be able to prevent such catastrophes from happening in the future by stabilising international relations and giving peace a more secure foundation. The UN is also widely seen as a successor to the failed League of Nations. It is yet another organisation which strives to seek international peace through cooperation with nations and resolving issues through peaceful means. title: End of the Cold War: Detente and External (Foreign) Factors
body: End of the Cold War Background In the late 1960s to mid-1970s, the Cold War entered a phase of Détente (French: "relaxation"), where both the US and USSR practised a policy of relaxing tensions and coexistence, rather than containment and confrontation. Pioneered by US National Security Adviser Henry Kissinger, alongside Nixon and Brezhnev, it helped manage Cold War competition without Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) and nuclear escalation, ensuring a brief peace and stability. Reasons for the Shift to Detente US: Focus on ending the Vietnam War USSR: Achieved Nuclear Parity Both: Avoid MAD Richard Nixon (POTUS) Visited Beijing in 1972, beginning the normalisation of relations with the PRC after 25 years of diplomatic isolation. First President to visit the USSR. Signed the Strategic Arms Limitation Talks (SALT) and the Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty with Brezhnev. In 1979 (referenced in the notes as 1974), the USSR invaded Afghanistan, starting the proxy Soviet-Afghan War, which stopped all talk of detente. External (Foreign) Factors Leading to the End of the Cold War 1. Military Buildup When Reagan took office as American president, he increased military spending and massively built up the US Armed Forces, knowing that the USSR's weak economy would not be able to catch up. This re-escalated the Cold War, shifting back from the policy of Detente to Rollback. Strategic Defence Initiative (SDI) [aka 'Star Wars Program']: Announced by Reagan in 1983, the SDI was a missile defence system that intercepted or destroyed any nuclear missiles fired at the US, protecting it from MAD. These measures made the US seem invulnerable to Soviet nuclear missiles, alarming the USSR, which did not have enough money to sustain an arms race. Pershing II Missiles: In 1983, the US announced that Pershing II missiles would be deployed in West Germany by NATO. These new missiles were mobile, more accurate, and within striking range of the western part of the USSR. This further exacerbated tensions and the arms race. Able Archer 83 Incident: A military exercise conducted by NATO members around Western Europe and the US was so realistic that the USSR thought it was a ruse for war and a first nuclear strike on the Soviets. In response, the USSR readied its nuclear forces and prepared for war — the second time a nuclear war was narrowly avoided. The incident made Reagan realise that aggression only made MAD more possible and that the Soviets, too, wanted peace. In the following year

title: Internal (Domestic) Factors Behind the USSR's Collapse
body: Internal (Domestic) Factors in the Collapse of the USSR Socioeconomic: Inefficient Economy — Poor Economic Systems By the late 1970s-80s, the USSR's command economy began to show its inefficiency. Excessive Military Spending: Years of Cold War and the arms race led to heavy spending on the military; in some years the military took up 50 per cent of government expenditure. As a result, there was little left to produce consumer goods, creating a shortage. Lack of Consumer Goods: The emphasis on heavy industry and the military meant little attention was paid to consumer goods; quality of life in the USSR was much worse than in capitalist countries. No Quality Control: The central government focused on targets that were easy to measure. Factory managers waited for instructions on what to produce and at what price. Targets were set only for quantity, not quality, so goods produced were often poor in quality, and many customers were unhappy with the quality of Soviet goods. Farms and Factories not improved: The central government had not improved farms with technology; factories still used obsolete methods and machines for production. Thus the USSR could not catch up with the West in terms of production. Inefficient Transport/Distribution System: The USSR's transport and distribution infrastructure was not organised efficiently, partly due to the vastness of the USSR — factories were located far from the raw materials they needed. Due to inefficient transport, much of the crops produced were wasted due to long waiting times. Inefficient Workers and Social Issues Alcoholism: A major problem in the USSR, caused partly by the relatively cheap price of alcohol and the lack of other consumer goods for workers to spend on. It created health-related and social problems, which had a bad effect on workforce productivity. No Working Incentive: In a communist society everyone worked for the state, so there was no reward or incentive to work hard since all were given the same benefits. All Soviet workers were guaranteed jobs for life, so Soviet workers became less efficient than their capitalist counterparts. Basic needs not met: The command economy could not provide the people with basic necessities. With increased demand for consumer goods, a 'black market' developed, which also meant the government lost a great deal of revenue. As a result, the USSR was bankrupt — the state had a 35 billion rouble annual deficit, and the military took 50% of the state budget. Political F

title: Mikhail Gorbachev: Glasnost, Perestroika and New Thinking
body: Mikhail Gorbachev Gorbachev was the last leader of the Soviet Union (1985-1991). Unlike previous Soviet leaders, although he believed in preserving the Soviet state and socialist ideals, Gorbachev knew that reforms were necessary. He also relied less on fear and oppression to rule the people, instead welcoming the voices of the people on how they should be governed. His role in the collapse of the USSR remains controversial both internationally and domestically. Though he was the recipient of many awards, including the Nobel Peace Prize, within Russia he is blamed for not stopping the fall of the USSR. Gorbachev's Policies When Gorbachev took office, he had 2 objectives: Restore the people's faith in the communist system of government and end corruption ( Glasnost ) Reform Soviet industry and agriculture by adopting elements of the free market system and moving away from central control ( Perestroika ) Glasnost ("Openness") Aim: End corruption and restore people's faith in the communist government. Make the Soviet government more open and forthcoming in its communication, which had long been restricted: Allowed public freedom of expression and sought to rid public information of propaganda and lies Consulted people about policies instead of just imposing them Allowed media to discuss problems of the nation, including the basic poverty of the Soviet people, waste of the country's resources, and the Chernobyl Disaster The Chernobyl Disaster (April 1986), where a reactor explosion resulted in the release of radioactive material around the region, was the first instance of Glasnost. Despite obvious health risks, little information was released to the public in the fallout zone, and some reporting was deliberately misleading. Shocked by this response, Gorbachev appeared on Soviet television and gave a speech with a serious admission of the facts of the accident. Encourage open debate and freedom of speech: Intellectuals, academics, writers and artists who had once criticised the state and were arrested or exiled were released — e.g. Andrei Sakharov, one of the most prominent critics of the communist regime, was allowed back into Moscow after being exiled More forms of media were allowed: banned Soviet fiction from the 1920s-30s was published, and Soviet citizens gained access to Western media outlets like the BBC History of the USSR was uncovered: a good deal of archival material on the Stalinist purges and the Great Terror was unearthed and published; in 1989,

title: Eastern Europe: Prague Spring and the Fall of the Berlin Wall
body: Eastern Europe Prague Spring (5th January 1968) Context: Antonin Novotny, the Stalinist ruler of Czechoslovakia, was succeeded as First Secretary of the Czechoslovakian Communist Party by Alexander Dubcek, a Slovak who supported liberal reforms. In the first few months of his rule, Dubcek introduced a series of far-reaching political and economic reforms, including increased freedom of speech and the rehabilitation of political dissidents. Effects: Dubcek's effort to establish "communism with a human face" was celebrated across the country, and the brief period of freedom became known as the Prague Spring. However, on 20 August 1968, the Soviet Union responded to Dubcek's reforms by invading Czechoslovakia with 600,000 Warsaw Pact troops. Prague was not eager to give way, but scattered student resistance was no match for Soviet tanks. Dubcek's reforms were repealed and he was replaced by the staunchly pro-Soviet Gustav Husak, who re-established an authoritarian communist regime in the country. In 1989, as communist governments folded across Eastern Europe, Prague again became the scene of demonstrations for democratic reforms. In December 1989, Husak's government conceded to demands for a multiparty parliament. Conclusion: The Prague Spring saw Czechoslovakian citizens gain more civil liberties following a nationwide liberalisation and move toward democracy. The USSR responded harshly to the crisis, but the citizens, having experienced the joys of civil liberties and a more democratic and liberal government, were prepared to reclaim their rights. The Spring was an obvious sign of the desire for freedom and democracy among communist subjects, and a general shift against communism, whether within or beyond communist states. Fall of the Berlin Wall (9th November 1989) Context: On 13 August 1961, the Communist government of the German Democratic Republic began to build a barbed wire and concrete "antifascist bulwark" between East and West Berlin. The official purpose of this Berlin Wall was to keep so-called Western "fascists" from entering East Germany and undermining the socialist state, but it primarily served to stem mass defections from East to West. The Berlin Wall also signified the divide between the communist and capitalist blocs, and stood until 9 November 1989, when the head of the East German Communist Party announced that citizens of the GDR could cross the border whenever they pleased. title: Social Movements in Southeast Asia: Introduction
body: Social Movements in Southeast Asia Social movements can be defined as loosely organized, purposeful groups striving to work towards a common goal. These movements can either create or resist change, providing a political voice to the disenfranchised. Unlike political movements, which aim to govern, social movements seek concessions from the state in the form of policy changes, protection or other forms of action. Southeast Asia consists of the Buddhist-majority Indochina Peninsula and the Islam-majority maritime SEA. Both regions house many different ethnic and cultural groups. Due to its wealth in resources, religious influence, history of colonialism and wide spectrum of political systems, Southeast Asia has long been a hotbed for social changes: Politics of social and cultural change Rapid social and cultural change in Southeast Asia has been afforded by power relations involved in the construction, functioning and transformation of cultural groups and societies The negotiation of power between the dominant and subordinated in society, each with their own versions of reality and practice, is often articulated through struggles over particular cultural sites, e.g. struggles over heritage sites Constructing identities Social groups emerge in relation to uneven political and economic arrangements wrought by processes such as globalization, migration and tourism, as well as how social and political institutions such as the family, paid employment and non-government organizations shape everyday lives and politics Social movements and influence Social movements cannot exist without a considerable measure of democracy Local social movements have been influenced by global social movement concerns and international discourse, e.g. war and environmental destruction, and causes such as civil rights, gender equality and the sexual revolution, shaped by funding and repertoires of action, and are able to leverage transnational networks to pursue local causes This multitude of factors has led to the manifestation of social change in movements such as the Free Aceh Movement and the People Power Movement. How are 'social movements' defined in the notes? Loosely organised, purposeful groups striving to work towards a common goal. How do social movements differ from political movements? title: Free Aceh Movement (GAM)
body: Free Aceh Movement Aceh is a province located on the northern tip of Sumatra in the Indonesian Archipelago. In 1976, Acehnese intellectual Hasan di Tiro established the Free Aceh Movement (Gerakan Aceh Merdeka; GAM) — a separatist group which sought the independence of Aceh from Indonesia. The insurgency, known to the central government as the Aceh Security Disturbance Movement (GPK), pursued its goals mainly through armed struggle with the Indonesian Army, lasting through the 1990s. In 2005, after a deadly tsunami devastated the region, a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) was signed, resulting in GAM giving up its arms and goals of independence in exchange for political power. Driving Forces Political: Fight for self-determination and the Acehnese identity: Under the Sukarno government, they were promised special benefits and their own land, but were incorporated under North Sumatra in 1950 and lacked autonomy After the Darul Islam rebellion in the 1950s, they were promised special territory status, but still lacked power to make decisions for themselves Suharto's 'New Order' in 1966 centralised power, causing political alienation of Aceh (little provincial power) Human rights abuses: Oppressed political voice — could not speak up about the violence occurring Operational Military Status (DOM) declared in 1991, leading to about 2,000 people being killed in the first 3 years of operations (1989-1992) Families who supported Aceh Merdeka were sometimes arrested without reason Social: Social identity: Historical roots as a powerful Islamic state Resistance to Dutch colonial rule (Aceh War: 1873-1942) Belief that they are a superior race, culturally distinct from the Javanese Compared to the secular government, wanted to establish an independent Islamic state under Sharia Law Political Islam was suppressed under Suharto Social tensions: Indonesia's transmigration policy led to many Javanese being displaced to the Aceh mountains and industrial coasts Due to tension between Javanese and Acehnese, the Acehnese could not go to the mountains or coastal zones, and were suffocating in the middle Immoral activities occurred, e.g. trafficking, cannabis cultivation and sexual assaults Religious: Strict adherence to Islam and religious identity: Had to safeguard this strong religious identity Threatened by the Sukarno Indonesian government's practices of secularism Wanted to turn Indonesia into an Islamic state Disagreements over the implementation of Islamic (Sharia) law

title: People Power Movement (Philippines)
body: People Power Movement (Philippines) Reasons/Driving Forces Political: Corrupt Marcos government: Martial Law declared in 1972 to keep Marcos in power A new constitution allowed Marcos to rule for 14 years instead of two (facilitated further by the rigged snap elections of 1986) 3,200 known killings and 35,000 documented cases of torture under the authoritarian Marcos regime Former Senator Benigno "Ninoy" Aquino Sr, one of Marcos' main political enemies, was shot and killed at the airport in 1983 Call for reform: Lack of freedom, oppression, living in a climate of fear Unable to carry out democratic elections and choose their own government Heavy political corruption Social: United society (civil): Over 2 million people condemned Marcos and launched the "Triumph for the People" campaign of civil disobedience All had a common goal of overthrowing the Marcos government Access to mass media: Celebrities and churches alike joined the movement, making it widespread The Catholic radio station, Radio Veritas, became a major control centre for the People Power movement's communications Economic: Economic recession: 1980s economic collapse brought about by extravagant spending in the 1960s and over-reliance on debt Economy contracted by 7.3% over the following 2 years The peso lost about 80% of its value By 1982, the Philippines' debt was about $24.4 billion Religious: Involvement of the Catholic Church: The Catholic Church's support led to mass mobilization, with many churches calling for followers to demonstrate and support the movement Impacts Political achievements: Short-term democratic reforms: 1987 Constitutional Reform removed and changed many repressive laws, shifting from a regimentary to a parliamentary system Intended to strengthen democracy and freedom for the people Power was split into 3 arms of government: executive, legislative and judicial Cannot sustain political achievements: Cases of political corruption continued to occur Some of Aquino's promises were not kept, such as the dismantling of US Army bases in the Philippines Social and civil successes: Legacy of the People Power Movement: Other movements were inspired by the effectiveness of the People Power Movement, e.g. the Arab Spring (2010), Hong Kong protests (2019) and the Burmese Civil Disobedience Movement (2021) Economic benefit: Recovery efforts for the title: Urbanisation: The Growth of Cities and USA Urbanisation (19th-20th Century)
body: Urbanisation The Growth of Cities The industrial revolution of the 19th and 20th centuries transformed urban life, giving people high expectations for improving their standard of living, and its developments encouraged migration to cities: Improved transportation moved goods and people quickly and easily Industrialization allowed for more goods to be produced cheaply by machines Commercialisation allowed for the production of goods for a mass market, meeting high demand from the people USA Urbanisation, 19th-20th Century Reasons Technological Advancement: Rise in the number of cars and the motor industry: facilitated immigration and urbanisation; created greater employment in the motor and manufacturing industries; eased transportation, allowing city boundaries to expand as workers could travel beyond walking-distance commutes Communication technology, particularly the development of telephones: eased communication, boosting efficiency and helping fuel the rise of larger national companies and corporations Long-distance transportation: rail and ships facilitated international immigration, especially from Europe given the context of WWI and WWII, as people escaped war and religious persecution Immigration Push and Pull Factors: Push factors: religious persecution (e.g. of Eastern European Jews during the European wars); poverty and conflict (WWI, WWII, Korean War); poor working and living conditions (e.g. the Great Irish Potato Famine of 1845) Pull factors: economic opportunities — a safe haven with high demand for labour and financial/economic security Political factors: laws from the United States (a country built by immigrants); immigration quotas Economic Opportunities: New products and new means of production (e.g. assembly line manufacturing) meant new industries formed and old industries flourished Workers were attracted by jobs and higher wages High employment meant more labour was needed: in 1929, the auto industry employed 500,000 workers; in 1921, 12% of Americans were unemployed, so more rural residents decided to move to urban areas in search of employment Dense city populations attracted business, with stores moving to cities (agglomeration economics) WWI and WWII: the USA supplied the European war effort Given the reduced economic significance of the farming industry in the 1920s, more rural farmers moved to cities in search of employment Effects Growth of cities City planning Movement of people Rising income gaps Impacts Social: Overpopulati

title: Question Approach and Source Analysis
body: General Approach to Source-Based Questions Look out for symbols and messages in the source. Look out for source provenance (when the source was created and who created it). Identify the characters and what is going on in the source. Identify possible hidden messages. Your analysis of the source must always be accurate and clear. Be discerning to interpret the source accurately and quickly. Always look out for the question issue/main issue in the source (above background information) and address it - this is your inference point, what you need to infer about. Example: "What can you learn from this source about the Korean War?" - the focus must be on the Korean War itself, not on China's role or America's actions specifically. Require sufficient facts (1-2 lines) to support your inference. What two things about the source's provenance should you look out for first? When the source was created and who created it. Besides provenance, what four things should you look out for in a source? Symbols and messages, characters and what is going on, possible hidden messages, and the question issue/main issue. Where should you look for the question issue/main issue? Above the background information, in the source itself - this is your inference point, what you need to infer about. How many lines of facts are typically needed to support an inference? 1-2 lines of sufficient facts. If a question asks 'What can you learn from this source about the Korean War?', what should the focus be? The Korean War itself, not on a specific country's role or actions (e.g. not just China's role or America's actions). What quality must your analysis of a source always have? It must always be accurate and clear. What skill is needed to interpret a source accurately? Being discerning, so you can interpret the source accurately and quickly. What are the two main things a source's provenance reveals? The time the source was created and the identity of its creator. title: Inference
body: Types of Questions What is the message? What is the cartoonist trying to convey? Other Possible Questions Sentiments (feelings - e.g. proud, patriotic, pity, disgusted, etc.) Attitudes (similar to tone - e.g. critical, harsh, pessimistic, condemnatory, etc.) Tone (e.g. sceptical, cynical, optimistic, pessimistic, melancholic, frustrated, anger, disapproving - note that 'positive' and 'negative' are not considered tone) Structure Single paragraph with context, or 2 paragraphs with context included. The number of paragraphs depends on the richness of the source. Message (Infer) Evidence (provide a quotation or description of the source) Explanation (elaborate the link between your quotation and inference) Link (can be before or after context) Context (support with contextual knowledge, which must be in sync and relevant/aligned with your inference) Example starting sentence: "The message of the source..." Notes [6 Marks] (spend about 10-12 minutes on this question, but no more) Also known as 'Message' questions. Always look for the bigger picture of the entire written or picture source. Don't point out only one small aspect of the source. Do not make one-word inferences. Ensure you do not repeat any of the words found in the source in your inference (do not describe the source). Repeat keywords found in the question (always answer or link back to the question). When the source is a picture or cartoon, always infer first and then describe the source. If there are speech bubbles, or accompanying text like a caption, you must quote them in your answer. Always think about a factor or perspective that you have learnt and try to make an inference that relates to it (avoid absurd or overly simple inferences). How many marks are Inference questions typically worth? 6 marks. How much time should be spent on an Inference question? About 10-12 minutes, but no more. What is another name for Inference questions? 'Message' questions. What are the four components of the Inference structure? Message (Infer), Evidence (quotation/description), Explanation (link quotation to inference), Link/Context (contextual knowledge support). What is a good starting sentence for an Inference answer? "The message of the source..." What other types of questions fall under Inference besides 'What is the message?' Sentiments, attitudes, and tone questions. title: Inference with Purpose
body: Types of Questions Why was this cartoon published? What is the intention of the cartoonist in publishing this source? Is the cartoonist an opponent or supporter of the issue? Structure One paragraph will suffice if well written and elaborated upon. Example starting sentence: "The source was published to influence/educate/persuade/criticise/justify..." Notes [7 Marks] (spend about 10-12 minutes on this question, but no more) Also known as 'Why' questions. Do not make one-word inferences. Ensure you do not repeat any of the words found in the source in your inference. Avoid the following verbs: to show, to portray, to tell, to illustrate, to depict, to inform. How many marks are Inference with Purpose questions worth? 7 marks. How much time should be spent on this question type? About 10-12 minutes, but no more. What is another name for Inference with Purpose questions? 'Why' questions. Give an example of an Inference with Purpose question. "Why was this cartoon published?" or "What is the intention of the cartoonist in publishing this source?" How many paragraphs are needed for this answer if well written? One paragraph will suffice if well written and elaborated upon. Give a good starting sentence for this answer type. "The source was published to influence/educate/persuade/criticise/justify..." What verbs should you avoid using when describing the cartoonist's purpose? To show, to portray, to tell, to illustrate, to depict, to inform. Why should you avoid the verbs 'to show, to portray, to tell, to illustrate, to depict, to inform'? Because they describe content rather than convey the source's actual persuasive purpose/intention. title: Comparison
body: Types of Questions How similar/how different are the sources? To what extent do the sources agree with Hitler? How far do the sources agree on the League of Nations? Structure 3 Paragraphs First and Second Paragraph - One paragraph on 'agree' and another on 'disagree' (whether similarity or difference comes first depends on what the question asks for first). Basis of comparison/overarching statement: e.g. Sources B and C agree that the peacekeepers enforced a harsh peace settlement on Germany/dictated peace/did not invite Germany to the negotiations. Message: source evidence + inference (evidence must match/support the basis of comparison). Third Paragraph Agree or disagree based on the purpose and perspective of the source, with support of source provenance. Must include purpose and outcome as well as the audience in relation to both sources' perspective of the issue. Ideally, compare the audience outcome and the purpose. However, if the audience outcome is too generic (e.g. so that the British can understand the situation), focus instead on comparing the speaker's intention. Purpose has to focus on the verb used (refer to Inference with Purpose), and show how it impacts as well as the change in the audience. Example (Treaty of Versailles): both sources disagree - one is to criticise the Allies, in hopes that the Allies will reconsider the terms; the other is to justify the terms, in hopes that people will find it fair. Example starting sentence: "Sources B and C agree..." Note: use the exact word given in the question - if it says 'similar', use 'similar'/'different', not 'agree'/'disagree'. Notes [7 Marks] (spend about 10-12 minutes on this question, but no more) Follow the question phrasing exactly. Do not compare descriptions (what the source says) - compare an inference made about the issue, either chosen by yourself or directed by the question (e.g. "To what extent is Source A similar to Source B on its views on the benefits of Hitler's policies" requires an inference on the views on the benefits of Hitler's policies). Answers must start with an overarching idea (a similarity or difference) and then go on to explain each source. Avoid starting like "Source A says... and Source B says..."; instead use a connecting phrase like "Source A and Source B differ on..." Do not simply quote the sources - provide ample explanation after each quote to show similarity or difference. Do not assume all sources share a similarity or difference in tone. There is no

title: Reliability
body: Types of Questions How reliable is Source A? To what extent can Source A be trusted? To what extent is Source A reliable? Do you believe Source A? Other Possible Questions Credible Trustworthy Believe Prove Accept Structure 3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'reliable' and one on 'not reliable', or vice versa (rarely all reliable or all not reliable). Use the exact word given in the question (e.g. if 'trustworthy' is used, use 'trustworthy' not 'reliable'). First Paragraph Answer the question by making an inference with source content (e.g. Source A is reliable as it shows that Hitler disliked the Jews). Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description of the source to support your inference. Elaborate on your quotation/description to support your inference and answer the question. Link your explanation back to the question - reliable or not reliable. Second Paragraph Answer the question by cross-referencing to contextual knowledge (e.g. Source A is reliable as, according to context, Hitler did indeed dislike the Jews, so the source/inference is supported by contextual knowledge). Explain. Link back by stating "Thus, Source A is reliable" or "Thus, Source A has limited reliability." Third Paragraph Answer the question through a closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source. Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs, refer to Inference with Purpose; the purpose must focus on the verb used and show how it impacts and changes the audience). Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance - the year or context in which the source was published, or the writer) and explain. Explain the bias (if any), reasons to be one-sided in an argument (if any), and the position of the speaker (unbiased or biased). Link back to answer the question (e.g. "Thus, Source A is ultimately unreliable"). Note: Useful words/phrases for tone and perspective include 'unbiased', 'objective', 'subjective', 'biased', 'official', and 'exaggerated to an extent where what it depicts may not necessarily be true and reliable.' Always note that meeting minutes or official documents are objective and unbiased. Example starting sentence: "Source A is not reliable/reliable as..." Notes [8 Marks] (spend about 10-12 minutes on this question, but no more) Always repeat the keyword used in the question (e.g. if 'believe' is used, use 'believe' in your answer, not 'reliable'). Must include purpose and outcome as well as the audience in relat

title: Usefulness
body: Types of Questions How useful is Source A as evidence about Hitler using terror on the Germans? How useful is Source A as evidence about the Policy of Appeasement? Structure 3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'useful' and one on 'not useful', or vice versa (rarely entirely useful or completely not useful). First Paragraph Answer the question by making an inference with source content (e.g. Source A is useful in showing how the Jews were mistreated by Hitler). Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description to support your inference. Elaborate on your quotation/description to support your inference and answer the question. Link your explanation back to the question - useful or not useful. Second Paragraph Answer the question by cross-referencing to contextual knowledge (e.g. Source A is useful as, according to context, the Jews were indeed mistreated by Hitler, so the source/inference is supported by contextual knowledge). Explain. Link back by stating "Thus, Source A is useful" or "Thus, Source A has limited usefulness." Also list the limitations of the source (e.g. "Source A only discusses one reason as to why the Policy of Appeasement was adopted, which is the fear of communism. However, it does not cover other reasons such as the need for time to rearm or the need to protect their economies and colonies.") Third Paragraph Answer the question through a closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source. Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs, refer to Inference with Purpose; the purpose must focus on the verb used and show how it impacts and changes the audience). Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance - year or context in which the source was published, or writer) and explain. Explain the bias (if any), reasons to be one-sided (if any), and the position of the speaker (unbiased or biased). Consider the source's reliability and how usefulness is affected (a source can be unreliable but still useful). Link back to answer the question (e.g. "Thus, Source A is ultimately unreliable"). Note: Useful words/phrases include 'unbiased', 'objective', 'subjective', 'biased', 'official', and 'exaggerated to an extent where what it depicts may not necessarily be true and reliable.' Meeting minutes or official documents are objective and unbiased. Important: just because a source is not reliable does not mean it is not useful. title: Testing Assertion
body: Types of Questions Study all sources. "Hitler was an effective leader." How far do the sources support this statement? Study all the sources. "Hitler's economic policies benefited the lives of the Germans." How far do these sources support this view? Explain your answer using sources and your knowledge. Structure First, separate the sources into two categories: 'agree with the statement' and 'disagree with the statement'. Agree with the statement Disagree with the statement Source A, Source E Source B, Source C and Source D Typically, try to make it balanced in a 2:2 ratio, but if not possible, a 2:3 or 3:2 ratio works as well. Even a 3:1 ratio will work. Most of the time, due to time constraints, it is best to work with only 4 sources. You must be clear and accurate about which sources agree and which disagree. 6 Paragraphs: Source A supports this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation Source E supports this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation However, Source B does not support this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation Source C also does not support this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation Finally, Source D also does not support this view... + Source Evidence and Explanation General analysis of the majority of sources (e.g. most of the sources do not support this claim); Context (confirm if the claim is accurate, and if not, challenge the claim subtly - only include this in the final paragraph, not at the end of every body paragraph, e.g. "In addition, according to context..."); Link back to the claim. Example starting sentence: "Source A supports this view..." Notes [12 Marks] (spend about 20-25 minutes on this question, but no more) How many marks are Testing Assertion questions worth? 12 marks. How much time should be spent on a Testing Assertion question? About 20-25 minutes, but no more. What is the first step in structuring a Testing Assertion answer? Separate the sources into two categories: 'agree with the statement' and 'disagree with the statement'. What ratio of sources should you ideally aim for when separating them? Ideally a balanced 2:2 ratio, but 2:3, 3:2, or even 3:1 also work. Due to time constraints, how many sources is it best to work with? Most of the time it is best to work with only 4 sources. How many paragraphs make up a Testing Assertion answer? 6 paragraphs. What should each of the first several body paragraphs contain? A statement of whether the source supports/does not support the view, plus source evidence

title: Hybrid Reliability - With a Primary Source
body: Types of Questions Does Source A prove that Source B is wrong about Hitler's rule? (There is a primary source - Source A) Big Idea Involves the critical analysis of the reliability of one source using another source. The skills are very much like reliability, but involve the use of more than one source. Structure 3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'can prove wrong' and one on 'cannot prove wrong', or vice versa (rarely entirely one or the other). First Paragraph Present an overarching idea with the comparison (look for a similarity or difference in content) - make an inference of both sources and compare the inferences to see if they say the same or different things. Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description to support your comparison. Elaborate on your quotation/description to support your inference and answer the question. Link back to the question - can prove wrong or cannot prove wrong. If the source content is similar -> cannot prove wrong/reliable. If the source content is different -> can prove wrong/not reliable. Second Paragraph Cross-reference the main source to contextual knowledge (e.g. "Upon cross-referencing Source A to contextual knowledge, Source A can prove Source B wrong..."). Source A has to be reliable in order to prove something. If context matches -> Source A is factually accurate and supported by context, meaning Source A is reliable and will continue to either prove wrong or cannot prove wrong (refer to first paragraph). If context does not match -> Source A is proven wrong, factually inaccurate, lacks credibility, and thus cannot prove anything. Summary table: If Paragraph 1 found sources similar in inference (cannot prove wrong) and CK matches -> cannot prove wrong; if CK does not match -> cannot prove anything. If Paragraph 1 found sources different in inference (can prove wrong) and CK matches -> can prove wrong; if CK does not match -> cannot prove anything. Explain, then link back stating "Thus, Source A can prove Source B wrong" or "Thus, Source A cannot prove Source B wrong." Third Paragraph Closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source. Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs, refer to Inference with Purpose). Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance) and explain. Explain bias (if any), reasons to be one-sided (if any), and the position of the speaker. Consider the source's reliability: if found unbiased/reliable upon analysing purpose and proven

title: Hybrid Reliability - No Primary Source
body: Types of Questions Can you trust Source A more than Source B? (There is NO primary source) Big Idea Involves the critical analysis of the reliability of one source using another source. The skills are very much like reliability, involving the use of more than one source. Structure 3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'can prove wrong' and one on 'cannot prove wrong', or vice versa (rarely entirely one or the other). First Paragraph Present an overarching idea with the comparison (look for a similarity or difference in content). Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description to support your comparison. Elaborate to support your inference and answer the question. Link back - can prove wrong or cannot prove wrong. If the source content is similar -> cannot trust Source A more. If the source content is different -> can trust Source A more. Second Paragraph Cross-reference both sources to contextual knowledge (e.g. "Upon cross-referencing Source A to contextual knowledge, Source A is supported by contextual knowledge while Source B is not, hence Source A is more reliable, so you can trust Source A more.") If context supports Source A but not Source B -> can trust Source A more (vice versa for Source B). If context does not support either source -> cannot trust anything (Source A) (unlikely scenario). Explain, then link back by stating "Thus, Source A can prove Source B wrong" or "Thus, Source A cannot prove Source B wrong." Third Paragraph Closer examination of the provenance and purpose of the source, doing a critical analysis of both sources. Start with the speaker's intention and explain (use purposed verbs). Show the speaker's context/situation (based on provenance) and explain. Explain bias (if any), reasons to be one-sided (if any), and the position of the speaker. Consider the source's reliability: if Source A is found unbiased/more reliable upon analysing purpose and provenance -> can trust Source A more; if Source A is found less reliable and Source B more reliable -> cannot trust Source A more. Link back to answer the question (e.g. "Thus, Source A is ultimately unable to prove that Source B is wrong"). Note: Useful words/phrases include 'unbiased', 'objective', 'subjective', 'biased', 'official', and 'exaggerated to an extent where what it depicts may not necessarily be true and reliable.' Meeting minutes or official documents are objective and unbiased. Example starting sentence: "Source A cannot be trusted more than Source B about Hitler

title: Separate Inference
body: Types of Questions Source A and B differ in their views about Germany. Does it make one of them useless? (Not a strong need for comparison) Big Idea Involves the critical analysis of the reliability of one source using another source. The skills are very much like reliability, involving the use of more than one source. Structure 3 Paragraphs. Either 2 paragraphs on 'can prove wrong' and one on 'cannot prove wrong', or vice versa (rarely entirely one or the other). First Paragraph - Make an inference from the content of Source A, cross-reference Source A to context, and critically analyse the source's purpose and provenance. Second Paragraph - Make an inference from the content of Source B, cross-reference Source B to context, and critically analyse the source's purpose and provenance. Third Paragraph - Analyse what you have found in the first two paragraphs to ascertain which source is useful/useless. What kind of question uses the Separate Inference structure? A question like 'Source A and B differ in their views about Germany. Does it make one of them useless?' - where there is not a strong need for comparison. How many paragraphs are used in a Separate Inference answer? 3 paragraphs. What does the first paragraph focus on? An inference from the content of Source A, cross-referenced to context, and critical analysis of Source A's purpose and provenance. What does the second paragraph focus on? An inference from the content of Source B, cross-referenced to context, and critical analysis of Source B's purpose and provenance. What does the third paragraph do? Analyse the findings from paragraphs one and two to determine which source is useful/useless. What skill does this question type resemble? Similar to reliability, but involves the use of more than one source. What kind of source relationship prompts the use of the Separate Inference structure? What does paragraph one of a Separate Inference answer analyse? What is the role of the third paragraph in a Separate Inference answer? According to the notes, what three things does paragraph 2 of a Separate Inference answer do, specifically regarding Source B? title: Surprised
body: Surprised vs Reliability Judgement for 'Surprised' questions is NOT based on reliability. Step Surprised Reliability Inference ABC (use the person's position/context to say why it is surprising - this paragraph is mainly for the inference; no judgement required) ABC (cannot be same wording as the question issue - e.g. for 'Is the source reliable in showing you that the US was to be blamed for the Korean War?', answer: Reliable, as it shows the US was to be blamed because [inference, e.g. the source shows they were overly aggressive]) CR to CK Support = not surprised (ABC); Challenge = surprised (not ABC) Support = reliable (ABC); Challenge = not reliable (not ABC) CAP Person's position + intention (criticise, praise, warn, etc.) + context. If you can understand why the person would say this -> not surprised. If you cannot understand why -> surprised. Person's intention (criticise, praise, warn, etc.) + context -> Is there bias? If you understand the bias using context, it is reliable. If you do not understand the bias using context, it is not reliable. (Bias does not instantly make it unreliable - you must consider the context.) Even in usefulness, if unreliable, check if the inference is still useful: ask how the inference is affected by reliability, and why it might still remain useful despite being biased. If you can justify why it remains useful, it is useful; if not, it is not useful. Types of Questions Are you surprised by what Source E says? Big Idea Similar skill to reliability with similar steps. Essentially and very simply looking at a source's content and seeing if it is contrary to what we commonly know or have learnt. Structure 3 Paragraphs First Paragraph Answer the question by making an inference with source content (e.g. Source A is surprising as it suggests that Hitler was kind to the Jews). Using source evidence, provide a quotation or description to support your inference. Elaborate to support your inference and answer the question. Link back - surprising or not surprising. Note: you must always discuss the element of surprise based on the person's position, not just "...is in the source so it means this...so it is surprising" - instead: "...said..., meaning..., so it is surprising." Second Paragraph Answer the question by cross-referencing to contextual knowledge (e.g. Source A is surprising as, according to context, the Jews were mistreated by Hitler, so the source/inference is challenged by contextual knowledge).
