title: Surprised with 2 Sources
body: Types of Questions Having read Source A, are you surprised about Source B? Big Idea Similar skills and steps to 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources, as well as hybrid skills. Structure First, identify the main source (the primary source you look at): Question Main Source Does Source A make you surprised about Source B? Source B Having read Source B, are you surprised about Source A? Source A 3 Paragraphs First Paragraph - Compare the sources and look for similarities or differences. If content is similar/both sources share similar views/perspectives -> not surprised by the main source after reading the other source. If content is different/sources differ in views/perspectives -> surprised by the main source after reading the other source. Substantiate your claim with evidence and elaboration from both sources to show the similarity or difference. Second Paragraph - Cross-reference the main source with contextual knowledge, with minor attention given to the other source. If main source is supported by contextual knowledge -> not surprised by the main source, as it is not entirely reliable when considering contextual knowledge (careful: it is still framed as not surprised because it's internally consistent/supported). If main source is not supported by contextual knowledge -> surprised by the main source. Substantiate your claim with contextual knowledge and elaboration. Give minor attention to the other source (a short sentence justifying its reliability), e.g. "Source F comes from President Truman, an official point of view, and thus after reading Source F which is most likely reliable, I am surprised by Source E as Source E itself is not entirely reliable based on my contextual knowledge." Third Paragraph - Check the reliability of the main source based on its purpose and provenance, with minor attention given to the other source. If the other source has a more objective purpose (less likely to have ulterior motives) while the main source is more biased (more likely to have other intentions) -> surprised by the main source, as it itself is not reliable based on closer analysis of its purpose and provenance, while the other source is more reliable. If the main source has a more objective purpose while the other source is more biased -> not surprised by the main source, as it is more reliable based on closer analysis, while the other source is not as reliable. Substantiate your claim with purpose, provenance and elaboration. Example starting senten

title: Hybrid Surprised
body: Types of Questions Does Source A make you surprised about Source B? Big Idea Similar skill to comparison and hybrid reliability questions with similar steps. Structure First, identify the main source (the primary source): Question Main Source Does Source A make you surprised about Source B? Source A Note: although this uses similar skills/steps to 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources, they are distinct question types: 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources (e.g. "Having read Source A, are you surprised by Source B") - main source is Source B; think of it as focusing on the effect. Hybrid surprise questions (e.g. "Does Source A make you surprised about Source B") - main source is Source A; think of it as focusing on the cause. 3 Paragraphs First Paragraph - Compare the sources and look for similarities or differences. If content is similar/both sources share similar views/perspectives -> not surprised by the main source. If content is different/sources differ in views/perspectives -> surprised by the main source. Substantiate your claim with evidence and elaboration, providing evidence from both sources. Second Paragraph - Cross-reference the main source with contextual knowledge. If main source is supported by contextual knowledge -> the main source does make me feel surprised by the other source, as the main source is in itself a reliable source when considering contextual knowledge. If main source is not supported by contextual knowledge -> the main source does not make me feel surprised by the other source, as the main source is in itself an unreliable source when considering contextual knowledge. Substantiate with contextual knowledge and elaboration. Unlike 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources, there is no need to pay minor attention to the other source here. Third Paragraph - Check the purposes and context of BOTH sources (another differing point from 'Are you surprised' questions with 2 sources). Using intention and context: if you can understand why the sources are similar, you are not surprised. If you can understand why they are different, you are also not surprised. If you cannot understand why they are similar, you are surprised. If you cannot understand why they are different, you remain surprised. Example starting sentence: "(Main source) does/does not make me feel surprised by (other source)..." Notes Always answer the question. Analyse the sources carefully and identify the right main source. Be careful not to confuse

title: Essay: Key Notes and Overview of Skills
body: Key Definitions Social transformation - changes in political, economic, social, and cultural structures in society. Social identity - essential qualities that determine membership in a certain social group (something that defines you and what you do). Social identity creation - a process of redefining the essential qualities of membership in a particular group and seeking legitimisation of this definition (i.e. "No, this is who I want to be instead and how I want to be treated in society now, please accept me"). Important Pointers for Writing Essays Directly answer the question and signpost ('link') each paragraph to the question. Avoid strongly focusing on comparing just because it is a comparative essay, and thereby failing to answer the question. Provide ample substantiation and/or discuss competing perspectives in detail. Include concrete details, context and explanations so it is clear why a factor was a driving force (evidence is important but need not be overly specific). Overview of Essay Skills Overall Guiding Questions for Essays What were the major forces and developments during this period? What caused these major forces and developments? Who were the key players involved? How did the developments influence people's decisions and actions, and vice versa? How did people's views and perspectives shape their interpretation of these developments? How did these developments impact societies? Overall Guiding Rules for Essays Identify the factor in the question (e.g. the need to create a new social identity), usually flagged by a weighing word like 'most', 'key', or 'primarily driven'. Answer the question - address the given factor/reason first and state your argument for why it is a factor. Pump in content knowledge to back up your argument. Answer why the chosen factor is more important than the other factors. Time given: 1 hour 30 minutes (spend roughly 45 minutes on each essay, no more than 45 minutes each). 3 questions are given, of which Question 1 is compulsory, and you choose 1 of Question 2 or Question 3 - you must know your case studies well. title: Level 1 Essay Questions
body: Extreme/Relative Importance Questions Example questions: "Assess which term of the Treaty of Versailles was the most unreasonable." / "'The reason for the start of WWII in Europe was due to XYZ.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer." (i.e. questions asking for the most unreasonable/most important reason) Identify the factor in the question (e.g. the need to create a new social identity), usually with a weighing word like 'most', 'key', 'primarily driven'. Answer the question - address the given factor/reason first and state your argument for why it is a factor. Pump in content knowledge to back up your argument. Answer why the chosen factor is more important than the other two factors (requires weighing). Balanced Perspective Questions Example questions: "'War is inevitable.' How far do you agree with this statement? Explain your answer." / "Assess the importance of XYZ in the outcome of the civil movements in the USA." / "'X is more Yes than No for Y.' How far do you agree? Explain your answer." Identify the factor in the question, usually with a weighing word like 'most', 'key', 'primarily driven'. Answer the question - address the given factor/reason first and state your argument for why it is a factor. Pump in content knowledge to back up your argument. NEVER use a hypothetical situation (especially for questions on whether war was inevitable). Answer why both sides can happen (provide a balanced perspective). Structure Introduction : Short, about 3-4 lines - briefly discuss the issue the question raises and what your essay is about. 3 Body Paragraphs Point: must be specific (e.g. Discrimination -> Education, not just 'discrimination'). Evidence: a case study (an event, or an action taken by a group of people/single person - just 1, with an adequate description of relevant information, 4-5 lines). Elaboration: link the information of the case study to the point. Link: link the point made in the entire body paragraph to the question. Conclusion : reiterate your stand and evaluate your points using a basis of comparison (e.g. long term vs short term, or extent). Give an example of an Extreme/Relative Importance essay question. title: Comparative Essay Questions
body: Overall Guiding Rules for Comparative Essays Identify that the question requires you to use 2 case studies to support your argument (you need to make a judgement - choosing similarities/differences, or choosing case studies to illustrate your argument). Answer the question through: (a) content match - comparison of reasons, cause and effect, impact/consequence; (b) analysis based on criterion - social/political/economic, country, situation, people, government. Direct Compare and Contrast Questions Example questions: "Compare and contrast any 2 conflicts in the Cold War." / "Compare and contrast any two Cold War conflicts and their impacts." / "Compare and contrast any two Cold War conflicts and their causes." Comparison is important - need to show explicit similarities and differences (choosing similarities and differences). Possible comparative topics: power and authority; reasons for the rise to power; policies for the control of people/consolidation of power/securing power; impact of the dictatorship. Structure Introduction : include a short context about the case studies and the question, and a thesis statement that answers the question and lists your arguments. 3 Body Paragraphs : Point (answering the question - either a similarity or difference in a specific area); Evidence (relevant details about both conflicts to highlight the similarity/difference); Elaboration (elaborate and explain how details show the similarity/difference); Link (link the point back to answering the main question). Conclusion : short conclusion to reiterate your stand and evaluate the similarities and differences/provide additional comments, going back to answer the question. Evaluative Comparative Questions Example questions: "Assess if social movements in Southeast Asia were valid. Use 2 case studies from the period of 1970s to 2000s to illustrate your argument." / "Evaluate the impact of social transformations in Southeast Asia. Use the case studies of at least 2 countries to support your argument." No need for explicit comparison (choosing case studies to illustrate your argument). The idea is to illustrate an argument using 2 case studies. Key Things in an Evaluative Comparative Essay Content match: When comparing the 2 case studies, be careful not to just list a chunk of information. Avoid simply comparing similarities and differences. Instead, compare with varying criteria and perspectives - can compare causes and effects, or things of different values like extent or me
